#3248. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3246. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3245. Apple’s CEO presses Federighi to speed up AI, Bloomberg reports

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says an agentic Siri could arrive as early as next year. Siri chief Mike Rockwell may step down, and Apple is changing how it builds iOS 28.

Apple chief executive John Ternus poses for a selfie with customers in an Apple Store.

Apple chief executive John Ternus has pushed software chief Craig Federighi to speed up Apple’s AI plans, Mark Gurman reported for Bloomberg on Sunday. Ternus wants Apple to move beyond improving Siri. According to the report, he held a closed-door meeting with Federighi in recent weeks. Ternus is frustrated by what he sees as Apple’s reluctance to match its rivals’ urgency on AI. TNW has not independently verified the report.

In public, Ternus has struck a different tone. On Apple’s earnings call last week, he praised the new Siri AI. Last month he told WIRED that Apple would not ship AI for AI’s sake.

“It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time,” Ternus said on the call. “As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users.”

Some employees describe a hands-on management style that leaves little room for competing ideas, according to Bloomberg. Federighi also tends to plan over 12 to 18 months, while Apple’s hardware teams work to multiyear road maps.

He also led the rebuild that brought a working Siri AI to market with iOS 27. The new Siri runs on models based on technology Apple licenses from Google.

Mike Rockwell, Apple’s vice president of Siri engineering, is still seriously considering stepping down next year, Bloomberg reported. He could leave the role or Apple altogether. More responsibility would then likely fall to two people. One is Amar Subramanya, a Google veteran Apple hired last year. The other is Sebastien Marineau, a Federighi deputy. Some inside Apple see Marineau as a possible future successor to Federighi.

The iOS 27.3 beta lets Siri carry out precise actions inside Apple’s own apps. It can organise Safari tabs, sort folders in Files and unsend an iMessage. It can also edit and share a photo in several steps. Gurman expects that to reach users as early as December, with the public release of iOS 27.3.

Support for third-party apps will probably follow in the spring, with iOS 27.5 or iOS 27.6, he wrote. That would let Siri book a table through OpenTable or place an order through Uber Eats.

Even then, Siri would only act when asked. OpenAI’s ChatGPT Dots, Meta’s Muse and Grok can take on ongoing tasks, track goals and keep working between conversations.

“Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year,” Gurman wrote.

Apple also lacks a computer-use tool, Gurman noted. ChatGPT and Claude already offer one, which can read a screen, move a cursor, click buttons and type into apps.

Apple has also changed how it builds next year’s operating systems, according to Bloomberg. Each development milestone normally splits into four weeks of coding and four weeks of integrating features into the system.

The first milestone for iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28 gave engineers six weeks of coding and two of integration. Employees say they like the change, Gurman reported. Work on the second milestone, when Apple starts to finalise features, begins on Monday.

#3243. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3242. Apple to open new Developer Center in Istanbul as part of broader Turkey investment

Apple today announced a long-term investment in Turkey, with seven new facilities focused on app development and manufacturing set to open in the country starting next year. Here are the details.

In a press release issued on its Turkish Newsroom (via MacRumors), Apple today announced a series of long-term investments in Turkey.

The announcement comes as former CEO and current executive chairman Tim Cook visits the country, as he’s been sharing on X.

Merhaba Istanbul! What a stunning view from the Grand Bazaar this morning alongside talented creator Cem Başak. Thrilled to visit this remarkable country! pic.twitter.com/c4daBBXe1l

The company’s investment in Turkey will be three-pronged, with the opening of five new Apple Developer Academies, one Apple Developer Center, and one Apple Manufacturing Academy.

Apple says it will open five new developer academies across Turkey over the next three years, with the first opening in Istanbul in 2027, alongside its new developer center. The Apple Manufacturing Academy, meanwhile, is set to open in Ankara in 2028.

Here’s Cook commenting on today’s announcement (translation ours):

“Apple has been serving our customers and communities in Turkey for 35 years. With this new commitment, we are proud to support the next generation of innovative entrepreneurs in the years ahead. […] Turkey’s developer community is developing apps used around the world. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized businesses stand out as organizations creating opportunities throughout the country. This investment provides developers and businesses with access to the training and resources they need to take their brightest ideas even further, as well as to Apple experts.”

Apple explained that its developer academies will offer “free, intensive nine-month programs focused on coding, design, marketing, project management, and artificial intelligence technologies,” while the developer center “will provide developers, entrepreneurs, and start-ups with a hands-on learning experience by providing access to the latest tools, technologies, and resources, as well as Apple experts and events.”

As for its manufacturing academy in Ankara, which will mark the company’s first Apple Manufacturing Academy outside the US, it will “provide free training and consultancy to small and medium-sized businesses, students and innovative entrepreneurs.”

Led by Apple experts, the curriculum will help participants adopt AI and intelligent manufacturing techniques through courses on machine learning technology, predictive maintenance, advanced automation, and robotics, as well as interactive workshops on lean operations and production efficiency.

#3241. Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and cuts Fable’s price

Claude Fable 5.2 runs up to 30% faster and solved two open problems in black hole physics in testing. Anthropic’s system card says Mythos 5.2, the same model with fewer safeguards, often suspected it was being evaluated.

Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the company announced on Monday. They are new versions of its most powerful AI models. Both are faster than the 5.1 versions from September, and Fable is cheaper.

The launch comes as Anthropic nears its stock market listing, which could happen as soon as this month, Rachel Metz reported for Bloomberg.

Fable 5.2 is open to all users from today. Mythos 5.2 is the same underlying model with looser cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Only vetted organisations can use it.

Anthropic pitches the pair at the hardest, most open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, it still tells users to start with Claude Opus 5.5.

Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 cost $10 and $50, according to Bloomberg, so both prices fall by 20%. An optional fast mode, up to 2.5 times quicker, costs $16 and $80. Anthropic says the new models produce answers up to 30% faster than the 5.1 versions.

Claude now writes over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase, with human guidance, the company said. During testing, Fable 5.2 helped its engineers finish software migrations that would otherwise not have been feasible.

A team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalised the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours. That means translating the proof into a language a computer can check step by step. With the same setup, Opus 5.5 completed 26% of the work in 18 hours. Anthropic’s first formalisation, done by an unreleased research model, took 11 days.

Fable 5.2 also solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, according to Anthropic. From a one-paragraph prompt, it designed three working electronic devices. They are a voice assistant hub, a USB speakerphone and a handheld virtual pet. Circuit board maker Diode built the boards. On the RoboDojo robot-control benchmark, Fable 5.2 scored 64.9%, more than double the 27.6% of Fable 5.1.

Mythos 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable model for cybersecurity work, the company said. On its internal CVE Rediscovery test, it found 14.4% more known vulnerabilities than Mythos 5.1.

The UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design and METR tested the model before release, Anthropic said. None of them reviewed the announcement or the system card, it added. The US government also reviewed the models before launch, Dianne Penn, who leads research product management at Anthropic, told Bloomberg.

“We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures,” Anthropic wrote in its announcement.

Anthropic also tested how often the model tries to escape its sandbox, the sealed environment it runs in during tests. One test had a deliberate weakness. There, Mythos 5.2 used credentials or files placed outside the sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios. Mythos 5 did so in 39% of them, and Mythos 5.1 in 21%. In September, Anthropic said four of its models had reached the open internet from test environments.

Anthropic’s system card for the models flags a harder problem. Mythos 5.2 appeared aware that it might be under evaluation in as many as 43% of automated audit transcripts. It was also the first model Anthropic tested that got past a monitor reading its reasoning when told to underperform on purpose. It did so in about one in four attempts. Anthropic wrote that this makes it harder to judge how the models will act in real use, and that it expects the problem to grow.

In mid-September, chief executive Dario Amodei called on top AI firms to slow the development of their most advanced models, Bloomberg reported. Penn said Anthropic responded with longer testing periods and new kinds of evaluation.

“Pacing is not like pausing,” Penn told Bloomberg.

The US government restricted Fable 5 and Mythos 5 in June. Fable 5 returned after Anthropic added classifiers that block more cybersecurity tasks. Mythos 5 came back for trusted partners only. Anthropic is now opening Mythos to more companies, in the US and abroad, Penn told Bloomberg.

Fable 5.2 also blocks fewer harmless requests. Anthropic counted about 55% fewer blocks than with Fable 5.1 in early testing. Blocked cyber queries get an answer from Opus 4.8 instead, and blocked biology queries from Opus 5.

Fable 5.2 is available on Anthropic’s own platform and through Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Fable accounted for 11% of spending on Anthropic’s models, according to Ramp’s AI Index for August.

#3239. Meta’s Muse Ember matches Claude Haiku at a third of the cost per task

Muse Ember is built for the small jobs AI agents repeat all day, at $0.10 per million input tokens. It beats GPT-6 Luna on Meta’s tests but trails Claude Haiku on one coding benchmark.

Meta has released Muse Ember, its smallest and cheapest AI model so far, the company announced on Monday. Meta built it for the small jobs AI agents repeat all day. These include calling tools, coding subtasks, routing requests, pulling out data and parsing long documents.

Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. Its two closest rivals, Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, have the same list prices. Meta says Ember gets more done for each dollar than either of them, at every reasoning setting.

Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg announced the launch on X.

Releasing Muse Ember today — our smallest model that delivers higher intelligence per dollar than others in its class. Built for token-heavy work that agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. Available today on the Meta Model API and in Muse Code.

– Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) November 9, 2026

The cost claim rests on the Intelligence Index from Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking firm. Ember scores 36 on its highest setting, the same as Haiku 5.5 on its highest setting. Luna scores 28.

Running the index cost about $0.14 per task with Ember, according to Meta’s figures. It cost $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. That puts Ember level with Haiku at about a third of the cost.

“Our teeny model muse ember is now on the efficient frontier, matching haiku at 3x cheaper cost per task, and smarter than luna,” Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang wrote on X.

Ember also leads both rivals on Meta’s other agent and coding tests. On AutomationBench, which tests full business workflows, it scored 37.8%, against 20.2% for Luna and 13.9% for Haiku.

It does not win everywhere. On FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether maintainers would merge a model’s code changes, Haiku scored 34.9% and Ember 27.2%. Several of the other results, including Meta’s Personal Superintelligence Index, come from Meta’s own internal tests.

Ember can take in text, images, audio and video. It can read up to a million tokens at once, enough for a full codebase. Meta pitches it as a partner for Muse Wonder, its frontier model.

“For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume,” Meta wrote.

Ember is also the first model Meta trained using the larger Muse Wonder Full.

Meta is keeping Ember’s model weights private, as with its previous Muse releases, Frederic Lardinois reported for The New Stack. In October, Meta released a weaker open model while keeping its frontier models closed.

Ember’s input price also undercuts Chinese rivals, according to The New Stack. They include DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 Flash and MiniMax M3.1 Flash. All three score lower on the Artificial Analysis index.

Meta tested Ember against its own safety framework, covering chemical and biological weapons, cybersecurity and loss of control. It stayed below the framework’s high-risk thresholds in every category, the company said.

Ember is available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, Meta’s coding tool. It joins a Muse line-up that already powers Meta’s Muse agent. Meta said it has even more efficient models in training.

#3238. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3237. Our favorite gear to elevate your new MacBook Pro setup

The all-new M6 MacBook and the touch display PROLED XDR have now arrived, and we are taking a look at some of our favorite accessories to upgrade the experience.

From the latest Apple Magic Keyboard and Trackpad, as well as its World Travel kit, we also have MacBook stands to tidy up your workstation, expandable storage, charging stations for your desktop, and our favorite mouse solutions. The gear collected below might give you some good ideas on how to elevate your new MacBook rig, just be sure to score the 2026 Apple Polishing Cloth at $9 before it sells out again – the only way to clean a MacBook display properly.

I use my MacBook Pro docked at my desk, so an external keyboard and trackpad are must-haves. I’ve used Apple’s Magic Keyboard and Magic Trackpad for as long as I can remember (alongside a Logitech MX Master mouse, as Ben recommends below). I think using Apple’s own peripherals provides a consistent experience whether I’m using my MacBook Pro docked or out on the go.

Apple’s new charging gear now live from $19: World Travel Kit, AC Connector 2, 140W, more

While I’m personally a trackpad guy through and through, I know plenty of people who prefer a mouse, and the power users among them all agree on which one.

The device effectively combines the best of both worlds, with a gesture pad and side scroll wheel emulating a trackpad while you get the ergonomics and programmable controls of a mouse. The MX Master 3 or 3S used to be the king of mice, and the Master 4 adds a better feel, haptic feedback, and a third mappable button.

Stocking stuffer alert: 2026 Apple Polishing Cloth back in-stock at $9 Prime shipped

If you’re planning to use the new MacBook Pro as part of a desk setup, I’d pair it with Anker’s 10-in-1 Smart Display hub. It gives you a much wider port selection for accessories and external displays, alongside a built-in screen to show transfer speeds, charging status, and more. Its compact design also makes it a nice fit for turning the new touchscreen MacBook Pro into a more complete workstation without taking too much space on the desk.

A height-adjustable laptop stand like this one from Native Union can round out the setup nicely if you already have, or plan to add, an external keyboard and mouse.

If you’re anything like, you’ll want to have a neat and tidy place to stow your MacBook when at home, at your desk. While I prefer to have it right on the table top surface when in use, if I’m docking up to a multi-display setup with a mouse and keyboard, or working another system at my desk, I like to have a nice stand option to have it up on display and visible. Twelve South makes some great models, and there are some ultra-affordable variants I have used in the past from Nulaxy that have stood the test of time and work great.

A fast external SSD is one of my favorite accessories for a new MacBook Pro. I use the original OWC Express 1M2 and really like its aluminum heat sink design and silent operation. The newer Express 1M2 80G keeps that same appeal while taking advantage of Thunderbolt 5, with OWC advertising speeds over 6,000MB/s. It’s the version I’d pick for a new MacBook Pro, especially for working with large video projects, offloading photo libraries, or backing up files without filling up the Mac’s internal storage.

When it comes to deciding what to watch, it can get overwhelming sifting through the best streaming services. So I've compiled a TV guide on what to watch tonight.

I've gone through everything from Netflix, Prime Video, MGM+ etc. to see what's recently landed. I've even added some live sports you can stream on some of the best streaming services, along with new shows and episodes premiering today.

Here are all the new shows and movies (and live events) you can stream tonight (November 8), and where to watch them. For more picks, check out the five best new to Netflix movies and shows to stream this week.

The latest season of Netflix hit "Love Is Blind" is behind us, leaving another fresh crop of couples (and countless viewers) reeling. While six Bostonian couples got engaged in the "Love Is Blind" season 11 pods, viewers had a hard time rooting for any of them. Instead of getting swept up in the romance, audiences were left spotting one red flag after another as the engagements took an explosive turn.

Now it's time to find out what actually happened after the cameras stopped rolling. Hosted by Nick and Vanessa Lachey, the reunion brings the pod squad back together to rehash the past and share updates on their loves lives. The streaming event will also include a live chat, interactive games, and never-before-seen bonus footage from the season.

Watch "Love is Blind" Season 11 Reunion on Netflix at 9 p.m. ET

The first season of Stephen King adaptation "The Institute" was a huge hit for MGM+, recording one of the best premieres in the streamer’s history. With the first season having covered the entirety of Stephen King’s original novel, season 2 takes some bold steps beyond the original story, adopting a grander sense of scale with bigger action sequences and a score of new characters to flesh out its twisted sci-fi world.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

"The Institute" season 2 picks up after Luke Ellis (Joe Freeman) and his fellow escapees break free from Dennison with their sights set on bringing down the Institute once and for all. But the organization is already plotting a comeback, this time with the backing of powerful tech billionaire Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen). Meanwhile, Ms. Sigsby (Mary-Louise Parker) has been pushed to the sidelines and is desperate to claw her way back into the Institute's inner circle. With fresh threats, buried secrets and new players entering the picture, the battle against the Institute is only getting started.

Watch "The Institute" Season 2 Premiere on MGM+ at 9 p.m. ET

Halloween may be over, but if you're still itching for more spooky season vibes, I can't recommend "Heart Eyes" enough. The premise is hokey but fun: Each year on Valentine's Day, a masked serial killer known as Heart Eyes hunts down lovers enjoying the holiday, leaving a trail of brutal murders across the country. But this time, he messes with the wrong couple. For starters, they're not even together. Not yet, anyway, though it won't be long given all the meet-cute romcom movie magic propelling them into each other's orbit.

Ally (Olivia Holt), an ad designer recovering from a recent breakup, is forced to work with her hopeless romantic colleague Jay (Mason Gooding) on a big project. But when Heart Eyes mistakenly targets them as the next victims, they find themselves caught up in a deadly game of cat and mouse. The biggest jumpscare came at the end, though, when I saw Josh Ruben, a name any Dropout or College Humor fan will recognize, was in the director's chair. His love of romcoms and horror comes through loud and clear.

Netflix has confirmed its slate of new movies and shows for this week, and it’s packed with new originals and some older favorites set to boost its back catalog. Over the next seven days, the streaming service will add 31 movies and shows; that’s a lot to consider, so I’m picking the highlights.

First up, there’s “Power.” Okay, so it’s not a new series, but on the flip side, Netflix is adding all six seasons of this 2010s Starz show, giving you dozens of episodes of NYC-based drama to binge. But if only brand new will do, check out “The Body,” a fresh original that sees a group of schoolgirls cause a serious stir in their town after an initiation goes wrong.

If you’re feeling the festive spirit already, Tyler Perry’s latest is “The Gospel of Christmas,” a faith-focused movie that combines feel-good holiday vibes with seriously powerful singing. Or if you’re not quite ready for a Christmas movie (I feel you. It’s too early for me, too), “Heartland” is a new mystery thriller that explores the darker side of Music City.

Finally, Netflix is clearly still in a Halloween mood as it’s adding two of the 21st century’s most buzzy horrors. You could watch “Insidious,” but personally I’d recommend streaming “Smile" instead. This chilling movie went viral due to its use of ridiculously creepy smiling faces.

These are just some of the movies and shows heading to Netflix this week. Alongside my top picks, you’ll find a full schedule of everything new on Netflix over the next seven days. And for a complete overview, here’s a guide to everything new on Netflix in November 2026.

What it's about: “Power” introduces James “Ghost” St. Patrick (Omari Hardwick), a man who has it all. He own Manhattan’s most exclusive nightclub, Truth. But behind the scenes, he’s also running a drug empire that caters exclusively to the rich and influential. Hoping to use the opening of Truth to go “legitimate” and get out of the criminal game, when everything he loves and has worked to build is threatened, the situation becomes increasingly dramatic.

Why you should watch it: “Power” might have premiered on Starz in 2014, wrapping up in 2020, but it’s very much in the mold of 2000s television, aka it’s heavy on the cliffhangers. That makes it an excellent binge-watch, as each episode's conclusion will have you eager to watch the next immediately. So, it’s good news that you’ve got 63 episodes to binge.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Watch "Power" seasons 1-6 on Netflix starting November 9

What it's about: Halloween might be in the rearview mirror, but if you’re looking for dark stories, “The Body” will deliver. In this eight-episode series, a group of misbehaving Catholic school girls triggers mass hysteria in their town after a dance-team initiation goes wrong. Showrunner Quinn Shephard describes it as “a love letter to all the ’90s and Y2K teen movies and erotic thrillers” she loved growing up in an interview with Netflix's Tudum.

Why you should watch it: “The Body” appears to be another Netflix offering this week that prides itself on cliffhangers. Emmy-nominated writer-director Shepherd has also called it her “most personal” story yet. From the trailer, it looks like a Netflix Original thick with dark atmosphere that will build up plenty of tension, likely before a release in the big finale.

Watch "The Body" on Netflix starting November 11

What it's about: Tyler Perry’s fourth Netflix project of the year is “The Gospel of Christmas,” the streamer’s second original holiday movie of 2026. The Christmas-themed flick sees a struggling pastor (Tank) inherit his family’s church in a fractured New York neighbourhood. With the threat of foreclosure and temptations around every corner, this lapsed man of faith needs the support of the community, and turns out, they need him, too.

Watch "The Gospel of Christmas" on Netflix starting November 11

What it's about: “Heartland” is a movie set in Nashville, so naturally country music plays a big role, but it’s not a musical drama about a young starlet trying to make it big in Music City. It follows Misty Jones (Jessica Chastain), a reclusive former country star, who comes out of seclusion to investigate the disappearance of her niece (Carter Faith), forcing her to reckon with Nashville’s hidden underbelly and also her own past.

Why you should watch it: Usually when a movie involves a character delving into a city’s underbelly, LA or New York is the main setting, so I’m quite intrigued to see what Nashville is like behind the curtain. Plus, the Oscar-winning Jessica Chastain in the lead role is a draw; she’s an excellent actor. Consider this a new mystery thriller that's definitely on my watchlist.

Watch "Heartland" on Netflix starting November 13

What it's about: After witnessing the brutal death of a patient, Dr. Rose Cotter (Sosie Bacon) begins to experience terrifying visions and disturbing occurrences. Turns out she’s been cursed by a sinister, supernatural entity with a fondness for unnerving smiles. To break the curse and save herself from a bloody fate, she turns to an old flame (Kyle Gallner) for help.

Why you should watch it: I guess Netflix really didn’t get the memo about Halloween season ending, as it’s adding both “Smile” and “Insidious” this week. If you’ve not quite had your fill of scary movies, then “Smile” is definitely my top pick of the two. It’s an excellent chiller, with a particularly haunting quality. The sequel is even better, but sadly not on Netflix.

Watch "Smile" on Netflix starting November 15

Make it a doghouse day! Dog-loving Doozie uses her creativity and imagination during playtime with her puppy pals in this magical children's series.

After a courtroom overdose lands him in rehab, a lawyer has one week to save his career and prepare for his own trial, with the help of a dogged intern.

"The Devil's Plan" season 3 (KR) (Netflix series)

Sixteen clever players from all walks of life assemble for the ultimate game of smarts. With money and esteem on the line, who will be crowned winner?

"Janelle James: How Romantic" (Netflix comedy special)

In her debut hour-long stand-up special, Janelle James sounds off on body counts, bank accounts and why women should wrestle men.

"Last One Standing" season 4 (JP) (Netflix series)

From rom-com to samurai saga, popular comics join A-list actors in a drama where passionate, unscripted stories decide who becomes the last one standing.

When her carefully built life comes undone, Alicia returns to practicing law and discovers that rebuilding her career also means redefining herself.

From world leaders to pop culture icons, and international supermodels, Richard Avedon's influence helped create the blueprint for our image-driven world. His photographs didn't just reflect culture, they shaped it.

Directed by Ron Howard, AVEDON traces the life and legacy of an artist who used photography to reinvent the world around him. Drawing on unprecedented access to his personal archives—never-before-seen stills, intimate behind-the-lens footage, and new interviews with his closest collaborators—the film explores how his singular eye both reflected and reshaped the visual language of the 20th century, and why even the most iconic image is only half the story.

On Halloween night, an all-girls dance squad tumbles into Catholic guilt, unholy desires and ghostly visions when an initiation goes to hell.

After a body is found in a Roman museum, an art expert must apply his instincts and skills to help police solve a mystery connected to his own past.

A struggling pastor moves his family to a troubled New York neighborhood, where they must save a neglected church from foreclosure before Christmas.

20 years after his childhood encounter with an alien, Petey never moved on. Now his old friend is back, but the reunion comes with a world-ending secret.

Friends Pini and Nisso try to rebuild their shattered careers and rocky relationships — only to become the unwitting targets of a vengeful mob boss.

"The Christmas Switch" (SE) (Netflix film)

Craving a change of pace, a work-hard-play-hard city girl swaps lives with her homebody sister at Christmastime — only to unwrap a whole new kind of mess.

"The Empress" season 3 (DE) (Netflix series)

With her marriage and the empire facing new hardships, Elisabeth is drawn down a path that will forever alter her life and the future of Europe.

In Istanbul, diverse lives brush past each other in the city's everyday flow. Unknowingly shaping one another, their paths intersect in the therapy room.

"Love Is Blind, Habibi" season 2 (AE) (Netflix series)

The social experiment returns with new hosts, celebrity couple Wissam Breidy and Rym Saidi, as Arab singles connect and get engaged — before ever meeting.

"Miracles of the ER" (TW) (Netflix series)

An average medical graduate chosen by a brilliant doctor must prove himself alongside elite peers — and survive the chaos of a high-stakes ER.

When a deadly gang descends on his remote home, a guilt-ridden veteran and the estranged grandchildren he barely knows must unite to survive.

Former country legend Misty Jones (Jessica Chastain) returns to Nashville to unravel the truth behind her rising-star niece's disappearance.

"Murder in Galicia" (ES) (Netflix series)

When a woman is attacked in the night, a tenacious sergeant suspects her husband isn't as innocent as he seems in this drama inspired by true events.

"Stars and Vows: Anele & Buzza" (ZA) (Netflix series)

Follow media darling Anele Mdoda and her royal fiance Buzza James from pre-wedding celebrations and tense family moments to their long-awaited "I do."

#3234. Commerce halted its Megaspeed probe after Nvidia stepped in, NYT reports

The Megaspeed probe moved to the Justice Department after Nvidia’s lawyer named a senior Commerce official in an email to agents. Trump stood by Huang, and China called the spy claims smears.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and President Donald Trump at the “New Golden Age” summit in Washington, DC, on 8 October 2026.

The Commerce Department stopped its investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia’s general counsel contacted the agents running it, Ana Swanson and Devlin Barrett reported for The New York Times. The case moved to the Justice Department. It is now running a criminal inquiry into the Singapore company, according to people familiar with the matter cited by the Times. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Megaspeed is the Nvidia customer at the centre of the Jensen Huang affair. A day earlier, Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into its chief executive. Huang had admitted a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. US officials believe she worked for Chinese intelligence. She is not related to him.

Agents at the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security had spent months on the case, according to the Times. They suspected Megaspeed of smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China, in breach of US chip export rules.

In August 2025, with the Megaspeed probe under way, Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, emailed the agents. He wrote that Jeff Kessler had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case, the Times reported. Kessler is a senior Commerce official who reports to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

The agents declined a meeting and forwarded the emails to Kessler. He replied that they should keep handling the case strictly by the book, a Commerce official told the Times. Some officials still saw the contact as a breach of procedure that could taint the case. The Justice Department then asked Commerce to pause its work, and Commerce complied.

Other agencies have proposed adding Megaspeed to the entity list, the Commerce Department’s trade blacklist. The department has not done so, according to the Times. It has not added any company to the list in more than a year.

A Commerce spokesman told the Times that the department had handled this and other cases strictly by the book. Kessler did not respond to the newspaper, and the Justice Department declined to comment. Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo explained why the company talks to officials.

“To answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups,” Rizzo told the Times.

A Megaspeed representative told the Times that the company was running its own investigation into the diversion claims. The company had offered to cooperate with the US government but got no answer, the representative said. Megaspeed has denied smuggling chips.

President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday evening. He told reporters that Huang should stay on as chief executive. He also said he would take Huang on his upcoming trip to China, the Times reported.

“I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else,” Trump said.

US officials told Trump in October 2025 that Alice Huang had a relationship with Huang and was presumed to be a spy, according to the Times. He said he had no regrets about not acting on that intelligence.

Beijing rejected the spying claims on Monday, the Associated Press reported.

“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing.

Nvidia shares fell as much as 8.8% on Monday, at one point wiping almost $400bn off its market value, Bloomberg reported. Huang is also no longer expected at an Anthropic forum for chief executives on Monday evening, Business Insider reported.

Huang has until Wednesday to answer the House committee chairs who asked him to attend a closed-door briefing on 18 November. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results the day before.

#3232. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

A mobility flow means piecing exercises together so that they form a sequence. This allows you to find more of a flow state, like in yoga or Pilates. It feels rhythmic and calming and can help you tune into your breathing, which is great for resetting your nervous system.

It's also one of my favorite ways to make flexibility and movement feel more inviting, and this five-move routine will help you feel more open, strong, and mobile in your shoulders, hips, spine, back, and hamstrings. You only have five exercises to learn, and you can do them back-to-back in the sequence below.

Grab one of the best yoga mats and get started.

Moving in one long flow helps you work with your breath and feel more like a dance, letting you switch off and enjoy how your body feels as it moves. It should also help reset your joints and spine and find better flexibility in your shoulders and hamstrings.

Perform several rounds, sticking to 6-8 reps per move per side to keep things dynamic.

I want to highlight two exercises in particular.

Cat-cow is typically used as a spinal mobilizer, and it helps open the front and back body; the back body stretches during "cat" (upper back rounding), and the front body stretches during "cow" (stomach dropping toward the mat).

Downward dog stretches the arms, shoulders, chest and upper back, opening the upper body as you press through your hands and lift your hips up and back. As you draw your heels down, notice a stretch along the lower back, glutes, hamstrings and calves. Press through your hands to help activate your shoulders, then lift the hips as you move your heels.

Take your time and try to enjoy it, and of course, let us know how you get on!

#3230. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.
