#3210. Motorcar Parts (MPAA) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Delayed orders hit sales, but new awards point to a stronger second half.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Motorcar Parts of America, Inc. (MPAA -26.62%) reported a decrease in quarterly revenue attributed to delayed customer orders and lower tariff pass-throughs, prompting management to lower its full-year sales guidance. Despite these near-term headwinds, the company secured significant new business awards and completed a strategic manufacturing relocation to Mexico to improve cost structures. Management expects a stronger second half of the fiscal year as new programs launch and inventory liquidations from competitors subside. The company remains focused on leveraging its diagnostic technology and expanding its brake product line to drive long-term market share gains.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Motorcar Parts of America, Inc. Fiscal 2027 Second Quarter Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Gary Maier, Vice President of Corporate Communications and Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Gary Maier: Thank you, Kay, and thanks, everyone, for joining us. Before I turn the call over to Selwyn Joffe, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer; and David Lee, our Chief Financial Officer, I'd like to remind everyone of the safe harbor statement included in today's press release. The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 provides a safe harbor for certain forward-looking statements, including statements made during today's conference call regarding future financial performance, sales growth, margin improvement, operating efficiencies, customer demand, new business strategies, capacity utilization, working capital liquidity, debt levels, cash flows, strategic initiatives and market conditions. These statements are based on current expectations, estimates, forecasts and assumptions and are not guarantees of future performance.

Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied in these forward-looking statements due to risks and uncertainties, including changes in customer ordering patterns, customer concentration, competitive conditions, supply chain constraints, inflation, tariffs, interest rates, credit availability, labor and production costs, inventory levels, operational execution and macroeconomic conditions and other risks described in the company's most recent Form 10-K, 10-Q and other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company undertakes no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements, except as required by law. For a more detailed discussion of some of our ongoing risks and uncertainties of the company's business, I refer you to the various filings.

With that, I'd like to begin the call and turn the call over to Selwyn Joffe.

Selwyn Joffe: Thank you, Gary. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. As outlined in our earnings release this morning, our second quarter results reflect delayed customer orders. There were also delayed orders relating to the realignment of inventory at certain customer distribution centers. Also, there were lower tariff pass-throughs compared with the prior year. While these conditions have affected our near-term performance, we remain confident in the underlying fundamentals of our industry and most importantly, in the substantial opportunities we are developing to expand our business and improve profitability. I want to focus today on several developments that we believe will strengthen Motorcar Parts of America's competitive position and provide a foundation for meaningful future growth.

First, we have secured nearly $60 million in incremental annualized new business awards from both existing and new customers. These awards represent product programs we were not previously supplying with anticipated annual volumes based on customer requirements and historical sales activity. This is an important distinction. We are not simply forecasting opportunities. We have been awarded business that we expect to translate into additional revenue as the programs launch and mature. Small initial shipments have already commenced, and we expect all these programs to launch during the second half of this fiscal 2027, with the majority of these programs launching towards fiscal year-end.

We also currently anticipate approximately $25 million in incremental annualized sales by the end of March, with additional contributions expected as these programs ramp during fiscal 2028. We believe these awards demonstrate our ability to gain market share even during a period of softer industry demand. Turning to our Brake business. Brakes have become our second major product category, building on more than 50 years of experience and our established leadership in rotating electrical products. We believe this is particularly attractive because Brakes represent an essential nondiscretionary wear category with multiple replacement opportunities over the life of the vehicle.

Our brake-related product offerings, including calipers, pads, rotors, master cylinders, power boosters, wheel hubs and brake shoes provide opportunities to expand our relationships with major retailers and professional aftermarket customers. The relaunch of our Centric Parts brand represents an important additional opportunity. Centric is an established name in the professional brake aftermarket, and we believe that combining that brand with our existing manufacturing capabilities, product coverage and distribution infrastructure significantly strengthens our competitive position. Importantly, potential Centric sales are not included in our current incremental growth estimates. We also believe increased utilization of our existing brake manufacturing capacity can contribute to improved operating leverage and profitability as these volumes grow.

We are also encouraged by the expansion of our business opportunities beyond the United States. Mexico is becoming an increasingly important growth market for us. Some of our largest customers are expanding their operations there, creating additional opportunities for Motorcar Parts of America to supply products through our established relationships, capability and performance. Some of these opportunities are included in our current new business expectations, while others represent additional potential growth. We also see opportunities as major aftermarket customers expand geographically into Canada. Our established North American relationships, combined with our manufacturing and distribution capabilities provide a strong platform to support these exciting developments. Turning to our heavy-duty rotating electric business.

We have completed the relocation of this operation from Canada into our existing manufacturing facility in Mexico, where production has commenced. This initiative is an important part of our continuing efforts to improve our manufacturing competitiveness. By leveraging existing infrastructure, manufacturing resources and operating capabilities, we expect to reduce costs, improve production efficiencies and benefit from operating synergies. We believe this will strengthen our competitive position in the heavy-duty aftermarket and improve our ability to pursue additional business. Another business demonstrating continued positive momentum is our rotating electric diagnostic testing equipment program. Our JBT-1 diagnostic testing equipment has an established presence with major automotive aftermarket customers across the United States, Mexico and Canada.

We continue to expand installations within existing customer networks while pursuing additional opportunities, including international markets. We believe there is significant long-term potential for broader deployment of this technology throughout the automotive aftermarket. Stepping back, we remain constructive about the long-term fundamentals of the automotive aftermarket. The average age of vehicles on the road continues to increase and consumers are keeping their vehicles longer. Higher new vehicle prices also reinforce the economic incentive to maintain and repair existing vehicles. These dynamics are particularly relevant to our business because we supply essential components required for vehicles to start, stop and operate safely. Although repairs and purchases can be deferred temporarily, the underlying need for replacement parts remains.

While we see temporary deferrals, we believe that a catch-up is ahead as the economy stabilizes. We believe our broad product coverage, manufacturing capabilities, customer relationships and global operating platform uniquely position us to participate and meet the long-term demand. In summary, while the current operating environment remains challenging, we are making progress on several important fronts. We have secured significant incremental new business. We are expanding our brake platform through Centric. We are pursuing additional opportunities as major customers expand geographically. Our rotating electrical diagnostic business continues to gain momentum, and we have completed an important heavy-duty manufacturing relocation designed to improve our competitiveness. These developments are not dependent solely on an industry recovery.

They reflect initiatives we are undertaking to strengthen our market position and improve our long-term operating performance. We remain focused on converting these opportunities, improving manufacturing utilization, generating cash flow and delivering sustainable profitability. With that, I will turn the call over to David to review our financial results and updated outlook.

David Lee: Thank you, Selwyn, and good morning, everyone. Let's start with analytics for the fiscal second quarter. Fiscal second quarter ended September 30, 2026, net sales of $169.2 million were impacted by delayed customer orders and a reduction in tariff pass-throughs. Broader economic uncertainty, including inflation, tariffs and uneven consumer spending also contributed to a cautious operating environment. Additionally, net sales for the prior year reflect $14.8 million of core revenue in connection with the realignment of inventory at certain customer distribution centers. We believe higher sales and a continued focus on efficiency and cost reductions will favorably continue to favorably contribute to results for the second half of fiscal 2027.

From a sales perspective, as sales momentum increases, combined with new business commitments that Selwyn referenced earlier, which has had a small impact through September 30, 2026, as well as other meaningful opportunities, we believe the company will benefit in several ways near term, including favorable impact to gross margin, continued annual cash flow generation, net debt reduction and opportunities to increase shareholder value. In short, we believe the fundamentals of our business are strong. Regarding gross margin, let me first discuss the second quarter in more detail. Gross margin was 24.2% compared with 19.3% a year earlier.

Gross margin was impacted by noncash expenses of 2.8 percentage points and benefited from onetime items of 5.7 percentage points, including approximately $11.1 million of IEEPA tariff refunds as detailed in Exhibit 3 of this morning's earnings press release. In addition, gross margin was impacted by unfavorable foreign exchange rates of approximately 1.4 percentage points or approximately $2.4 million due to the weakening of the U.S. dollar versus the Mexican peso. Excluding the noncash expenses and onetime items as well as the foreign exchange impact, gross margin was approximately 22.7% for the quarter. Fiscal 2027 gross margin is expected to be favorably impacted by increased sales and overall cost reductions and efficiencies.

Overall, regarding gross margin, we remain focused on overall margin accretion supported by strong momentum and greater utilization of brake-related capacity from both existing and new business. We are also focused on positive impacts to overall margin from further improvements in operating efficiencies supported by benefiting from our tariff mitigation initiatives, better pricing for scrap sales as we gain more market share for our products, additional opportunities to relocate certain operations to our low-cost facilities globally, including Mexico and further strategic cost reductions. These initiatives are expected to positively impact overall gross margin.

Our cash flow, balance sheet and liquidity for the quarter was impacted by working capital inventory ramp-up for new business, and we used cash in operating activities of approximately $4.1 million for the second quarter. The company's revolver loan of $126.6 million, less cash of $20.8 million at September 30, 2026, resulted in net bank debt of $105.8 million. For the prior 3 years ended March 31, 2026, the company generated cash from operating activities of approximately $103.8 million. While quarters fluctuate, the company continues to expect to generate positive cash flow. Our liquidity of total cash plus revolver availability was approximately $104.8 million as of September 30, 2026.

We remain focused on increasing operating profit and gross margin and generating positive cash flow, supported by growth and operating efficiencies from our global footprint. In addition to our goal of generating increased operating profits, including benefits from our gross margin expansion initiatives previously explained, we expect further opportunities to neutralize working capital, supported by customer product demand planning, enhanced inventory management and extending our vendor payment terms, including growing our supply chain finance program offered to our vendors. Recently, MPA received a highly commended award in the category for best use of supply chain finance by a leading provider of supply chain programs.

Regarding our debt leverage, based on information in our filing today, EBITDA for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, was $58.9 million. EBITDA before the impact of noncash and onetime cash items was approximately $70 million for the same period. To recap, our net bank debt was $105.8 million at September 30, 2026, compared with EBITDA before the impact of noncash and onetime cash items mentioned above of $70 million for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, resulting in a net bank debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 1.5. I should mention that under the company's authorized share repurchase program, there was approximately $20.1 million available to repurchase shares at September 30, 2026. Turning to our outlook.

We are revising our fiscal 2027 guidance to reflect delayed customer orders in both our existing business and contributions from new business awards. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, we now expect net sales of $715 million to $740 million compared with our previous guidance of $780 million to $800 million. The revised outlook reflects a challenging ordering environment and the timing of new program launches. As Selwyn discussed, we expect all of the awarded programs to launch during the second half, with most launching toward fiscal year-end and continuing to ramp during fiscal 2028. We expect full year operating income of $37 million to $44 million.

This outlook reflects approximately $30 million in noncash expenses, approximately $5 million in expenses associated with relocating our heavy-duty operations to Mexico and excluding approximately $11 million in IEEPA tariff refunds recognized in the second quarter. In addition, full year depreciation and amortization is estimated at approximately $9 million. To put the revised outlook into perspective, our guidance implies second half net sales of $378 million to $403 million. This compares with $380 million in the prior year period, representing a decline of approximately 0.5% to growth of approximately 6.1%. The prior year second half included $19.9 million in core revenue in connection with the realignment of inventory at certain customer distribution centers.

Excluding that revenue from the prior year comparison, our projected second half sales represent growth of approximately 5% to 11.9%. We expect second half operating income of $23 million to $30 million, reflecting approximately $14 million in noncash expenses. In addition, second half depreciation and amortization is estimated at approximately $5 million. Our expected second half improvement is supported by contributions from new business, better utilization of our manufacturing capacity and continued cost reductions and operating efficiencies. While the timing of customer orders remain a source of uncertainty, our focus is clear: execute the scheduled launches, improve margins and convert sales to cash. With that, we will open the call for questions.

Operator: Your first question comes from the line of Brian Nagel with Oppenheimer.

Brian Nagel: I was hoping, Selwyn, you could just go into more detail with the -- I guess, I would always call the sales dislocations that happened here in the quarter and then we've given the guidance look like they'll persist through the balance of the year. You mentioned -- I guess, activity on part of your customers and then some tariff dynamic. But I guess the first one is you just want more detail on what happened here and what disrupted so significantly the sales run rates?

Selwyn Joffe: Yes. So let me sort of focus on three major points. We had a reallocation where we moved our business opportunities from certain warehouses to newer different warehouses. The ramp-up in the newer warehouses is, I think, the economy affected, but the number of stores in those newer warehouses has been slower than was anticipated. We believe that's going to catch up. So what happens is you lose -- you give up certain warehouses and you get certain warehouses and that ramps up slower, I mean, there's a sort of gap between the revenue. Now we're starting to see that change.

Just as a matter of backdrop, Brian, is that certainly in the last 4 weeks, we're seeing more vibrancy coming back to the entire categories that we're in. So that was number one. Then number two is we picked up a nice amount of new business from the First Brands' bankruptcy or liquidation in the brake business. And in that brake business, what happened is that the First Brands' inventory got -- it was being liquidated. And so a number of the existing customers bought inventory in that liquidation. So that deferred the ramp-up volume in what we received. Now we think that, that's substantially over, and we're receiving that now.

We're receiving that now, and we think that, that is going to be vibrant. And then last but not least is we've had some softening in the -- just in basically in the fundamentals, mostly in the DIY business. We're a big supplier to the DIY business, and some of those orders have got deferred. Now we're starting again to see some more vibrancy in that area. And those are the 3 major items that really somewhat took us by surprise. I mean, we saw a couple of months of really soft revenue and then it came -- has come back now, and we're hoping to see that continue.

Brian Nagel: So as a follow-up to that, to the first point there with regard to, I guess, the warehouse movement, is this one customer? Or is this something you're seeing more pervasive through the sector?

Selwyn Joffe: That is one customer. That's one customer. That particular event is one customer. If you had to look in general, I'd say across the spectrum, we're seeing some softness. Again, in general, we're seeing a pickup as well across the spectrum.

Brian Nagel: Oh, go ahead. Sorry to interrupt. Go ahead.

Selwyn Joffe: No, no. I mean, I think in general, I mean, that certain customers are weaker than others. But in general, that's the trend.

Brian Nagel: And then I guess maybe more for David. So you had this -- I'm going to use the word dislocation here in the fiscal second quarter, but you took down guidance substantially for the year itself, and I hear you saying trends got better maybe in the last month of the fiscal quarter. So as you're thinking about the guidance and the thinking behind that guidance, what's embedded there? Is this reflect basically the weakness that was in the earlier part of the quarter? Or is it all embedded in some of the pickup we're seeing or saw late in the quarter?

Selwyn Joffe: No, I think what you're seeing in the guidance, and I'll turn it over to David, is that the first 6 months, obviously was significantly weaker than we thought, but we believe the back 6 months is going to return. So David, I'll turn it over to you to talk more about that.

David Lee: That's a good question. We're already seeing October sales have increased compared to the end of the trend in fiscal second quarter, and we expect that trend to continue. So we're already seeing orders pick up.

Selwyn Joffe: Yes. And I think that the guidance, we're assuming that the tide for our existing business will increase, but not all the way. We do think it's going to get stronger. And then the significant amount of new business that's coming on will further enhance that. So I mean, the question is how high is the tide going to come back to -- is it going to come back to our normal or even greater because there is, I think, some discussion in the industry that there may be some catch-up because these are -- when you say nondiscretionary, I mean, people are delaying these repairs.

Their cars don't work, but they're not scrapping their vehicles because they're not replacing a component in the vehicle. So there's a potential for some tailwinds catching up, but we're not assuming all of that. We're being -- we do think that there is a recovery coming, but not -- we're not assuming a significant tailwind at this point, but there is a possibility of that.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Derek Soderberg with Cantor Fitzgerald.

Derek Soderberg: So I wanted to start with the new business, the $60 million. I was curious how fast you can ramp that opportunity. It sounds like some of it is going to start shipping by the end of the fiscal year. But I was just wondering if you can kind of talk about how fast you can really ramp to that $60 million level. And then the $25 million announcement on new business, is that related to the $60 million? Is that the same kind of group of customers, same products? Can you talk a little bit more about the $25 million piece as well?

Selwyn Joffe: Yes. So the $60 million is firm commitments that we have right now. That's annualized revenue. We believe we'll begin shipping all of it this fiscal year. It's already started. I mean we're ready -- pretty much ready to go as the customer demand starts ramping now. Many of these, they have to transition between the old supply and the new supplier. And in some cases, you have a changeover where boxes have to be changed or replaced. So -- but we are very confident that all of that $60 million will begin this year. On the $25 million, that's incremental to the $60 million, similar story. That $25 million is very advanced discussions. The $60 million is firm commitments.

The $25 million is a very advanced discussions with the expectations. And we believe we can get to hopefully all of that $25 million by year-end as well, but that's going to be a little later in the year. There may be some of that, that goes into the following year. And then we've got a significant backlog lined up for next year, and that excludes the Centric opportunity. The Centric opportunity is really shaping up. There's a number of very large players that are interested in it. And certainly, we're evaluating how and what the most productive way is for us to launch that program, in particular, in light of the Quality-Built program that we already have out there.

That's doing quite well. So we'll see how that unfolds. More news or more guidance on that to come still as we get through that.

Derek Soderberg: Got it. And sticking to this -- sticking to the $60 million new business, is this accretive to gross margin? And David, I don't know if you can talk a little bit about kind of the near-term gross margin target or give us maybe some commentary on like a normalized gross margin target maybe for next fiscal year. Just maybe talk about kind of the pricing, what you're seeing on that front in this kind of maybe softer market, what we should expect on -- how should we expect -- how should we think about gross margin kind of from here?

David Lee: That's a good question. So with the additional business, gross margin should be comparable to what we've been reporting. So if we look at the most recent history, including last fiscal year, if you go through the tables in the back of our earnings press release where we exclude the items that impact the results that are noncash we've been averaging about 22-plus percent on gross margin. So we expect that when we bring on the new business, it's going to be comparable. However, with the increasing volume that we're adding and the overhead absorption that's going to be favorable and continued focus on cost reductions, we do expect to see accretion in the margins.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question-and-answer session. I will now turn the call back to Selwyn Joffe for closing remarks.

Selwyn Joffe: Well, I just want to thank everyone for their questions. I'd like to close by reinforcing a few important points. We recognize that our near-term results have been affected by delayed customer orders. We are focused on addressing these challenges and improving operating performance. At the same time, we believe the company's competitive position continues to strengthen. Our nearly $60 million in new annualized business commitments will generate additional revenue as these programs launch and ramp. We also see further growth potential through Centric Parts, the geographic expansion of our major customers, our rotating electrical diagnostic equipment business and our improved heavy-duty manufacturing platform and business.

We believe these initiatives provide multiple avenues for revenue growth, greater operating efficiencies and improved profitability. Our priorities remain clear: execute the new business launches, support our customers, improve margins, generate cash and create long-term shareholder value. I want to thank our employees for their continued dedication and our shareholders for their support, and we look forward to updating you on our progress during our next earnings call. Thank you, everyone.

Operator: Before we conclude today's call, we have one final question from George Berman with Cabot Lodge Securities.

George Berman: I'd say congratulations, a very elaborative conference call, and we'll be looking to use today's market price to add to our position substantially. Question I have is with the recent election now over, is there -- if we have any anticipated reduction in the tariff situation between U.S. and Canada, U.S. and Mexico, would that have a positive influence for you?

Selwyn Joffe: Well, clearly, I think the challenge that's out there today is that the cost of repair for the consumer has gone up substantially, in particular, in light of the tariff pass-throughs that have gone through. So to the extent the consumer can repair the vehicle for a lesser cost for them, our margins basically remain unchanged because we would reduce our prices to reflect the reduction in the tariffs. But the volume and the demand at the consumer level, I believe, will accelerate dramatically. So I think that's a very positive event. In particular, when you talk about the significant role that we play in selling new units, not only remanufactured new units.

And most of our remanufactured product is exempt because it's coming out of Mexico. But we're fast becoming leaders in the new unit business, both for brake calipers and for rotating electrical. And those are made in our Malaysia facilities, which are extremely efficient, but they have the burden of bearing some tariffs. So to the extent that those tariffs come off, it will be very advantageous to pricing and to our margins.

George Berman: Great. Maybe another quick question on Mexico. Over the last few quarters, you've alluded to the fact that Mexico is growing quite nicely for you. I saw that one of your customers, AutoZone has recently been also expanding into Brazil. Do you see the South American market in general being another growth opportunity for you?

Selwyn Joffe: That's a great question. I mean what's happening is because of the success in Mexico and all of the South American trade contracts and free enterprise zones between different countries between Mexico and South America as well as AutoZone going into Brazil, we think South America is probably the biggest opportunity as far as a new continent for us. Our Mexico sales are growing significantly, and we're seeing a lot of Mexican interest in them wanting to export into South America, which opens the door for us to move into South America as well. I think another exciting part of that is that our diagnostics equipment is all bilingual.

It's not bilingual, but right now, trilingual, but we have the flexibility of even adding Portuguese to our diagnostics. The diagnostics capability in the rotating electrical segment for us is extremely strong. And right now, to the best of my knowledge, we are the only tester that's available that can actually test the communication protocols. So to the extent you don't test communication protocols, you're getting false -- you may get false positives on testing. So having these testing units in locations where rotating electrical alternators and starters are sold is critical. And we're fast reaching the point where we have a majority of the locations in the United States.

We still have a lot more to go, but significant demand there. We have the same demand brewing in Mexico, the same demand brewing in Canada, where we have French and English and obviously, Spanish in Mexico. The diagnostics demand is -- continues to go up, and that's a pretty exciting opportunity as we get into multiple. And then the rotating electrical, I mean, we are one of the -- we have one of the broadest product offerings and our cataloging capabilities allow us to be able to reach these international markets fairly quickly and with a breadth that I think is world leading.

So I appreciate that question, but I definitely think that as you look into the future, that's a big growth opportunity. The other side is the Centric formulations. If you look at the formulations and the acceptance and the amount of Centric out at a time is around $400 million in revenue. And these brake pads, in particular, that unique formulation of these pads is so highly accepted by the installer that we have no doubt that as they start reaching reintroduced into the United States, which we already see the research that the installers are waiting to see this product, especially the professional installer market.

But we think that the applicability as we move into Mexico and other countries on the brake product line and the utilization of the Centric as well as our Quality-Built, we see a big opportunity across our whole product line spectrum in these new countries. So it's very exciting again for the future.

George Berman: And one quick housekeeping question. How many shares have you bought back in the current quarter? I saw that your interest costs are coming down dramatically as well.

Selwyn Joffe: That is true. Our interest cost -- I mean, unfortunately, that interest cost comes down because some of the sales is lower, and we don't use the supply chain finance programming as much. But we still got $20 million available on our buyback. We bought back, I mean, over -- I think, over $11 million or $12 million. David, more than that, what do we have?

David Lee: As of June 30, the trailing 12 months was about $11 million.

Selwyn Joffe: A little over $11 million. So we have still another $20 million in the current authorization available. And so we're optimistic about our potential and our future, and we continue to keep that as a potential for capital allocation.

George Berman: And I think you do have a poison pill in place, right?

Selwyn Joffe: No, we do not have a poison pill.

George Berman: That might be something you want to think about because it seems to me the equity valuation is extremely low right now.

Selwyn Joffe: Yes. Well, I certainly agree with that, yes. We'll take that under consideration. I appreciate that.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

Making sure you’re in tune with the basics behind AI

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In my line of work, as someone who’s constantly explaining what I do for a living, it can be a lot for someone to wrap their head around.

Explaining that I cover the world of AI, the abundance of chatbots & AI agents that exist and the companies & bigwigs that throw big swaths of money at the growing tech can be a lot for someone to take in. I can only imagine how much more confused they get when they look up AI as a general search term and come across a bunch of additional technical jargon that scares them away from the trending tech altogether.

I went ahead and offered up a 15-minute lesson on how to start out using ChatGPT (which helped my parents get a decent understanding of one of the most popular AI tools). Now I’m here to break down seven of the most vital terms every AI user should know.

Whether you consider yourself someone who’s just starting to give AI a chance or a power user whose base level of knowledge is already strong enough, it’s still worth learning or getting a quick refresher on the world of AI.

A Large Language Model can be broken down easily by delving into what each letter in “LLM” stands for. The “L” represents the “large” amounts of data that it's trained on, such as the words contained in books, on sites, in articles and across research papers. The second “L” pertains to the human “language” that it’s designed to understand, process and generate on its own.

And finally, the “M” represents the type of AI program that works as a “model” that interprets human patterns and relationships through words instead of just memorizing answers. For instance, an LLM taps into the patterns it’s learned during its training to properly respond to a user’s request to write a birthday message to their friend. Simply put, an LLM is the driving force behind a chatbot that helps it comprehend and generate human language.

Generative AI is a type of AI that can generate original content, such as text, images, audio, videos and computer code, based on the instruction you give it via a prompt. I’m sure you’ve come across all sorts of photos of people made to look like they exist in a neon-soaked 80s world, videos of dogs riding a skateboard like a human being and easily discernible AI-generated songs. Generative AI is used to produce those types of content as it's commanded to create something new instead of just retrieving pre-existing information.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Think of machine learning as a method in which computers are taught how to recognize patterns and make predictions based on all the data they’ve observed. Instead of having to be given specific instructions by a programmer to complete their task, computers can rely on machine learning to learn from examples to build knowledge over time.

Machine learning is comparable to the way Netflix brings up recommendations, as the streaming service analyzes what you’ve watched, what you’ve given a thumbs up to and what you've skipped to make educated decisions about what to suggest you watch next. The more information Netflix has, the stronger its recommendations will be. Machine learning is the core engine that’s crucial to the continued improvement of AI as a whole.

A neural network is a computer system that’s comparable to the human brain, as it contains layers of interconnected nodes that process information and identify patterns in the same way that neurons connect and communicate in our heads. It’s the system that helps AI recognize complicated patterns, with it being able to understand that you’re presenting it with a picture of a cat since a neural network helps it learn to recognize the patterns of that animal type.

AI is prone to making mistakes, which are defined as hallucinations. When a chatbot confidently gives you information that is clearly incorrect or entirely made up, you’ve just borne witness to your AI tool hallucinating. AI doesn’t automatically recognize whether the information it's giving you is true, which can lead it to produce made-up statistics and cite fake sources. As a tip, it’s always worth double- and even triple-checking the information AI feeds you. That rings especially true for those instances where a chatbot gives you medical, financial or legal advice.

Prompt engineering is super easy to comprehend: it’s the process of writing detailed instructions that can help a chatbot produce better results for whatever you’re requesting. Now, a prompt is simply what you write into an AI tool. Prompt engineering is what you need to master so you can properly phrase your command so that the AI tool understands exactly what you want and delivers on it.

Going from a basic prompt such as “give me dinner ideas” to a more fleshed-out one such as “Give me [number] dinner ideas that take less than [time] to prepare, cost under [cost] per meal and use ingredients I can find at [name of supermarket” highlights a stronger mastery of prompting chatbots.

I’m sure you’ve spotted instances of AI subscription plans that include a limit on how many tokens your current plan consumes.

Tokens are pretty much small chunks of text that AI models process when reading and generating language. Since chatbots don’t necessarily process an entire sentence as individual words, they break up portions of the text you put into it as tokens instead. A token can be classified as a single short word, a portion of a longer word, a punctuation mark and even a period. So a question you may type into ChatGPT will push it to break up that sentence into tokens before it processes it to generate a proper response.

Since some AI models have a limit on how much information they can process during a single conversation, tokens are brought up when looking at their subscription plans so you can understand how much they can take in before they reach their limit.

As someone who couldn’t even tell you the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent just a year ago, I’ve taken crash courses on the most important terms every type of AI user should know. I’m sure all the beginners out there won’t become pros at using ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or any other AI tools overnight. But over time, you’ll recognize its benefits while also keeping the core definitions around AI as a whole in the back of your mind.

Elton Jones covers AI for Tom’s Guide, and tests all the latest models, from ChatGPT to Gemini to Claude to see which tools perform best — and how they can improve everyday productivity.

He is also an experienced tech writer who has covered video games, mobile devices, headsets, and now artificial intelligence for over a decade. Since 2011, his work has appeared in publications including The Christian Post, Complex, TechRadar, Heavy, and ONE37pm, with a focus on clear, practical analysis.

Today, Elton focuses on making AI more accessible by breaking down complex topics into useful, easy-to-understand insights for a wide range of readers.

#3207. A Blue Tsunami in State and Local Government Elections May Have Just Driven a Dagger Through the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Data Center Trade

Democrats didn't just flip Congress; they won many gubernatorial races and flipped several state legislatures.

While Democrats are celebrating the midterm elections that enabled them to reclaim control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate, they may still be unable to make big changes over the next few years.

That's because President Donald Trump still holds veto power that requires a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate to override. Democrats didn't obtain 60 Senate seats, so it's unlikely they'll be able to override the filibuster, either.

That said, Democrats performed incredibly well on the state and local levels, including in areas that haven't gone blue in decades. The state and local "blue tsunami" may have just driven a dagger through the artificial intelligence (AI) data center trade.

Voters elected Democratic governors in Texas and Georgia, which haven't seen a blue governor in decades. According to the Associated Press, Democratic governors will preside in at least 28 states starting in 2027.

Furthermore, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures on Nov. 6, polling data suggest Democrats will flip at least 11 state chambers (House or Senate), although many results still aren't final.

Many Democratic governors and state lawmakers have promised either to ban data centers or to advocate for more regulation of them.

For instance, according to Reuters, incoming Texas Gov. Gina Hinojosa campaigned on halting new data center approvals until state lawmakers could pass laws "to protect Texans, so that Texans have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into our community."

Hinojosa defeated incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, who had been perceived as more friendly to data centers until he flipped his position on the matter in the final month before the midterms. Georgia's soon-to-be governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, also campaigned on a data center pause.

Dozens of municipalities also approved nearly all the data center moratoriums on midterm ballots.

While data centers do provide jobs, they can also drive up electricity costs and use tremendous amounts of resources, such as water. At a time when people are grappling with costs and worried about AI safety and AI taking their jobs, data centers are clearly not popular.

In stark contrast, President Donald Trump believes that AI and data centers should not be paused because the U.S. is in an AI race with other countries.

Now, I don't think many state and local governments will permanently ban data centers. It's tough to outright ban an industry, especially if it can provide economic value. That said, state and local governments can make the cost of doing business much higher and significantly delay them.

The hyperscalers may be able to afford to wait, but some of the neoclouds have deteriorating balance sheets, and the delays could prove costly for their stocks.

Consider a company like Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies, which has significant data center capacity and plans to build more. Musk reportedly spent $224 million on Texas races in favor of Republican candidates.

On SpaceX's most recent earnings call, on Oct. 20, Musk said he expected the company to build and bring online an incremental 10 gigawatts of AI compute in 2027 alone, even suggesting that the number could be closer to 20 GW.

While it's hard to know how much of SpaceX's planned data centers are already underway, local restrictions could slow the build-out, and data centers are the company's biggest revenue generator right now and a near-term driver of growth.

If SpaceX experiences further delays and analysts revise revenue and earnings estimates downward, that could be a tough blow to the stock.

Building data centers may become more expensive, and investors are already concerned about whether such spending will yield adequate returns will likely be even more worried.

Netflix is a goldmine for crime dramas. You can find some of the most acclaimed original series the genre has ever produced there, the kind that rack up impressive IMDb scores. But which of Netflix's crop of originals are some of the best-rated and most worth your time?

If you’re not sure where to start, we’ve got your back. We’ve taken care of all the digging so you can skip straight to the good stuff. The three shows below are among the best crime dramas Netflix has ever made, as rated by IMDb users.

Something tells me you’ll be recommending at least one of these to someone else before long. And if you somehow haven’t gotten around to any of them yet, my advice is to fix that as soon as possible. Check them out as soon as you finish reading and get started on remedying that now.

One of the original Netflix powerhouses, “Narcos” kicked off the streamer’s run of must-watch crime dramas. It chronicles the bloody rise and fall of Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar (Wagner Moura) and the DEA agents, including Javier Peña (Pedro Pascal), who spend years trying to bring him down. Blending dramatized events with real archival footage, it explores the cocaine trade’s explosive growth and the violence it unleashed across Colombia. “Narcos” is a gripping crime epic that doubles as a crash course in one of modern history’s most infamous criminal empires. So if you want something gritty and realistic, this might want to be your first stop.

Executive produced by master of suspense David Fincher, "Mindhunter" is one of Netflix’s most chilling achievements. Set in the late 1970s, it follows two FBI agents, Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) who sit down and interview imprisoned serial killers to understand how their minds work. There are no car chases or shootouts here. But there are plenty of long, unnerving conversations with some of history’s most notorious murderers. And they're starting to take a psychological toll on the men conducting them. This adventure into the minds of killers is a cerebral, slow-burn crime drama that gets under your skin, and it definitely didn't last long enough.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Jason Bateman stars as Marty Byrde, a financial advisor who launders money for a Mexican drug cartel, until a deal goes wrong. Then, he's forced to uproot his family to the Lake of the Ozarks to make good on his debt and, most importantly, stay alive. As Marty and his wife Wendy (Laura Linney) sink deeper into the criminal underworld, they get tangled up with local crime families, the FBI, and young hustler named Ruth (Julia Garner). Bleak and gripping, this slow-burn thriller is unnervingly easy to lose a weekend to, and you probably will.

The HomeView Ultra is expected to feature a robotic arm and 9-inch display. Shades of Amazon's discontinued Echo Show 10?

The Apple HomeView is the company’s first dedicated smart home display, and new reports of how Apple plans to improve the product are already circulating. Apple is reportedly planning to announce a HomeView with a robotic arm as early as next year. The dynamic display is expected to cost up to $1,000.

The HomeView isn’t even on the market yet — it will be available for purchase next week, starting at $299. This 7-inch smart panel features a speaker that doubles as a stand, and Apple will also sell a wall-mounted option.

As a smart home device, the HomeView is designed to serve as a platform for interacting with your Apple ecosystem, including Apple Home and Siri. It’s a smart dashboard that lets you view all your smart home devices and security cameras, as well as your calendar, messages, and other integrated apps.

The Information reported that Apple is rumored to be working on a higher-end smart display for 2027, with shipments starting in 2028. The new device, codenamed J595, may be branded HomeView Ultra and feature a robotic arm and a 9-inch display.

The new HomeView’s screen would be mounted on an articulated mechanical arm to swivel the display, tracking users during FaceTime calls to keep them on-screen. The device could feature proactive smart home automations, such as turning on devices or triggering a room scene when someone walks into the room.

While there’s reason to doubt whether most smart home users would welcome such technology in their homes or consider it too invasive, premium robotic smart displays indicate that companies are standardizing interactive central hubs for the home.

#3204. OpenAI and Anthropic Drop New AI Tools for Cybersecurity, Images and Finance

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Here are three AI product drops you might've missed this week.

Every week is a busy week in the artificial intelligence industry, and this week is no exception. As voters expressed serious concerns about AI and data centers at the ballot box, OpenAI and Anthropic — makers of ChatGPT and Claude, respectively — each dropped new updates to make their chatbots a little more capable.

All these changes come amid rapidly changing government and financial environments. The midterm elections, in which Democrats handily beat Republican candidates across the country, showed that anti-AI and anti-Big Tech campaigns resonated with voters. Tech critics told CNET this week that there is a clear desire for government officials at every level to change how they interact with technology companies — to keep their campaign promises. The election results are also shaking up Wall Street, as investors’ fears about AI’s long-term financial viability grow.

Smaller updates like these are helpful for everyday AI users, and there’s a benefit for AI companies, too. They can prove they’re competitive in a market that is losing confidence in AI. Here are the three biggest AI updates to ChatGPT and Claude.

Gone are the days when every new AI tool got an immediate general release — and that’s probably for the best. Now, when a major AI lab has a new frontier AI model, it slow-rolls its access, and it starts with cybersecurity defenders. That’s exactly what OpenAI did with its newest model variant, GPT-6 Cyber.

Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber: a major advance in security research that pairs stronger capabilities with better model alignment.The model powered the Linux kernel research we announced yesterday, and security teams at companies like Mozilla, Palo Alto Networks, Calif, and… pic.twitter.com/34uAeNnhwP

GPT-6 Cyber is a version of OpenAI’s newest flagship model that’s specifically made for security research and work. OpenAI says it’s best at finding vulnerabilities and staying in its secure container. Those two things matter a lot. Earlier this fall, an OpenAI model was partially responsible for helping researchers identify a major vulnerability in PHP, a programming language that’s used in the majority of websites. And any improvements to keep AI secure are necessary. We saw many instances this summer of AI agents breaking out of their testing environments and making cybersecurity experts fear future autonomous hacks.

You won’t be able to use GPT-6 Cyber unless you’re a cybersecurity expert who’s part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program. Cisco and Mozilla teams are already using the model, according to OpenAI.

OpenAI also added a minor model update to its AI image model, called ChatGPT Images 2.6. The biggest improvement is its speed; OpenAI says the new model is 50% faster than before. That matters for AI enthusiasts who are generating multiple variations of a prompt. The new model also lets you animate your AI images into short GIFs. It’s available globally now for all ChatGPT users.

This isn’t the return of the long-dead Sora AI video model, but it is a sign that OpenAI isn’t giving up on the creative AI space entirely. Anthropic, by comparison, has never had a traditional AI image or video generator and opted for a design tool that’s better suited for mocking up websites and apps.

Anthropic is teaming up with fintech platform Plaid to help you bring your financial information into its Claude chatbot.

Both companies say they have strong security measures in place to keep your information safe. But CNET always recommends a cautious approach when it comes to sharing your financial information (or any sensitive information) with an AI product.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

I'm Erin, and welcome to The Coffee Lab Episode 25, the series where we forget coffee snobbery. The Coffee Lab is all about making coffee fun. Join me as I help you kickstart your coffee journey!

I'm just going to rip off the Band-Aid: the xBloom Studio coffee machine is $599. Alright, now that's out in the open, let's get to the bottom of what the xBloom Studio actually is.

Although it looks like something you'd find in a minimalist NYC apartment (life goals), the xBloom Studio is a maximalist coffee machine. It's a pour-over, scale, and grinder in one. It's even app-compatible, so you can customize your drink down to the milliliter.

Like the Ratio Four ($279), it's an automated pour-over, but unlike the Ratio Four, it's got the aforementioned built-in grinder, built-in scale, and app control. Is that extra $329 worth it? That's the question we're trying to answer this week on The Coffee Lab. Is the xBloom Studio one of the best coffee makers, even at $599?

The xBloom Studio is three products in one.

There's a grinder, a scale, and an automated pour-over. If you buy the Ratio Four, you would need to buy one of the best coffee scales and one of the best coffee grinders separately. These could easily set you back a grand — grinders are particularly pricey (especially my favorite grinder, the $1,500 Mazzer Philos).

However, you could also get a cheap setup; I always recommend the Wacaco Exagram Pro ($49) and the Timemore Chestnut C2S ($60) for seriously low budgets. With the Ratio Four ($279), this would cost $388. That's still $211 cheaper than the xBloom Studio, though it adds more clutter to your coffee space.

Would you pay the extra 200 bucks for an all-in-one? I'm not sure I would, but of course I can't tell you how to think.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

One of the best parts of the xBloom Studio is its customizability. You can make pour-over, xPod (like a fancy Keurig), or even a big batch of pour-over. And every step of those brewing processes is customizable — you can adjust temperature, volume, ratio, and grind speed.

This coffee maker is for serious coffee lovers. You can get incredibly granular, and the xBloom app (more on that later) can literally graph your flow rates. Yep, this isn't a machine for the everyday coffee drinker. I'd recommend this one only for self-professed nerds. While there's nothing wrong with this at all — different strokes for different folks — it's just worth noting if you're a total beginner. If you are a total beginner, I might suggest something like the pod coffee Lavazza Tabli, or if you want a pour-over, start cheap with the Chemex or Hario V60 — definitely the best pour-over coffee makers.

It's not just coffee, either — you can brew tea! Specialty tea is just as delicious as specialty coffee, and with adjustable temperature control, the xBloom can go as low as 100°F (perfect for some types of white tea, for example).

Yes, the xBloom Studio has an app. Because why wouldn't it? It's a new(ish) coffee gadget. Of course it has to have an app.

I'm so sick of apps in general. Why do I need a different app for my speaker, my soundbar, my air fryer, my coffee maker, my watch, my headphones, my earbuds, my alarm clock? Can't we just put a stop to this madness?

Jokes aside, I suppose the xBloom app has a few useful functions. You can customize the NFC card (pictured above) with your go-to recipe. You can also adjust brew volume, brew temperature, and flow rate on the app. You can also program the built-in scale and grinder and configure the pouring direction.

So, I suppose, in the grand scheme of companion apps, the xBloom one is pretty useful. I just wish we didn't need apps at all — I wish this were all built into the machine. I have companion app fatigue. What if I didn't have a smartphone? I'd miss out on 90% of xBloom's USPS.

What do you think? Would you spend $600 on this coffee machine? Let's do a quick rundown of its features again.

As I'm sure you're aware by now, the easiest way to describe the xBloom Studio is as a grinder version of the Ratio Four ($279). The Ratio Four is an automatic pour-over, so you get the delicate flavor of pour-over without the effort. The xBloom Studio makes the same type of coffee, but with a built-in grinder.

Would you pay $600 for an automated pour-over with a built-in grinder? Or do you think that's way too expensive?

As much as I like the appearance and ambition of the xBloom, it's way too expensive for me. There's a lot going for it, but it'll cost you. Let me know what you think in the comments, and check back next week for the next episode of The Coffee Lab.

#3202. Barrick Mining (B) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Gold and copper output held guidance while buybacks and net cash stood out.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Barrick Mining Corporation (B +4.22%) reported third quarter results that matched or exceeded the company's operational targets across its gold and copper portfolios. Management stated that safety and operational execution allowed the business to capture higher realized metal prices, leading to a 41% year-over-year increase in adjusted net earnings per share. The company reported a net cash position of $900 million and confirmed its 2026 production guidance ranges for both gold and copper. Management also indicated that the company is proceeding with a restructuring of North American assets, including an initial public offering for a new entity to hold those interests. Capital allocation remains focused on growth projects like the Lumwana expansion and returning cash to shareholders through dividends and a $3 billion buyback program.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Barrick Third Quarter 2026 Results. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Emily Chieng, Senior Vice President, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Chieng: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. We hope you've had an opportunity to review the press release we issued before market opened this morning. This presentation deck is also now available to download on our website. Presenting our results today are Mark Hill, Barrick's President and CEO; Seb Bock, CEO of Barrick International, which we previously referred to as Barrick Rest of World; and Helen Cai, Senior EVP and CFO. Other members of Barrick's management team will be available after our prepared remarks for Q&A. Before we begin, please note that we will be making forward-looking statements.

This slide includes a summary of the significant risks and factors that could affect Barrick's future performance and our ability to deliver on those forward-looking statements. This material is also available on our website. I will now hand over to Mark.

Mark Hill: Thanks, Emily. We had our fourth quarter in a row with improved safety and excellent operating and financial results. Once again, we delivered against all 4 of our priorities. We continue to focus on safety, which remains our #1 priority. We delivered higher gold production than last quarter and continue to manage our costs. That allowed us to capture the benefits of higher metal prices and deliver strong financial results. We had adjusted net earnings of $0.82 per share and consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $3.5 billion, and consolidated free cash flow of $1.2 billion. As we announced last quarter, we have restructured the management of the Fourmile project and NGM which has already produced significant synergies.

On the growth projects, we continue to advance the Pueblo Viejo resettlement and tailings expansion, and the mine continues to be on track and on budget. Finally, we expect to complete the IPO of our North American gold assets by the end of this year or early next year, subject to market conditions and regulatory review. So as I said, safety is our #1 priority. Our goal is for everyone to go home safe and healthy every day. In Q3, our leaders continue to get out in the field to identify and manage risks. We conducted over 24,000 Critical Control Verifications. Our recordable injury rate decreased quarter-on-quarter from 0.77 to 0.71. We're also working hard to reduce high potential incidents.

So turning to our Q3 highlights. We delivered 816,000 ounces of gold. As we flagged last quarter, gold production was higher in Q3. The strong ramp-up of Goldrush underground and Loulo-Gounkoto more than offset the weather disruptions at Veladero and Porgera. Third quarter copper production was 50,000 tonnes, which Seb will provide more details on shortly. We continue to manage our gold costs. While we are seeing pressures in Africa from fuel, other consumable costs, and foreign exchange, we expect to remain within our full year guidance range. Our adjusted net earnings of $0.82 per share is up 41% year-over-year. Our attributable adjusted EBITDA is up over 20%, and our year-to-date capital returns of $3.2 billion are double last year's.

We're also on track to deliver full year production guidance, and we expect to further extend our track record of strong operational execution. So in North America, we had another increase in production this quarter with almost 0.5 million ounces of gold, with NGM and Pueblo Viejo generating 67% and 72% EBITDA margins, respectively. We saw record throughput at the Gold Quarry roaster. We progressed the ramp-up of Goldrush underground and mined record tonnes from Turquoise Ridge underground. Gold production from Pueblo Viejo was softer in the third quarter due to planned autoclave maintenance. Also in North America, we continue to evaluate a number of growth opportunities.

At NGM, we're assessing options to optimize infrastructure, including new processing capacity at Cortez and rail infrastructure, which could drive a step change in production over the next decade. At Cortez, we're advancing drilling along one of the most prospective corridors in Nevada down the Goldrush trend. And at Carlin, we turned our focus to drilling at Greater Leeville. We are also looking at optimizing process capacity, which could extend open pit life well beyond 2050. Turning to Pueblo Viejo, where the resettlement and advancement of the TSF construction continues on schedule. We have 99% of the resettlement packages accepted and have resettled more than 97% of the families.

We continue to advance the engineering work for the addition of a third flotation train, which will deliver improvements to recovery beyond 2030. And we expect to share more information regarding that work in Pueblo Viejo with our upcoming IPO filings. So with that, I'll turn it over to Seb to discuss the performance of Barrick International. Thanks, Seb.

Sebastiaan Bock: Thank you, Mark, and good morning, everyone. Barrick International produced 319,000 ounces in the third quarter, up 6% on Q2, with strong performance at Loulo-Gounkoto, Kibali, and Bulyanhulu more than offsetting weather disruptions at Veladero and Porgera. The increase came from 2 places. Loulo-Gounkoto continued to perform well, up 16% on higher throughput and grade, with mining and processing consistently running ahead of the original restart plan. And Kibali, up 20%, delivered its highest quarterly production since Q4 2023 as the underground brought more ore at higher grades. Moving to Tanzania. Bulyanhulu stepped up again as the Upper West development resulted in greater mining flexibility.

North Mara was up on the quarter despite an extended plant shutdown and some power instability. Veladero and Porgera were affected by El Niño weather events. Severe winter storms suspended operations at Veladero on several occasions, while drought-related water shortages at Porgera limited plant operating rates. We've seen these conditions continue into early Q4. We manage Barrick International as a portfolio, and the performance across the rest of the operations keep us on track for our full year gold production guidance. On costs, higher volumes at Kibali and Bulyanhulu brought unit costs down. Veladero, Porgera, and North Mara went the other way, with impacts from the storms adding to Veladero's costs. Royalties and fuel remain the main pressures year-to-date.

Despite that, Barrick International generated over $800 million of attributable adjusted EBITDA from the gold operations in the quarter with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 59%. Moving to copper. Production remains on track for full year guidance. We produced 50,000 tonnes in the quarter, with Lumwana completing a planned mill reline in late September, which sets us up for a clean run through the fourth quarter. Our other copper operations were flat on a combined basis, with higher grades and recoveries at Jabal Sayid offsetting lower throughput and grades at Zaldívar. Costs were higher in the quarter, driven mainly by diesel prices, local currency appreciation, higher royalties on the stronger copper price, and some additional waste stripping on top.

For the full year, we expect our copper cost to be around the top end of the range, given the same diesel and currency pressures. The Lumwana expansion will take production to 240,000 tonnes a year with a mine life of more than 30 years, and it remains on track for first copper from the expansion at the end of Q1 2028. Since the start of the project, we've spent $795 million on the expansion, and total expected project capital remains on target at $2 billion. Procurement of all major long lead equipment is complete. The mill building, which sits on our critical path, is scheduled for completion in Q4.

To close, quarter 3 shows the portfolio delivering where we control the variables and doing what we can to mitigate the external pressures on costs. We remain on track to deliver full year production in line with guidance for both gold and copper. With that, I'll hand over to Helen.

Hongyu Cai: Thank you, Seb, and good morning, everyone. We produced a strong set of financial results this quarter with solid operational execution, allowing us to capture more of the favorable gold and copper prices. This more than offset the increasing cost pressures we face. Compared to last year's Q3 results, we delivered a substantial increase in earnings, highlighting our leverage to rising prices and robust operating cash flow. Adjusted net earnings rose 37% year-on-year, and attributable adjusted EBITDA increased 22%. Operating cash flow was in line with last year, and we stepped up investments in our growth options across the portfolio. This includes executing on the Lumwana expansion project, increasing stripping at Loulo, and developing NGM optionality.

Free cash flow was strong at $1.2 billion with $154 million of additional growth-related CapEx compared to this time last year. We closed Q3 with $0.9 billion of net cash on the balance sheet, up $586 million over prior year despite higher return to shareholders, still leaving us some flexibility to invest in our future growth opportunities. A disciplined approach to capital allocation is a top priority, particularly when the business is generating significant cash. We have a clear framework for deploying capital. Our first priority is balance sheet strength. With $0.9 billion of net cash and an undrawn $3 billion revolving credit facility and no meaningful debt due until 2033, we are in a strong position.

Our second priority is sustaining the business and earnings accretive growth. Lumwana and NGM optimization are 2 clear examples where we are deploying capital into low-risk brownfield opportunities that we believe will generate superior returns. Our third priority is returning cash to shareholders. Our new dividend policy implemented earlier this year prioritizes a quarterly base dividend of $0.175 per quarter topped up at year-end to target a total payout of 50% of attributable free cash flow. This quarter, we completed $0.8 billion of share buybacks, and we continue to return excess cash to shareholders. Since 2021, Barrick has returned $10.4 billion to shareholders. And this year, we are set to deliver record annual returns with $3.2 billion returned so far.

With that, I will turn the call back over to Mark.

Mark Hill: Okay. Thank you, Helen. So for 2026, production and cost guidance remain unchanged. As we round out the year, we expect the fourth quarter gold production to be slightly higher than Q3. We expect copper production to also increase as we process material stockpiled during the quarter at Lumwana. We also expect to remain within our full year guidance for costs. So in conclusion, for the fourth quarter in a row, we have improved our safety, although we acknowledge there's more work to do. We delivered on our production and cost. We advanced our growth projects on time and on budget, and we advanced our North America IPO.

So with that, I will hand it back to the moderator for Q&A. Thank you.

Daniel Major: Okay. And then yes, maybe the second question, just how you're thinking about CapEx into next year and the projects.
