#3154. Fervo Energy (FRVO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First GeoBlock is commercial and contracted backlog nears a gigawatt.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Fervo Energy Company (FRVO +26.09%) reached a major operational milestone during the third quarter by placing its first utility-scale geothermal unit into commercial service and expanding its binding contract backlog to over 1 gigawatt. Management reported that the company is transitioning from pilot-scale validation to industrial-scale power production through a modular "GeoBlock" design and horizontal drilling techniques. Financial results reflected significant capital investment in the Cape Station facility, balanced by a strong liquidity position following the company's initial public offering. Strategic focus is now centered on the 400-megawatt Cape Google project and achieving long-term targets for reduced installed capital costs per kilowatt.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to Fervo's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions]. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Paxton Bentzinger, Senior Director of Corporate Development and Investor Relations. Please go ahead, sir.

Paxton Bentzinger: Thank you. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Fervo Energy's Q3 2026 Earnings Call. Joining us today are Tim Latimer, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer; and David Ulrey, Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of applicable securities laws. These statements reflect management's current expectations and assumptions and involve known and unknown risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to the forward-looking statements and risk factors disclosed in today's earnings release and in our filings with the SEC. Additionally, today's discussion may include certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliation tables are provided in the appendix of the earnings release as applicable.

Timothy Latimer: Thank you, Paxton, and good morning, everyone. I'll start with the most important development of the quarter. Our first GeoBlock case station is in commercial operation, delivering power to the grid and generating revenue under our power purchase agreement. A few years ago, enhanced geothermal was an idea recently proven with a pilot that had just begun operating. Today, it is a 33-megawatt power plant consistently delivering clean, firm electricity. When we last spoke in August, I said we judge our progress on 4 things: First, the strength of our pipeline; second, how well and how quickly our modular approach serves customers; third, our license to operate in the communities where we build; and fourth, our execution in the field.

This quarter, we advanced on all 4, and Cape Station is the clearest evidence. Cape Station's first GeoBlock is the first greenfield enhanced geothermal system development in the world to reach commercial operation, and it was built in just 23 months. It demonstrates that enhanced geothermal can deliver reliable, carbon-free power at utility scale. We firmly believe that integrating modularity and best-in-class continuous improvement into infrastructure construction will drive tighter delivery time lines, and we're proud to have taken the first step in delivering this promise by completing our first GeoBlock ahead of schedule.

During this call, I'll elaborate on the start-up of operations before turning to our recent PPA with Google, which we believe is the largest enhanced geothermal PPA signed to date. I'll also speak about continued operational success at Cape Station, policy tailwinds and progress across our pipeline. Before we go further, I want to talk about safety. Nothing we build matters if we don't build it the right way. Our trailing 12-month total recordable incident rate now stands at 0.10, even as we scale up construction and operations at Cape Station. This quarter, our facility construction crew also reached a major milestone, 1 million hours worked without a recordable incident.

The men and women building our GeoBlocks do complex demanding work, including work at heights, hot work and exposure to the [ elements ]. so that reliable clean energy can be built in America. We are deeply grateful for their efforts. 1 million hours without a recordable incident reflects the seriousness with which we approach this work and the tools and processes that let it be done safely. At Fervo, we've said that we want to show that you could be at the forefront of innovation and still lead in health, safety and the environment. This milestone is strong evidence that innovation and safety can go hand in hand. Now back to Cape Station.

On September 30, we declared commercial operation at our first GeoBlock ahead of our contractual deadline. We synchronized to the grid on September 24, and today, GeoBlock 1 is generating revenue under its PPA. In just 23 months, we turned an empty plot of land into a fully operational power unit. This milestone sends a clear message to customers, utilities, regulators and other developers, Enhanced geothermal is now delivering at utility scale. We took science and intellectual property validated at Project Red and built a 33-megawatt full-scale GeoBlock that is delivered on our PPA, supported by project finance, and we delivered it on time. We're still early in our overall Cape Phase 1 operational life cycle.

But while our pilot proved the building blocks of EGS, Cape Phase 1 data is beginning to confirm the benefits of operating EGS at scale. GeoBlock 1 is performing in line with our operational expectations, including both production performance and power delivered under our PPA. Said simply, brine is arriving at the power plant at the designed volume and temperature and electricity is being sold as planned. GeoBlock 1 has given us the playbook. It has taught us about commissioning sequence, equipment and controls, contract coordination and regulatory approvals. We've run that playbook once, and now we run it repeatedly, improving each time we do.

GeoBlocks 2 and 3 are on track with the time line we laid out during our IPO. Both have reached mechanical completion. GeoBlock 2 has achieved grid stake, a major milestone which marks the end of hot commissioning. The plant is now in its tuning and early operations phase, exporting test energy to the grid. GeoBlock 3 is close behind in cold commissioning, where we are testing the mechanical and electrical systems prior to introducing brine. We continue to expect commercial operation for these GeoBlocks by January 1, 2027, which puts us on track to deliver approximately 100 megawatts of firm clean power from Fervo's first 3 GeoBlocks by 2027.

As we deploy our repeatable GeoBlock delivery model across other geo clusters, both in Utah and in other states, we expect efficiencies to compound in terms of both speed and cost. Over time, we are confident we can build and commission GeoBlocks in fewer than 18 months. This brings me to what we are now calling Cape Google 400, GeoBlocks 4 through 11, the next 8 units from our factory model that will deliver to Google in 2028 under our recently signed PPA. These GeoBlocks are on track for mid-2028 delivery. Let me turn now to the details of that agreement. In September, we announced what we believe is the largest enhanced geothermal power purchase agreement signed to date.

It is a 15-year take-or-pay agreement, meaning Google is committed to paying for this power irrespective of the Beaver County data center plans on terms that are fixed for the life of the contract. The agreement covers approximately 396 megawatts delivered in 4 tranches of 99 megawatts each, with commercial operation targeted to begin in mid-2028 and the full set of GeoBlocks targeted to be online before the end of 2028. Construction is already underway, and I will share that progress shortly. Beyond the 396 megawatts contracted, we also committed to offer Google an expansion option of approximately 600 megawatts, which would bring the total to 1 gigawatt.

Let me explain how delivery works under this agreement because the structure is as important as the size. The signed 396 megawatts is the first layer, and it is initially grid connected. For Fervo, it is a firm binding and financeable contract that we can build against today with parent guarantees from both Fervo and Alphabet behind it. For Google, we believe grid connectivity means the power they are buying has value regardless of how much of the power they consume as Google can monetize power in the broader market. That is the point of this structure. It lowers project on project risk. We build Cape station on our schedule.

Google can develop a potential data center on their schedule and neither party is waiting on the other. The second layer, the 600-megawatt expansion option is behind the meter. Unlike the 396 megawatts, which are grid connected, Fervo and Google are pursuing direct-to-load delivery for this expansion to the potential regional data center. This would be under Utah's SB132, a framework that lets large load customers connect directly to new generation with protections for existing ratepayers. Our joint work to seek regulatory approval is underway, and we'll share updates as this progresses. We are working on all of this with the same commitment to transparency and high-quality stakeholder engagement as we conduct with the rest of our business.

Our partnership with Google adheres to the Geothermal Sustainable Development Pact, the voluntary standards I spoke about last quarter. In October, we were at Google's community event in Milford High School, where 250 neighbors came to learn about the potential data center and asked questions. We are pleased with our progress to date, proud to partner with Google and honored to operate in the community of engaged invested citizens. Of course, everything we do comes back to execution in the field. So I will turn to construction. Work on Cape Google 400 continues on track across all 8 50-megawatt GeoBlocks, our standard design going forward.

As I mentioned, we expect first power from these GeoBlocks in mid-2028, ramping to approximately 400 megawatts by the end of that year. Since last quarter's call, the first set of 50-megawatt turbines has passed factory acceptance test, and we've accepted delivery of major equipment in line with our development plan, including recuperators in over 60% of all Air-Cooled Condensers. On the subsurface side, we now have 4 H&P Flex 3 rigs running the Cape Station. Drilling for GeoBlocks 4 through 11 is approximately 18% complete. Our drilling results continue to improve as we drill more wells with our 3.0 design.

Recall that our 3.0 design includes extending laterals to 7,500 feet, stepping up the lateral diameter 8 5/8-inch casing and targeting an average reservoir temperature of 430 degrees Fahrenheit. Each of these changes result in more power capacity through higher flow rates and higher temperatures. Reducing costs and increasing production aren't the result of any single breakthrough. There's a result of intentional measure improvement where small changes compound into large increases in productivity. Dissolvable Plugs and redesigned Toe Prep reduced completion time and complexity. Rotary Steerable Systems and insulated drill pipe allow us to reach deeper hotter rock without slowing down.

Procurement at scale is driving cost efficiencies on our surface equipment, where our ORC Framework with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries through its [indiscernible] and subsidiary provides better pricing and firm delivery time lines on the equipment at the heart of each GeoBlock. No single action will win the day on cost reduction. But what Fervo is demonstrating is that through our methodical approach to development and our dedication to continuous improvement, we continue to remove costs from the system. And as a result, we are positioned to achieve $5,500 per kilowatt of installed CapEx for GeoBlocks 4 through 11. Our long-term target remains at $3,000 per kilowatt.

We maintain a keen focus on returns-oriented deployment of capital, where each dollar spent must justify its economic value. Last quarter, we spoke about using small amounts of capital toward this effort. And one area we've identified is that by pairing relatively small amounts of solar with our GeoBlocks to power our station auxiliary load, we increase the amount of high-value geothermal power that is available for sale under our PPAs. We expect to continue identifying opportunities like these where through our repeatable approach, we drive costs down and improve returns. Next, I'd like to cover policy updates. We continue to see bipartisan support for geothermal at the federal level, support that has been notably broad and durable across administrations.

The Department of Interior recently directed the Bureau of Land Management to allow certain early exploration activities with expedited approval. When we announced our 396-megawatt power purchase agreement with Google, Interior Secretary Burgum congratulated Google and Fervo, calling it "A powerful example of how geothermal can deliver more reliable, affordable, secure around-the-clock American energy." The Department of Energy further bolstered that support by selecting Fervo for 2 potential grants totaling approximately $20 million to support exploration drilling activities. Subject to finalizing definitive funding agreements, these awards would accelerate capital to evaluate prospects in Idaho and Nevada for full-scale enhanced geothermal development.

The Idaho award is notable in that it would fund our first appraisal wells in that state, marking our entry into new geography for Fervo and giving us the opportunity to appraise new geothermal resources there with government support. In recognition of geothermal's extraordinary potential, Congress has taken action to advance impactful bills on permitting, commercial deployment and R&D, all with broad bipartisan support. Next, let me step back and comment on our commercial pipeline. We now have 1,054 megawatts of binding power purchase agreements, representing approximately $11.9 billion of contracted revenue. With the addition of the Google PPA, that is an increase of 396 megawatts or about 60% from last quarter.

That binding backlog is only part of the picture. Beyond those signed agreements, we have an active pipeline of discussions across utilities, industrial customers and hyperscalers. This broad demand reinforces just how acute the need for firm power that can be delivered quickly really is at this moment. Approximately 35% of those ongoing discussions are with utilities and load serving entities, 15% are with large load industrial buyers and 50% are with data centers and hyperscalers. Our approach to power delivery will continue to blend front of the meter and behind-the-meter development. Grid-connected assets remain the foundation, though behind the meter gives customers a faster path to power when transmission time lines lag their need.

Every one of our geo clusters is planned for eventual grid interconnection. So this isn't an either/or choice. It's about giving customers power as quickly as possible. Before I hand it over to David, I want to note that it's been just about 6 months since our IPO. And so it feels like a good opportunity to look at where we started versus where we stand today. We started with a 3-megawatt commercial pilot. Today, with our first GeoBlock online at Cape Station, we have a total of 36 megawatts installed. We had 658 megawatts of contracted power purchase agreements. And today, we have 1,054 megawatts, and our revenue backlog has grown from $7.2 billion to roughly $11.9 billion.

We raised our 2030 capacity target from 1 gigawatt to 1.1 gigawatts. We've grown our estimated resource potential from about 40 gigawatts to over 58 gigawatts. We've expanded our net geothermal lease portfolio from roughly 610,000 to 670,000 acres. And finally, we went from 2 drilling rigs to 4. What hasn't changed is our conviction. When we rang the NASDAQ bell 6 months ago, we believe that the subsurface technology behind the shale revolution could unlock geothermal at enormous scale. That remains our belief today. Only now we have a fully operational commercial asset and over 1 gigawatt of binding contracts to back it up. With that, I'll hand it over to David.

David Ulrey: Thanks, Tim. I'll cover our third quarter results, then capital spending and liquidity and finish with a few items related to near-term expectations before turning to our pipeline. With GeoBlock 1 placed in service on the last day of the quarter, our third quarter results primarily reflect our ongoing construction and development activities. General and administrative expense was $39.4 million compared with $27.4 million in the second quarter. About $14 million of Q3 G&A was noncash stock-based compensation, up from about $8 million in Q2. Excluding stock comp, G&A rose about $6 million to about $25 million, reflecting public company costs and continued hiring.

We ended the quarter with 306 employees, up from 261 at the end of June, with most of that growth in operations and construction as we bring Cape Station online. Operating loss was $43.7 million. Net income was $11.7 million, reflecting $15.4 million of interest income and 2 nonrecurring items and $11.8 million noncash gain on interest rate swaps and $29.9 million tax benefit from tax credits earned as Phase 1 assets were placed in service.

While I call out these items as nonrecurring because they affect comparability between quarters, I want to remind you that our tax credits have considerable economic value, and we have a binding agreement to monetize the tax credits for GeoBlocks 1 through 3 with the proceeds supporting repayment of our tax credit bridge loan. Net cash used in operating activities was approximately $12 million in the quarter. The difference from operating loss primarily reflects noncash expenses, interest income and working capital movements. Capital expenditures were $256.7 million compared with $226.5 million in the second quarter, primarily for drilling, completions and surface facilities at Cape Station.

For the fourth quarter, we expect capital expenditures of approximately $450 million to $500 million, bringing CapEx in the second half of 2026 to $700 million to $750 million compared to our prior expectation of $850 million to $900 million. This is driven by more efficient capital execution for Cape Google 400, primarily because we now expect certain spending to occur later while staying on schedule. Our engineering and construction teams have identified opportunities to shorten the construction period, allowing us to deploy that capital closer to the expected 2028 commercial operation dates. The commercial operation dates remain unchanged as does the approximately $2.2 billion, we expect to invest in the Cape Google 400 GeoBlocks through 2028.

The revised spending plan reflects our relentless optimization of construction time lines, which helps us improve returns by deploying capital closer to revenue generation. One balance sheet item to note. Our expected total cost for GeoBlocks 1, 2 and 3 remains approximately $7,000 per kilowatt. When GeoBlock 1 was placed in service on September 30, we transferred approximately $514 million from construction in process to property, plant and equipment. That amount is not the stand-alone cost of GeoBlock 1 and includes a larger share of Phase 1's wellfield costs and shared infrastructure that serves all 3 GeoBlocks, including our own substation, [indiscernible] and administrative facilities as well as capitalized interest and financing costs.

As GeoBlocks 2 and 3 are placed in service, the shared costs will be spread across more capacity. We ended the quarter with $1.9 billion of unrestricted cash and cash equivalents and current and long-term debt of $301.6 million. Now a few items related to near-term expectations. The fourth quarter will be our first full quarter of revenue from Cape Station under our PPA. As Tim mentioned, GeoBlock 1 is performing in line with expectations. We anticipate fourth quarter 2026 revenue to be in line with what we discussed on our Q2 call. GeoBlocks 2 and 3 remain on track to progress through commissioning, grid sync and into operations following the same sequence as GeoBlock 1.

We continue to expect commercial operation for GeoBlocks 2 and 3 by January 1, 2027. Looking ahead to 2027, our expectations for revenue remain unchanged from what we discussed on our Q2 call, and we'll share more guidance when we report full year 2026 results. To close, I want to talk through our development pipeline because every milestone we've covered today started years ago as acreage and early-stage resource. That pipeline is the engine of our growth. I'll go from most mature development to earliest development.

Today, we have 36 megawatts in operation at Cape Station and Project Red, another [ 66 ] megawatts encompassing GeoBlocks 2 and 3 in commissioning and an additional 400 megawatts encompassing GeoBlocks 4 through 11 is under construction. Our ready-to-build capacity remains at 550 megawatts, supported by our continued expansion at Cape Station beyond what is currently in construction as well as our Corsac GeoCluster, where we have contracted PPAs with Google and [indiscernible] Community Energy. Fervo's advanced development pipeline remains at 3 gigawatts and early development grew to 54.7 gigawatts, up from 48.6 gigawatts. I want to pause here. A large part of that increase reflects our drilling advances at Cape Station.

Our 3.0 well design is going deeper and hotter than the Phase 1 wells that underpinned the initial DeGolyer and MacNaughton initially in place report at Cape. Reflecting those drilling results in incremental lease acquisitions and updated DeGolyer and MacNaughton study now supports 8.4 gigawatts of capacity potential at Cape Station, nearly double the prior 4.3 gigawatts and roughly 18x the megawatts we have under construction today. This is the same dynamic that played out in shale. As well designs improve, the resource base grows and the inventory of development locations expands.

At Cape, every generation of our well design is going deeper and hotter and with 8.4 gigawatts of potential alongside a clear regulatory pathway to develop behind the meter, we have a long runway to keep drilling, building and driving costs down on the same footprint. Separately, an update on our appraisal campaign. As we outlined on our Q2 call, we've begun drilling appraisal wells across several of our geoclusters. These wells will assist in pinpointing and prioritizing specific locations for future development. This work is currently underway, and we'll have more to share in future periods. Underpinning all of this, we continue to expand our land holdings, which now total 670,000 acres, up from 650,000 acres last quarter.

Every stage of this pipeline is moving as we build option value across our portfolio. We have 36 megawatts operating, 466 in commissioning or under construction, 550 ready to build, 3 gigawatts in advanced development and more than 54 gigawatts in early development, all built on 670,000 acres. This is the process through which we will turn resource to megawatts, and we continue to expect this to advance. Before we open the line for Q&A, I'd like to invite you to join us at Cape Station for our investor open house on Thursday, November 19. You can walk the site, see the drill rig and power plant and talk with our team.

Space is limited, so please request a spot through the link in our October 16 press release. For those unable to make it, we expect to host more visits in 2027. With that, operator, you may now open us up to Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions]. Our first question comes from the line of Derek Podhaizer with Piper Sandler.

Derek Podhaizer: Appreciate all the updates here. Maybe just wanted to start by asking you to expand a bit more on the performance of the Cape Station, specifically GeoBlock 1, the first 33 megawatts you brought online. You noted it's operating as expected. But if you could point to specific results and maybe some of the initial data that encourages you on the performance that you're seeing so far?

Timothy Latimer: Yes, definitely, Derek. I appreciate the question. And on a personal note, for someone who's been working on utility-scale enhanced geothermal systems for over a decade now, it's just thrilling to see the flow results of Cape Phase 1 and GeoBlock 1 come in line very much within our expectations. As we mentioned on the call, the brine is arriving to the power plant, and we're meeting both of our flow rate targets as well as our temperature targets, very in line with our modeled expectations.

And that's why we're so excited to be able to achieve that 33-megawatt net number right out of the gate in terms of our September 30 COD that we disclosed in that press release there. And in terms of other performance metrics, I think the most important thing at this point is how many megawatt hours are we producing and what does that translate to in terms of revenue. And I'll just reiterate what David mentioned there, which is that we're very in line with our prior disclosures on the Q2 call in terms of our Q4 2026 revenue target, which means that things are tracking exactly as we expected there.

Derek Podhaizer: Great. That's helpful. And then I want to ask about that heat and place study on Cape Station. You basically doubled your potential capacity to 8.4 gigs from 4.3. What does this mean for Fervo longer term if Cape Station is a bigger asset than you initially expected? Like you said with Shale, you're accessing more resources than you planned. I have to imagine this adds maybe additional GeoBlocks, but just some additional color on the increased capacity would be helpful.

Timothy Latimer: Absolutely. And as you noted, Derek, and as we said in the script, this is not a unique feature of resource place. A lot of times, initial estimates of heat in place or whatever resource you're looking at are oftentimes very conservative because it's an unknown technology and there's not a lot of data. But then what we saw in shale is as more wells were drilled and efficiency gains were captured and a more understanding of the original resource in place was there and spacing assumptions got updated, the shale developers discovered that there was more and more hydrocarbons at each play. And we're seeing this play out exactly in geothermal as well.

So this independent report roughly doubled the capacity that we expect there to be from a technical basis in terms of heat in place at Project Cape and in large part, it's because we've been able to prove out deeper drilling and more efficient operations. And the more data we get, the more comfortable third-party assessors are to give us credit for these advanced designs and these greater drilling depths and greater drilling temperatures, and this is a reflection of that. And I think a couple of things is, one, we don't think it's going to be unique to Cape. We think we're going to be able to repeat this playbook potentially across other prospects.

The more we drill, the more we learn, the more efficient we get, the more resource we believe could be available. So we're excited about what this means across the whole portfolio with really just Cape being more advanced in terms of data collection being the first example of that. And then in terms of Cape as well, we are seeing no shortage of customer demand, both through traditional front-of-the-meter customers or behind-the-meter customers and understanding that we have confidence and there being more resource available as well as third-party verification of that will give us more confidence to market additional expansion at Cape beyond what we've already disclosed.

And so we're -- those efforts are ongoing even as we look at the rest of our portfolio and get excited about what these new efficiency and spacing and depth and temperature numbers mean for growing the total size of the prize across our acreage position as well.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Dendrinos with RBC Capital Markets.

Christopher Dendrinos: Congratulations on the strong progress here. Maybe to start, I wanted to follow up here on just some of the kind of key debates that we've seen out there and specifically maybe some of the longer-term expectations around water loss and thermal declines. And so can you maybe spend a few minutes here talking about how we should or shouldn't extrapolate some of the performance that Project Red over to Cape Station? And then just what gives you confidence in the long-term performance expectations?

Timothy Latimer: Yes, definitely. Maybe I'll start by tackling water loss and sort of how we think about this. And we published an enormous amount of material on this. I can direct you to our website in terms of multiple blog posts explaining water and the importance of water stewardship in our operations. And that effort to be great stewards of the water resources led us to make really intentional design decisions like a commitment to using only dry cooling and no evaporative cooling in the power plant and also by targeting drilling deeper wells to target deeper brackish layers, not freshwater for use in our operations.

And so when we think about water and what we learn there, are we being good stewards of water? Is it impacting cost structure? And do we have the right permitted and allocated amounts to continue our growth. And the new data we've seen from Project Cape confirms us on all dimensions there. This continues to be something where there's minimal -- little to no freshwater use in our operations or construction at all. We're seeing that in line with our expectations, it's not a material driver of OpEx or cost.

And we're also seeing that within our permitted amounts that we can -- the levels we're already seeing at Project Cape, we can support years and years of expansion and growth there given the early results we've seen so far and the position we have in terms of water rights and allocation. So everything that we've seen on production of water in early Cape operations is exactly in line with our prior disclosures, and our confidence remains that this is a problem that we can address through good water stewardship. And then as we turn to thermal decline, it's good to remember how valuable of an asset Project Red is.

This is a first-of-a-kind test, a horizontal EGS system that had never been done before. And it has been designed from day 1 and continues to stay to maximize learnings. And as a result, we have observed after a period of stable temperature, a decline in the production temperature. This was expected. And as we've disclosed on many other calls and other forums, a decline in reservoir temperature after operating an asset for a given period of time is exactly what you expect in a geothermal reservoir. The most important question is how does that impact project viability and economics.

And I'll also note that this information, in particular, how thermal decline shows up and what drives it is now proprietary information to Fervo. We're starting to see competitors design and permit some of their first horizontal EGS projects and they're years behind us. And no one in the world has an asset that now has 3 years of operational history and gives us insight into both the causes of thermal decline and also allows us to test techniques to mitigate thermal decline and improve operational performance. So we continue to believe that this is going to be a very high-value asset for Fervo.

And even to this day, we're doing logging trials and other intervention work at Project Red to maximize learnings that we can apply to Project Cape. And as we turn to these results in Project Cape, as any good resource play, the real-world modeling results we see at Project Red directly informs the reservoir forecasting and expectations we see at Project Cape. And that information is, of course, shared with our underwriters and the debt process as well, how those history match models at Red inform Cape. And again, we're seeing lots of positive indications of the system there. And it's useful to remember, Cape is a very, very different resource than Red.

Red was an isolated double system designed to prove out the concept and maximize learnings. Cape is an operational asset designed for economic returns. We discussed the Gen 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 well system and things like radically longer lateral lengths, improved well spacing, more efficient completion, larger casing diameter, higher temperatures are all things that mean the Project Cape results are going to be categorically improved from Project Red, and we're very excited about the early data, as I mentioned in the prior question, everything at Project Cape from a temperature and flow rate standpoint coming in line with our expectations. So we continue to really see enormous value in Project Red in terms of maximizing learnings and data.

But at the same time, we're incredibly excited about the operational and engineering improvements that we've already executed at Project Cape, and that continues to go really well and have clear evidence that the results of our pilot have improved our operation and execution at Project Cape very substantially.

Christopher Dendrinos: Got it. And maybe as a follow-up here, and I think you mentioned going larger, longer and deeper and then making tweaks to the frac design. I guess my question would just be, do you have ways of measuring downhole once the fracs are laid that you're avoiding kind of like channeling? And is there ways to track, I guess, maybe just performance even from GeoBlock 1 today that the water is flowing maybe uniformly across the network?

And then how long does it take for you to get maybe some level of performance data that you can come back to the table at a later date and kind of say, "hey, look, this first set of wells here is performing in line with what we've expected and we're going to make." It confirms basically the thermal decline assumptions that we laid out maybe at the time of the IPO.

Timothy Latimer: Yes, definitely. And I mean, the short answer is already. We have -- we are collecting and have collected that data. That's one of the things that's really great about Project Red and why we think it's such a unique asset in the space and will drive a significant competitive advantage. We have original flow test results for Project Red that go back 3.5 years ago, and we've done -- continue to do significant logging and characterization work to measure things like flow conformance and thermal decline.

And what's fascinating now is we can go back and map what do we measure in the early flow test results and see how it manifests 2 or 3 years later in changes in flow distribution or temperature. And that's a really unique data set that we have.

And of course, we've conducted, as we've mentioned in prior cases, we've spent tens of millions of dollars now, specifically on unique data acquisition at Project Cape through some of this downhole logging, measuring production flow, flow conformance, temperature profile -- and the combination now of having several wells online, soon to be dozens of wells online, being able to collect and map data across all of them and then go back in history match it against Project Red is really powerful. So we can identify what are the key design attributes, not just in things like well spacing, but in completion design that really do drive best-in-class performance when it comes to flow rates and thermal decline.

And so yes, the answer is we've already collected that data. We will continue to collect that data. And as mentioned, even though we only have now a few weeks of flow data at Project Cape, everything is fitting within our modeled expectations. And I think we can confirm a lot of the assumptions that we have laid out over the last year are playing out in practice. And I think as time goes on, we're just going to collect even more data to make that case. But it's all very confirmatory to what we have expected on really every dimension of the technical road map.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of David Anderson with Barclays.

John Anderson: So Tim, I was wondering if you could talk a little bit about the progress you're making on bringing down the CapEx costs at Cape Google. As we talk, seeing the shale, things always improve over time. And I'm presuming most of the drop from the 7,000 down to 5,500 is subsurface. So I was wondering if you could just kind of talk about the 2 sides of that, one on the drilling side. Where are you today in terms of drilling? How much -- like where do you need to be, I guess, I'm curious, like along that path? How is that progressing?

And then secondarily, curious on the DeGolyer & MacNaughton study that increased heat in place, how does that -- does that change the math on Cape 2? In other words, is the megawatts being produced per well, is that now higher in your expectations? How do we think about that in terms of the more immediate development?

Timothy Latimer: Yes. I appreciate the questions. And to start off on CapEx, you're right about drilling and production results. We are certainly seeing great efficiency gains. And I think in the earnings presentation, we gave some really great concrete examples of where we're seeing gains both in days of drilling and also in things like deployment of dissolvable plugs. But maybe before I get into that, I'll point out in terms of is it subsurface or surface. In geothermal, it's really hard to disentangle those things. It's a complex system-wide optimization. And first and foremost, I want to reiterate what higher temperatures does across the entire CapEx cycle.

Higher production, as we've mentioned, we've increased our target temperature by about 30 degrees Fahrenheit between Cape Phase 1 and the Cape Google 400 project is sort of an overarching lever that reduces CapEx across the board. And that means because you produce more energy per flow of brine, you need fewer wells and then also the power plant is more efficient. And that's part of why we've been able to go from 33 net megawatts to 50 net megawatts from the GeoBlock first-generation design to what we're doing today.

So we're actually seeing CapEx reductions on both the surface and subsurface in part because of things like supply chain efficiency, construction optimizations like David mentioned, but in part because you just get more bang for your buck as you increase the temperature. And we're continuing to see great results there. We're already -- in terms of where we are on the drilling costs, we do expect to -- as we learn these longer laterals, different hole designs to continue to improve, like you mentioned, just like shale, each iteration of that well, as we draw out dozens of these wells, we're going to get more efficient.

But we're already seeing the cost structure, drilling days versus depth, completions numbers very much tracking our expectations and driving -- which is why we were excited to reiterate that $5,500 per kilowatt target. We're already really very much in line with what we need to see there. In terms of the [indiscernible] heat in place report, I would say a lot of this just comes down to collecting more data. And as I mentioned before, also being able to get credit for deeper depths. Typically, when you do these studies, you -- like I said, you do this in a conservative fashion at the beginning, you really only get credit for what you demonstrated is possible so far.

And as we've drilled deeper wells, this is sort of the third dimension. You can drill longer laterals, you can drill those laterals over a larger dimension and you can also drill deeper, so you get more benches of production. And now that our Cape Phase 2 wells are so much deeper than the Cape Phase 1 wells, it's allowing us to get credit for a lot more geology that we always knew was there, but wasn't included often in the initial heat and play studies because we needed to sort of demonstrate the viability of drilling those wells. So that's a big part of it.

I would say the heat and place study itself is not going to drive a design change in the Cape Google 400 where a lot of those wells were in plan already. It just means that as we've long stated, as the technology improves, there's just more geology we can access and access it more efficiently. And that's really what this study reflects. And it's not a major driver of changes to the Cape Google 400 planned wells at this point in time.

John Anderson: Okay. That makes sense. Just separately, obviously, politically data centers became a rather hot topic during this election season. So I'm kind of curious, you touched on this in your remarks, but kind of where does geothermal now fit in this argument? Are conversations with the offtake companies and communities, is that changing? And maybe sort of how is that changing? And how does that impact interest in additional developments as you're looking forward?

Timothy Latimer: Yes, it's a great question. And honestly, public awareness of the importance of developing data center or any other industrial infrastructure the right way with the right sustainability standards and the right community benefit standards and the microscope that's on that now has only benefited Fervo and our discussions with offtakers. I think some of the things that were done fast and loose in the early boom days of this data center revolution where communities were not engaged the right way and projects didn't meet the right emission standards and other things are now well-known, hard lessons learned to data center developers about the importance of doing things the right way.

And as a result, a resource that's 24/7 carbon-free electricity that has great attributes like enhanced geothermal systems plus a developer that has a track record of being in the community early, discussing community benefits, being a good steward of the local environment is really compelling. And I can tell you, a project like what we're doing with Google and Utah wouldn't have come about if we were a [ dirty ] energy resource or we hadn't done the right community engagement work.

So I would say that this microscope on making sure that if you are going to do data center development, it's done the right way is something that is accelerating our conversations with offtakers because honestly, clean and sustainable is back in the conversation in a way that it hadn't been. And I think that's going to be an enduring shift, and we have the right sustainability metrics to be a fantastic community environmental partner. And we're seeing ourselves being relative winners in this discussion and an acceleration of our offtake discussions as a result.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Dylan Nassano with Wolfe Research.

Dylan Nassano: Just wanted to check on the roughly 400 megawatts of PPAs that I think got kind of reshuffled when you, I mean Google PPAs. Just any update there in terms of when those customers are expecting or want to receive that power and how you guys are planning to deliver it with interconnection?

David Ulrey: Yes. Dylan, I appreciate the question. The short of it is that we're working through those amendments as we speak and having really constructive dialogues with those offtakers. And so there's obviously a pretty lengthy process when it comes to working with, with the load turbine entities like those. And so we're continuing to work through it. But I think the punch line is that we're still kind of circling 2032 for delivery of those PPAs. There are some transmission opportunities that are opening up specifically to get power back into California and expect that those PPAs are going to be great candidates to take advantage of some of that capacity.

Dylan Nassano: Got it. And then just a quick follow-up on the CapEx efficiencies, specifically the ones that you're kind of saying is allowing you to shift your CapEx spending profile timing. Just curious, are there any opportunities there for using those efficiencies to maybe drive earlier upside or CapEx savings upside relative to the plan there?

David Ulrey: Yes. You're asking the exact right question. And this is what our teams are constantly focused on or how do we put these time lines together to manage both construction as well as the capital outlay that comes with it. And I'd say that this is a core facet of what we're asking our teams to do, which is challenge every assumption. And as our teams do that, they're looking for ways to apply learnings to modular GeoBlocks, and that is certainly coming through as we speak.

Just to kind of give you one firm data point that we're already seeing for commissioning from GeoBlock 1 at Phase 1 to GeoBlock 3 at Phase 1, we're already expecting about a 50% improvement in that commissioning time line. So as we roll that through our broader construction time lines, that's going to really help us achieve these growth targets that we want while also kind of improving returns. And if you think about what we're doing, we alluded to this, but the overall construction budget is not changing. What is changing is the time with which we deliver that same amount of CapEx.

And so by pushing dollars to the right closer to when we generate revenue, just by taking advantage of time value of money, we're already improving returns. And we're seeing opportunities like that kind of across the board.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Joseph Osha with Guggenheim Securities.

Joseph Osha: I've got 2. First, if you look at Page 11, there's a lot of new stuff going on, dissolvable plugs, rotary steering systems, insulated drill pipe. Has all of this been successfully deployed already? And is all of this necessary to get to 5,500? And then I do have a follow-up.

Timothy Latimer: Yes. This has all been deployed successfully. We decided just to share a small subset of the improvements and things that our team has been working on and decided in this case to go with already implemented and successful improvements that we've seen over the last couple of years at Cape. And this is all stuff that puts us on track for that 5,500, but certainly is not an exhaustive list of the improvements that we've already implemented and are working on. But as I mentioned before, we're very -- we feel very good about our trajectory to the 5,500 based off of these improvements and others.

Joseph Osha: Okay. And then my follow-up, you're having really good luck with the 8 5/8 casing. At what point does it make sense to go to the 9 5/8 that you've talked about as opposed to just going deeper and longer and hotter with the current casing because obviously, as your bigger boards have another set of problems. So I'm just wondering how -- if I look at this 3.0 design you've got on Page 10 here, how much more room do you have to improve on that before you've got to go to the bigger casing?

Timothy Latimer: It's a great question, Joe, and something our engineering teams are wrestling with every day. I would say that our gains in drilling and completions and production efficiency at the 8 5/8 level, we're still very optimistic of being able to drive significant improvements there. And at this point in time, all of the Cape Google 400 wells are planned to be in the 3.0 design with the 8 5/8-inch casing. And so we think we can hit these cost targets within the Generation 3.0 well design. And we will evaluate in the future kind of based off of the data we see, if we -- when and if we're going to move to that larger casing design.

But we do not believe it's necessary to achieve our cost targets. It's just a question of is do we think it's going to be an even larger lever for efficiency gains going forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Julien Dumoulin-Smith with Jefferies.

Unknown Analyst: This is Carter on for Julien. Just a quick follow-up on Google. Thanks for all the color on the PPA there. Just on the 600-megawatt option, when do they have to decide on that? Just trying to think through, given you've got 550 megawatts ready to build and now the Cape asset at over 8 gigawatts, kind of when that option could get exercised if they were to decide to do that?

Timothy Latimer: Yes. Carter, thanks for the question. We're obviously really excited about the progress that we're making in the community with Google, and we've been working with them for several years, and they just continue to be just an outstanding world-class partner. And so we're really excited about what we're seeing there. When it comes to the 600-megawatt option, you pointed to the additional capacity that we have at Cape. There's obviously multiples of capacity there to host that 600 megawatts. So that's certainly not the question. Really, this will come down to working through the various requirements to build a data center, and we expect that Google is going to continue making progress on that into 2027.

Unknown Analyst: Great. And I think in Tim's answer to some of the questions around thermal decline, you referenced data that the lenders get to see around Cape performance that we don't. I'm just curious if you could provide some color on latest project financing discussions in general as we think about CapEx for the Google Cape 400 ramping into next year. Just color on how those discussions are evolving and when we could see an update on project financing would be helpful.

David Ulrey: Yes. Happy to share a little bit of color. We did our initial project financing on Cape Phase 1, which is the facility that we refer to as a Granite Facility. And that was a $421 million loan that we closed in March of 2026 earlier this year. And that was a really intentional loan. It was a broad syndicate of lenders. So now we have a whole set of banks that are accustomed to thinking about enhanced geothermal systems, what that means from a production forecasting standpoint, what it means for permitting and all the various requirements.

We did all of that so that we could start to have these conversations earlier when it came to the 400-megawatt project, which we're now calling Cape Google 400. We expect that Cape Google 400 is going to be ready for project finance debt probably in mid-2027. When we think about the right type of debt, we're really circling that 70% loan-to-value that we've been relatively consistent on. And so as we look at kind of the right time to place that, it's probably going to be mid-'27.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Justin Clare with ROTH Capital Partners.

Justin Clare: I just wanted to start on the 2027 outlook here. So you maintained the revenue expectation of $60 million to $80 million. Just wondering if you've gained any additional visibility into the potential transmission-related curtailments that you had talked about last quarter? And then just with Cape Station Phase 1 progressing on schedule, is the transmission availability really the key variable determining where revenue falls? Or are there other key variables we should be considering such as the timing for the ramp-up of GeoBlocks 2 and 3?

David Ulrey: Yes. Thanks for the question, Justin. And just to remind folks, what we're talking about here is a really unique onetime outage at the substation that we tie into where there's a third-party solar project that needs to physically tie into that same substation. And so while that's happening, we obviously can't be passing energy through that physical asset. We're continuing to work with the counterparty and starting to put what we think are going to be good bookings on the outcomes there. Nothing additional to report right now. We'll have a little bit more detail when 2027 rolls around. But we're finding a counterparty that's really willing to work with us. Our interests are well aligned.

The same counterparty owns other wind and solar assets that tie in the same substation. And so when it comes to limiting that downtime, we're all incentivized to make this happen in a short amount of time as we can. And then on your second question related to revenue from GeoBlocks 2 and 3 and what we're seeing from a time line perspective, I think we still expect these GeoBlocks 2 and 3 to be ready when they need to be on January 1. Certainly, the substation outage occurring in early '27 is going to be a piece of that.

But with GeoBlock 1 working as intended and presumably GeoBlocks 2 and 3 following a similar track, we expect that the Cape Phase 1 is going to be at its 400 megawatts in 2027.

Justin Clare: Got it. I appreciate that. And then just one other one here. So you recognized almost $30 million in tax benefit in Q3 here as you placed the Cape Phase 1 assets into service. So just wondering if you could clarify what tax credit election you're using here. So is that the ITC? Or are you potentially going to use the PTC? And maybe just speak to the tax strategy that you're expecting for future assets here.

David Ulrey: Yes. So this one is a little bit unique, and it's the only one that will work this way. But for Cape Phase 1, we'll have an ITC on the subsurface assets and a PTC on the surface assets. And the reason is that those fall under previous definitions of those various tax credits. And so what you're seeing in that $30 million right now is an investment tax credit related to some of those well field assets. As we move down the road into the future, kind of our base case on a high-capacity factor resource like EGS would be that we're monetizing production tax credits for future GeoBlocks.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from the line of Jeff Grampp with Northland Capital Markets.

Jeffrey Grampp: I wanted to circle back on the solar installations that you guys referenced. Can you give us a sense of what kind of scale you're looking at? I don't know if it's -- if solar per GeoBlock is the right KPI, but like how scalable are these? And how impactful could those be to cost savings with respect to the longer-term capital targets you guys have laid out?

David Ulrey: Yes. Thanks for the question, Jeff. When we think about solar, it's a pretty modest amount of solar that we're talking about here. And this is something that other geothermal developers have employed at other assets, and it seems like it's worked for them as well. Where we see an opportunity is really just the power pumps and various station load. And when you think about the summertime, in particular, solar is really, really effective during the summer. We expect to realize some benefit there.

But when we look at this, each asset is going to be a little bit different depending on where it is, but you can think about this being 20% to 25% of the nameplate capacity of the EGS system itself. And so it's really not big dollars, though we do like the returns that we expect on those dollars. And so we think that this is going to be a really complementary addition to the asset.

Jeffrey Grampp: Great. That's super helpful. And for my follow-up, obviously, a lot of focus on Cape for obvious reasons. But outside of Cape, I think you mentioned some different exploration targets some DOE funding, things like that. Are there any main kind of catalysts or exploration activities that we should be thinking about getting some news flow or updates on as you guys progress into and through next year?

Timothy Latimer: Yes, definitely. We discussed previously that we will be doing an appraisal campaign on one of our next Nevada assets, Corsac. So we expect to be able to provide updates likely next year on some of those early results. And we're also very excited. One of the developments this last quarter was getting awarded 2 different Department of Energy enhanced geothermal system demonstration project grants, one for a product site we have in Idaho and another for a product site -- an additional product site we have in Nevada. And likely, we would expect some incremental updates on our appraisal work there also sometime in '27.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Sean Milligan with Needham & Company.

Sean Milligan: Thank you for all the commentary on the operations side. I just wanted to ask a question about the corporate cost side heading into 4Q and next year. I guess a couple of quarters out now, costs are a little bit higher than we expected on the G&A side. But is there a run rate that we should think about? Or were there any onetime items included in this quarter that we should back out on a forward basis?

David Ulrey: Yes. Thanks for the question there, Sean. We'll be back with more detail in '27, obviously, as we provide a little bit better guidance there. But as we think about what we've been experiencing right now, public company costs are high, and that's maybe the punch line. We've added additional employees. Quite a few of those additions are really focused on the construction, the GeoBlock factory side of things. But certainly, we're also adding folks on the back office administrative side. In addition to that, we have been using various service providers to help us kind of fill the gap while new employees get up to speed on the administrative side of things.

As we shift into 2027, what we expect is some of those employees that we have hired are now bearing more of the burden. And so hopefully, some of that service work will come down in the future.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jed Dorsheimer with William Blair.

Jonathan Dorsheimer: I joined the Q&A little bit late. But -- so I apologize in advance if you've already answered this. I wanted to just dig into the Google option a little bit more. And I guess if I took a cynical view on the PPA that they signed, their ability to resell that could be looked at as more of a protective, I guess, put, if you will. But building that data center or filing for a permit seems like it would be a clear signal triggering the option of the additional 600 megawatts. I guess I just wanted to ask that out loud and see if you would have any -- would view that differently or would agree with that?

David Ulrey: Yes. Thanks for the question, Jed. And you're right. When it comes to the 400-megawatt portion of this, like Tim mentioned, that's a firm contract. Our goal when we wrote that PPA was to have a 400-megawatt PPA that looks and feels like most PPAs and is financeable with counterparties and lenders in the sort, and that's what we ended up with there. When it comes to the 600 megawatts, yes, that's more tied to the outcome on the data center. The trigger for the option is not quite as clear as kind of any kind of specific permit or anything like that.

But we feel good about the progress that we're making there and certainly been in community with Google quite a bit. And think that they're doing a really nice job making progress, and we're excited to be standing beside them.

Jonathan Dorsheimer: Great. And then as a follow-up, there's this BAAJA or the Bipartisan American Affordable Jobs Act that's kind of going through the legislative process right now. There's a lot of language and one of the co-authors of that is Senator Mike Lee from Utah. And there's a lot of language specific to geothermal in there. And I'm just curious your thoughts if that were to go through, how that might change some of the regulatory framework around geothermal for you guys?

David Ulrey: Yes. We appreciate the question. We're incredibly excited about what BAAJA can do for our country's energy system in terms of its reliability, affordability and sustainability. And Fervo has been proud to endorse that legislation in multiple different forums. And we appreciate both the leadership of Senator Lee of Utah as well as his Democratic counterparties. And I think coming up with a really great bill that's just going to be very important for the future of the American energy system. As you mentioned, there's maybe one of the largest or most additive sections is fixes to geothermal, and we are excited about that.

Some of it is giving parity to things in federal permitting that oil and gas has enjoyed for decades that geothermal has been left out on. And other things are providing more financial resources and staffing offices better that we believe will lead to better permit time lines. The backdrop of this is that we've already seen significant improvements administratively over the last several years in geothermal permitting as it has become a larger priority for this country. And nothing in our go-forward expectations relies on the BAAJA. And the guidance we've given previously has been based off of our expectations on federal permitting time lines.

But if the BAAJA were to pass, both the geothermal provisions as well as the transmission provisions would be very additive to our business just in terms of creating a better regulatory backdrop and faster permit time lines for our projects. So for that reason, we stay keenly focused on it. Even though our growth plans don't rely on it, we are excited about it being a potential catalyst for even faster development as we move forward.

Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, I am showing no further questions in the queue. That concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

#3153. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#3152. Google’s AI Mode Will Soon Show Ads Even in Your Follow-Up Questions

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ads will start appearing in AI Mode’s follow-up answers in the US as Google expands AI Mode ads to more countries.

Sponsored results will soon appear in responses to follow-up questions in Google’s AI Mode in the US. Google announced the change, along with plans to show ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more people, after reporting that AI Mode searches generate less revenue than traditional searches.

The company says sponsored product listings in AI Mode already get clicked about as often as organic results. For publishers, the change adds paid competition inside AI answers, which a Pew Research Center study last year found already make people less likely to click through to websites.

You’ve probably seen how this works: Type a question into Google, and an AI-generated summary often appears at the top of the page. That can mean fewer clicks on the ads below, which underpin Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year.

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page.

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email.

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said.

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising.

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said.

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

#3150. 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

I’ve been a dedicated Pixel user since the beginning, so I was naturally excited to get my hands on Google’s latest iteration, the Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve been impressed with it overall, but I noticed that, as Google has done before, the device isn’t set up perfectly out of the box.

Also: Pixel 11 is $200 off in this early Black Friday deal

After spending a few weeks with the device, I found that several features are either turned off by default or need optimizing to work in the best way possible.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

The camera was the biggest reason I first joined team Pixel back in 2016, so it’s one of the first places I looked on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. You can change a number of settings, including contrast, shadows, tint, sharpness, and warmth.

Also: A week with the Pixel 11 changed my mind about Gemini

I’ve always loved the camera on any Pixel I’ve had, but I’ll admit that images can look a little over-processed at times. If picture quality is important to you at all, it’s vital to set this feature right out of the box because it applies to every image you take from that point on. You can find Camera Look by opening the camera app, tapping the settings icon in the bottom-right corner, and making your changes.

Pixel’s “At a Glance” lock screen widgets are one of the most sneakily useful features, and you’re missing out if you’re not using them. These widgets are off by default, but when you enable them, you can see real-time information without unlocking your phone. You can see weather info, sports updates, flight information, rideshare and food delivery updates, fitness information, and more.

Also: These tech gifts topped our experts’ 2026 holiday wish lists

To use these widgets, long-press on an open space on your home screen. To customize your widgets, go to Settings > Wallpaper & style > More lock screen settings > Widgets on lock screen. To access your widgets, you just swipe left from your lock screen.

Out of the box, your Pixel 11’s display isn’t set to utilize its full capability. The Pixel 11 series comes with a fantastic low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) display, but it’s slightly throttled in the name of battery life. You’ll notice the increased resolution most on text and in fine details. It won’t make a huge difference to your streaming or large display elements, though. If you read consistently, either articles or e-books, you’ll want to make the change.

To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

If you’re anything like me, your phone usually needs a quick charge some evenings. The Pixel 11 series introduced Extreme Charging Mode, which accelerates charging by pausing background activity and non-essential apps. Google says the mode should charge the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro to over 50% in 30 minutes, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL to 75% in 30 minutes. From my testing, that estimate was pretty accurate.

Also: After testing the Pixel 11, I feel fine about skipping the Pro models

There are a few caveats: this feature is only available when your phone is at or below 50% battery, and you do need to turn it on every time you use it. But after the first time you do it, it’s available in your quick settings. Head to Settings > Battery & charging > Extreme Charging to turn it on the first time.

If you have the newest Pixel, you might as well take advantage of one of its biggest selling points. I felt like this feature was gimmicky at first (and I’m still a little grumpy it replaced my beloved thermometer), but the more I use it, the more I like it. The multicolor LED on the phone’s rear camera bump can indicate who’s calling, serve as a status indicator for Gemini, and more — and it’s almost certain that more usability will arrive over time.

Where I found the most use was when I had my phone on silent. After assigning specific colors to contacts (you can do this from the contact information screen), I could easily see whether a call was worth picking up without reaching for my phone.

To make sure you’re getting the most out of your new device, head in and change your contact HiLight colors right away. It only takes a few seconds and makes deciding whether to answer a call a lot easier.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

Also: Google’s big flagship is more Pro than ever

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.
