#3149. GCM Grosvenor (GCMG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fee-related earnings climbed as infrastructure and absolute return platforms scaled.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

GCM Grosvenor Inc. (GCMG +6.24%) reported growth across its alternative asset management platform, primarily driven by double-digit increases in fee-paying assets and fee-related earnings. Management highlighted the scalability of its infrastructure and credit verticals, noting that specialized funds and customized separate accounts continue to serve as primary fundraising engines. The company achieved a higher fee-related earnings margin of 47%, reflecting technology-driven efficiencies and stable operating expenses. Strategic expansion into the insurance and individual investor channels has diversified the client base, with 30% of year-to-date fundraising originating from new relationships.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the GCM Grosvenor Third Quarter 2026 Results Webcast. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this call will be recorded. And I would now like to hand the call over to Stacie Selinger, Head of Investor Relations. You may begin.

Stacie Selinger: Thank you. Welcome to GCM Grosvenor's Third Quarter Call. Today, I am joined by GCM Grosvenor's Chairman and CEO, Michael Sacks; President, Jon Levin; and Chief Financial Officer, Pam Bentley. As a reminder, all statements made on this call that do not relate to matters of historical facts should be considered forward-looking statements. This includes statements regarding our current expectations for the business, our financial performance and projections. These statements are neither promises, nor guarantees and involve risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to the Risk Factors section in our filings for additional information. We will also refer to non-GAAP measures that are important in assessing our business.

Reconciliations to the nearest GAAP measures are available in our earnings presentation and supplement on our website. With that, I will turn the call over to Michael.

Michael Sacks: Thanks, Stacie. We are pleased to report another strong quarter for GCM Grosvenor. Our assets under management of $98 billion is up 13% year-over-year, and our fee-paying assets under management of $78 billion is up 11% year-over-year. Compared to the third quarter of last year, fee-related revenue grew 10%, fee-related earnings grew 15% and adjusted net income grew 20%. We raised $2.7 billion this quarter and $10 billion over the last 12 months.

Our fundraising was supported by 2 complementary growth engines: the first is our customized separate account business where high client retention, recurring re-ups and expansion into new strategies provide a consistent source of fundraising; the second is our growing specialized fund franchises, where we typically have 5 to 10 funds in market at any given time. We held several fund closings this quarter and looking ahead to 2027, we see meaningful fundraising opportunities across both separate accounts and specialized funds. Importantly, 30% of our year-to-date fundraising has come from new clients. As we illustrated at our Investor Day, our investor relationships are sticky and grow over time.

That dynamic, combined with our contracted not yet fee-paying AUM balance of $10.6 billion bodes well for future growth. Our fundraising pipeline is full with our near-term pipeline 20% larger than it was a year ago. We remain confident that second half fundraising will exceed first half fundraising and believe full year fundraising for 2026 will rival full year fundraising for 2025. With regard to investment performance, we believe we are well positioned to navigate an unsettled market environment, which is notable for high volatility, interest rate fluctuation and technological disruption.

Our fundamental diversification across investment strategies and within those investment strategies by asset class, geography, industry and investment style, benefits our clients and provides a stable growing firm for shareholders. Our absolute return strategies business is a good illustration of this. Our multi-strategy composite was down 2% in the third quarter on a gross basis, influenced in part by the movement in SpaceX. However, ARS has enjoyed excellent year-to-date and recent results with composite gross returns of 13% year-to-date, nearly 19% over the past year and 15% annualized over 3 years through September. Despite a tough October for hedge funds, our highly diversified approach continues to add value for clients and our ARS vertical continues to experience net capital inflows.

ARS fee-paying AUM was $28 billion at quarter end, up 18% year-over-year and an 11% compound annual growth rate since the end of 2023. ARS net flows have been positive for the last 4 consecutive quarters, and we expect positive inflows in the fourth quarter of this year. Our ARS pipeline is the strongest it has been in recent memory. Our accrued unrealized performance fees from ARS portfolios stood at $49 million at the end of October. In private markets, we've delivered for our clients with positive performance for every strategy and sub strategy over the last year. We have talked about how infrastructure and credit are firing on all cylinders, and that continues to play out.

In private equity, which generally has been the slowest of private market strategies across the industry, we see some promise as private equity represented approximately 1/4 of our fundraising over the last year. Private equity co-investment realizations are up approximately 50% by number of transactions and are also up nicely on a dollar basis in 2026. Within private markets broadly, we remain pleased with the quality of our investment activity and the opportunity set. Grosvenor continues to enjoy significant upside from incentive fees, particularly our unrealized carried interest balance. Unrealized carry at net asset value reached a new high of approximately $1.1 billion at quarter end.

Firm's share of unrealized carry at net asset value was $592 million, an increase of approximately $100 million from June 30. While realization timing cannot be predicted with accuracy, that balance represents strong embedded future earnings. The rapid pace of technological change is creating both opportunities and concerns across the market, particularly with regard to AI and the AI data center and power-related capital cycle. We've spoken for several quarters about why we believe our platform is well positioned in this environment, and we continue to hold that belief.

We spoke last quarter about our investment in SpaceX, which is a good example of our origination capabilities that resulted in the largest single investment gain in the history of the firm. We successfully monetized more than $500 million of that investment in the third quarter and firm-wide exposure was just north of $3 billion at the end of the quarter. Our emphasis on diversification in our infrastructure vertical, one of the fastest-growing areas of the firm, has enabled us to make good investments in digital infrastructure and power without taking lopsided risks in any particular sector.

As an example, when we look at our firm-wide AUM, data centers represent around 1% of our total AUM and 5% of infrastructure AUM. A substantial majority of that exposure relates to investments made more than 4 years ago. We remain confident in our Investor Day guidance, including with regard to 2028 adjusted net income and believe we have more upside than downside relative to that guidance. Our margins continue to grow and free cash flow generation can support stock buybacks or dividend increases in the future. We will continue to focus on delivering quality returns and service for our clients and growth in profits for shareholders. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Jon.

Jonathan Levin: Thank you, Michael. This quarter, I'm going to focus on investments we've made to create new sources of growth. We target opportunities where our investment capabilities and client relationships provide an advantage while maintaining financial discipline. There are several investments we've made over the past several years that highlight this approach. First, direct infrastructure. In 2018, we leveraged our established infrastructure platform and deep relationships in the multiemployer pension community to launch a direct investment strategy, leveraging our labor and government expertise to create a competitive advantage for infrastructure investing. Today, that strategy manages approximately $3 billion, contributing to our broader $20 billion infrastructure business, which has grown at a 24% annual rate since 2020.

It's a great example of building on existing strengths to create new growth opportunities, and we believe there's significant runway ahead for that business. Second, we've invested in credit for decades, but our recent growth reflects strategic decisions that we've made over the past several years. We integrated our public and private credit teams to leverage our full sourcing capabilities, expanded into small and emerging managers and strengthened our co-investment and secondaries expertise. In doing so, we positioned ourselves ahead of growing client demand for direct-oriented private credit strategies and greater portfolio diversification. The results speak for themselves. We've raised approximately $4 billion for credit over the last 2 years, nearly half in direct-oriented strategies.

We now manage approximately $2 billion in credit co-investments and recently closed our inaugural credit secondaries fund at $1.2 billion, including related vehicles. We believe these strategies are still in the early stages with meaningful growth potential ahead. We've taken a similar approach to expanding our distribution capabilities. In 2021, we launched a dedicated insurance solutions team and have since raised more than $4 billion through that channel. Insurance has contributed approximately 12% of our fundraising over the last 2 years despite representing just 5% of AUM. Today, we manage approximately $5 billion for 50 insurance clients, offering customized solutions through separate accounts, specialized funds and structured products, including 2 collateralized fund obligations.

Our ability to combine investment expertise with flexible structuring and delivery is a key differentiator. And again, we believe this is an area with significant opportunity for growth. Our individual investor channel provides another example of investing ahead of what we think is a long-term secular growth opportunity. While we've had success with wirehouses for over a decade, in recent years, we've invested in both distribution, such as with the launch of our Grove Lane joint venture, and in product. Since the start of 2020, we've raised nearly $5 billion from individual investors split evenly between ARS and private markets. Approximately $2 billion has come through wirehouses where we've built partnerships with most major platforms.

Our success has also been highly global. 41% of that capital was raised in the U.S., 36% in Europe and 23% in APAC. This channel will take time to scale, but momentum is building. We raised approximately $1.5 billion from individual investors so far this year or 23% of our fundraising and individual investor AUM has grown approximately 40% year-over-year to $5.3 billion. We're also investing deliberately in registered products and distribution, and we believe the opportunity remains very large relative to our current position. Combined with our recurring revenue base and scalable platform, our growth investments provide significant future upside and multiple paths to achieving our long-term objectives. And with that, I'll turn it over to Pam.

Pamela Bentley: Thanks, Jon. We are pleased with our third quarter results, which demonstrate continuing growth in recurring revenues and earnings across the platform. Private markets management fees were $66 million in the quarter, up 7% year-over-year. We continue to benefit from fundraising and the deployment of previously committed capital. Looking ahead, we expect fourth quarter private markets management fees to increase 7% to 9% as compared with the fourth quarter of '25. Absolute return strategies management fees were $47 million, up 19% year-over-year, driven by investment performance and positive flows. For the fourth quarter, we expect ARS management fees to increase in the mid-teens year-over-year. Taking these factors together, total fee-related revenue was $115 million for the quarter, up 10% year-over-year.

Turning to expenses. We continue to invest thoughtfully, while remaining focused on efficiency and operating leverage, and we are definitely seeing the benefits of optimizing technology. Third quarter FRE compensation and benefits remained relatively consistent from the prior quarter at $39 million. We expect fourth quarter FRE compensation and benefits to be approximately $1 million higher than the fourth quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP general and administrative and other expenses were $22 million in the third quarter, and we expect a consistent level of G&A expenses in the fourth quarter. Putting these elements together, fee-related earnings were approximately $54 million for the quarter, up 15% year-over-year, and our FRE margin expanded to 47% from 45% a year ago.

Adjusted net income was $45 million, up 20% and adjusted net income per share was $0.22, up 16% year-over-year. Turning to incentive fees. We realized approximately $25 million of gross incentive fees in the quarter, consisting of $23 million of carried interest and $2 million of performance fees. As of September 30, our gross unrealized carried interest balance was approximately $1.1 billion, with $592 million representing the firm share. As a reminder, private market valuations, including those relevant to the balance, are generally reflected on a 1-quarter lag. The majority of annual performance fees typically crystallize in the fourth quarter.

And as of the end of October, we had $49 million of accrued unrealized performance fees, driven by strong year-to-date performance in ARS. Actual fees will depend on investment performance and applicable fund terms through the relevant crystallization dates. Moving to capital allocation. Our balance sheet remains strong, and we continue to invest for growth, while returning capital to shareholders. Our Board has approved a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, and we ended the quarter with approximately $54 million remaining under our share repurchase authorization. We are pleased with the momentum in our business and our ability to deliver strong results, while continuing to invest in the platform. We are now happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our first question from Crispin Love with Piper Sandler.

Crispin Love: Just first on ARS, definitely a standout year so far, but just plenty of volatility in the last few weeks, rates, data center financing fears, the midterms. You did call out a tough October for hedge funds, and we've all seen the headlines. But just curious on your latest thoughts there and if you would expect a significant impact, whether it's from flows or performance kind of near term? Near term it looks pretty good based on your comments, but then it -- further as you look out to '27?

Michael Sacks: Yes. I think -- thanks, Crispin. It's Michael. I think that the picture today is a very good one. And I think you can look at our statements on ARS and almost view them as the most constructive statements that we've made. We're -- We are in a net inflow environment. We've experienced net inflows the last several quarters, and we were clear on the call, we see -- we'll have net inflows in Q4. In markets like this, hedge funds are a pretty good option. They have a lot of -- a diversified hedge fund portfolio has a lot of features that sort of naturally manage the volatility, naturally provide diversification.

And so there's a lot of good there in markets like this. And I think the sophisticated institutional investor base that we have, sees that, appreciates that, likes that. And the performance over any reasonable time period has been quite good for a while. There's been a lot of alpha there. And so we think we're in a constructive environment. And most importantly, we mentioned our pipeline, which is where we have the most short intermediate-term volatility, our pipeline is up a lot. So we're constructive there, even though we like our 3-year number of a 19% CAGR better than our 1-year number.

Crispin Love: Perfect. I appreciate that. And then your comments on fundraising on the call seem very positive kind of looking out. But drilling into that a little bit deeper, just specifically on the individual investor channel, can you just drill into that on fundraising and individual investor, the outlook over the near to intermediate term? It's definitely a growth area for you guys. So just curious on the outlook there?

Michael Sacks: Yes. Our outlook there remains -- so first, your interpretation of our comments on fundraising generally and our outlook is correct. And for us to say that we think the full year '26 can rival full year '25 is not an insignificant thing in terms of what that implies for Q4. It doesn't mean we get all the way there. But that's a pretty strong statement with regard to our expectations for Q4. The individual investor is -- offers a tremendous amount of opportunity and growth and -- for Grosvenor, for the whole industry, we've talked about that a lot.

We continue to raise there at a rate well in excess of what the individual investor represents in our total AUM. The rest of the firm is growing, so it's hard to flip those numbers, so to speak, but we continue to raise there at a very significant rate. I think it was 23% of our fundraising year-to-date, it's up 40% year-over-year. Our -- The AUM of the individual investors is up 40% year-over-year. And so we just think that space is going to continue to grow. And as we've talked about in the past, it grows through a number of different efforts, meaning product on shelf, but also meaning private label partnership, also meaning firm-level partnership.

So we have a lot of ways to win there, and we just look forward to continuing to build that out.

Operator: We will take our next question from Bill Katz with TD Cowen.

Ryan Langston: This is Ryan on for Bill. I was just wondering if we could expand on the commentary on the ARS pipeline? So is -- what's driving the growth, current clients increasing their allocations? Or is it also new clients signing on board? I know you called out that you're seeing good momentum there in the wealth channel as well.

Michael Sacks: Yes. So it's all of the above. We're winning new mandates from new clients. We're winning hedge fund mandates from existing clients. And we're seeing clients add capital -- existing clients add capital. So -- and that's not surprising. Typically, when these things happen, it's not like isolated particular channel. That's possible. But usually, there's just a market movement and hedge funds have delivered for a while. And again, the attraction is to some significant degree, just the inherent diversification, the inherent sort of shock absorbers inside the portfolios like these. And that combined with their recent performance makes it interesting.

Ryan Langston: Great. And also, if we could just stick on fundraising. On specialized funds, which funds drove the inflows in the quarter? And what's going to be -- what funds should we expect to be in the market next quarter and for next year, across which asset classes?

Michael Sacks: So we mentioned in the script that we have 5 or 10 funds in market at -- pretty much at all times. And so it's hard to sort of do -- each fund raised this much money in this period of time and is open until this period of time. I think that the growth of that business makes that a little more challenging to report out on and track and model. We do have, as we mentioned, a number of funds. From the beginning of the year, we've been seeing low catch-up fees this year. The funds in market are sort of freshly in market and/or don't have catch-up fees. So I don't expect that this year.

But next year we will have funds in market, that have been in market a little longer, that have catch-up fees or that are newly in market. So I think that next year, we -- a lot of funds in market where the momentum has started and we've had first closes and we're now moving on towards second closes, final closes, things like that. So we're anticipating, as we said, a good year for specialized fundraising next year.

Jonathan Levin: Just to give you a sense of it to put some further detail around it. For our private market specialized funds, if you look at it on a year-to-date basis, just to give you a little more sense than just 1 quarter, there was probably about 7 funds that contributed to the specialized fundraising. Some of the bigger ones I would call out would be our MAC fund. We are still in market with both, some direct infrastructure product as well as diverse infrastructure product. We're in market with secondaries product. And obviously, you have your evergreen funds like your Interval fund for infrastructure.

And then at all times, you have various evergreen products available in the ARS business as well. So it's pretty broadly diversified, to Michael's point. I would expect, as Michael said, like that will kind of be the story going forward as well, where there will be many different drivers of that number. And what we will always endeavor to do is to make sure that you all understand which of those funds are relevant from a catch-up fee perspective and the timing around that so that we can make sure people can understand that from a modeling perspective.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our next question from Ken Worthington with JPMorgan.

Kenneth Worthington: When we look at CNYFPAUM, $8.7 billion will become fee-paying as invested. Over what period is that $8.7 billion likely to be invested? And is that investment likely to be even over the term or more front-end or back-end loaded?

Michael Sacks: I think, Ken, a conservative way -- it's Michael, by the way. Thanks for the question. I think a conservative way for you to think about it is 3 years, maybe that equal weighted. The reality is, I think it probably is a little bit more front-end weighted. But I just think if you're modeling it, that, that's kind of a conservative way to think about it. It doesn't mean it couldn't stretch a little longer than that. But I think that's where I would -- how I would suggest you model it on a base case.

Kenneth Worthington: Great. And then you mentioned catch-up fees earlier and kind of highlighted that we still shouldn't expect much for catch-up fees in 4Q. As we're thinking about these funds being more tenured in 2027, is there a past year that 2027 might look like from a catch-up fee perspective that we can get a rough idea of what to expect for next year?

Michael Sacks: I think it's hard to pick out like a given -- a particular year, and we are not prepared today to give sort of guidance on that. But we will keep our eye on that and probably talk about that a little bit more next quarter.

Operator: We will take our next question from Jeff Schmitt with William Blair.

Jeffrey Schmitt: The -- On the SpaceX realizations, how much occurred in private markets funds that were already in a positive carry position? And can you help us think about how those realizations should translate into carried interest in Q4 and then the outlook for additional realizations from here?

Michael Sacks: Yes. I think the best way to answer that is -- and Jon, Pam can jump in and help me. But I think the best way to answer that is that the carry revenue that we've seen thus far is not significantly attributable to -- in private markets, it's not significantly attributable to SpaceX. When you start talking about in-carry position, you start to -- and by the way, first, it's hard to ever say anything is directly attributable to something unless you are both in carry position, which a lot of our funds are, but you're also through your waterfall on DPI where you're sharing in the carry, right?

So there's being in carry position and obviously, with a close to $600 million firm share of carry it in NAV, which is the amount of money that would come to the firm if everything were liquidated as of the last quarter. We're clearly in carry position in a lot of places, and that grew by $100 million in the quarter, and some of that is the SpaceX mark, and it's great. But you have to look at the fund level -- so you're in carry position, but where are you in the waterfall? And that's an equally important question as to being in carry position.

And so I think we still have our very best days ahead of us in terms of revenue -- realized revenue from carry. And I think that $600 million, $590 million firm share of carry is your biggest and best indicator there. We have sold, as we mentioned, SpaceX in Q3. We're continuing to sell SpaceX in Q4, and that is -- it has contributed to carry -- has or will contribute to performance fees based on marks. And it's obviously just an overall positive for the firm.

Jeffrey Schmitt: Okay. Great. And then the insurance, it continues to be a strong fundraising channel for you. And just given the scrutiny around private credit right now, have you seen any change in insurance company demand or a shift in their allocations toward infrastructure secondaries or other strategies?

Jonathan Levin: No, I think -- this is Jon. Thanks for the question. I think in general, we view the insurance opportunity in a similar manner to the individual investor opportunity in which you'll have, I'm sure, bumps along the road, whether it's private credit or whatever the concerns of the day might be, but you have a secular trend of a current asset allocation towards alternatives that is lower than what the target asset allocation towards alternatives is. And I think that, that will be a very strong driver of opportunity for us for a while.

And what I would say about the specific question on private credit, and we've talked about this on some of our previous calls, our goal with everything that we do, and I think it's particularly important in credit investing generally, is to provide diversified open architecture, broad solutions that's diversified on every kind of metric in terms of the different food groups within private credit, sponsor lending, asset finance, geography, size, all of those metrics that are very, very important. Also diversification with respect to implementation, fund investing, co-investing, secondary investing.

And so we closed -- when we closed our inaugural private credit secondaries fund, one of the big drivers of capital formation for that fund was insurance companies looking to create a diversified solution with some J-curve mitigation, with some return options, optionality to the upside relative to kind of a traditional implementation style. So will everything always be linear? No. Will there be different challenges that come along the way? Sure. But for us, we see that as still a great growth opportunity. And importantly, I think we see the way in which we can provide solutions to insurance companies gives us an advantage when you have dislocations or concerns, whatever the word might be in the market environment.

Operator: We will take our next question from Chris Kotowski with Oppenheimer.

Christoph Kotowski: I just noticed, like your customized separate accounts were still up growing like nicely double digits, like 11% or more. And a number of your peers, that has slowed down, in some cases down to the kind of low single digits as they say more institutions are going for the kind of evergreen fund structure. And I know you have a couple in the market, but I'm wondering, do you see that demand on the institutional side for the evergreen fund structures and maybe is there the demand there? And is it less of a heavy lift than doing the retail route for the evergreen fund structures?

Jonathan Levin: I'm happy to... Go ahead, Michael.

Michael Sacks: I'm going to take it, Jon, and then ask you to kind of finish up. What I will say is the wealth channel, the individual investor channels dominated by evergreen or open-end structures. The institutional channel is not. There has always been, and it is a kind of constant conversation, some debate between closed-end structure or evergreen structure. I think that -- and then the market has historically been dominated by closed-end. Solutions and custom separate accounts are a bit of a hybrid, and the clients are, I think, coming around very clearly to liking those custom separate accounts and liking a solutions approach.

It seems a lot of providers -- that everybody kind of wants to be a solutions company these days -- a solutions provider these days. And so our pipeline is full with no shift in the mix of what we provide, which is both Evergreen and closed-end and custom separate account solutions. And it is a -- the pipeline is full. There is demand, and we see plenty of growth, as we kind of pointed to in our comments. So I don't think there's a, like a real preference there or anything that I would call a market shift or materially easier to raise money institutionally in one place or the other or any change in that.

I think that has been a conversation for a while, and it almost comes down to preference of a particular investor or preference of a particular consultant.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the conference back to Ms. Selinger for any additional or closing remarks.

Stacie Selinger: Thank you very much for everyone who joined us this morning. We appreciate the questions and the engagement. If you do have follow-ups, very happy to take them offline. And otherwise, we look forward to seeing you next quarter.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for participating in today's conference. This concludes today's program. We hope everyone has a great day. You may all disconnect.

#3146. 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Most HR professionals say they believe employees can be reskilled for AI jobs, yet companies still often seek outside hires. Here's why.

HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.

“Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn’t consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible.”

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

Also: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.

Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

Also: Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

#3145. Affiliated Managers (AMG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record alternatives inflows and buybacks fueled a strong quarter for the manager.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Affiliated Managers Group, Inc. (AMG +5.56%) reported record quarterly results as the company continued its strategic evolution toward alternative investment strategies. Management reported that assets under management reached an all-time high, supported by record inflows into alternatives and strong investment performance. The company stated that alternatives now account for approximately two-thirds of EBITDA on a run-rate basis, up from approximately one-third seven years ago. Management indicated that its business model generates significant unencumbered cash flow, which the company intends to deploy toward new affiliate investments, supporting existing affiliates, and share repurchases. CFO Dava Ritchea noted that organic growth in the alternatives segment was driven by four specific secular trends: secondaries, infrastructure, absolute return, and tax-aware strategies.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the AMG Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I'd now like to turn the call over to your host, Patricia Figueroa, Head of Investor Relations for AMG. Thank you. You may begin.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that during this call, we may make a number of forward-looking statements, which could differ from our actual results materially due to a number of factors, including those described in today's earnings press release and our most recent Form 10-K and subsequent filings with the SEC. AMG assumes no obligation to update these statements. Also, please note that nothing on this call constitutes an offer of any products, investment vehicles or services of any AMG affiliate.

A replay of today's call will be available on the Investor Relations section of our website, along with a copy of our earnings release and reconciliations of any non-GAAP financial measures, including any earnings guidance provided. In addition, we have posted an updated investor presentation to our website and encourage investors to consult our site regularly for updated information. With us today to discuss the company's results for the quarter are Jay Horgen, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Dava Ritchea, Chief Financial Officer. Jay Horgen: Thanks, Patricia, and good morning, everyone. Today, AMG reported another quarter of record results. AUM, aggregate fees, fee-related earnings, adjusted EBITDA, economic earnings per share and organic flows into alternatives were all at record levels in the third quarter. On a year-to-date basis, AMG generated nearly $1 billion in adjusted EBITDA and $26 in economic earnings per share, representing growth of 41% and 56% year-over-year, respectively.

To put these impressive results in perspective, in just 3 quarters, our business generated economic earnings per share roughly equivalent to what we delivered in all of 2025, and nearly 95% of that was driven by fee-related earnings. AMG also delivered its sixth consecutive quarter of net inflows. With $21 billion in net inflows in the quarter and $85 billion over the last 18 months, our business continues to generate strong organic growth. And these results understate the exceptional momentum in higher fee, higher-margin alternative strategies, which attracted more than $31 billion in net inflows in the quarter and $150 billion over the past 6 quarters.

Assets under management increased to a record $974 billion, driven by our affiliates' growth through both net inflows and investment performance, setting the stage for ongoing earnings growth momentum in the fourth quarter and into next year. And given AMG's significant growth, our increasingly attractive alternatives profile and the compelling valuation of our shares, we stepped up our repurchases meaningfully, deploying $400 million in the quarter and bringing our year-to-date total share repurchases to $775 million. The momentum across our business is a direct result of the successful execution of our strategy to evolve our earnings profile towards alternatives.

After nearly 20 years at AMG, I am very proud of our team's many accomplishments, but the one that stands out the most is the transformational impact of the strategic shift towards alternatives that we embarked on in 2019. In just 7 years, we will have evolved from generating less than 35% of our earnings from alternative strategies to nearly 70%. It is a remarkable transformation, underscoring the power of disciplined and deliberate capital allocation and the advantages of our unique business model, particularly our strong cash flow generation and our ability to redeploy that cash to areas of secular growth.

Today, AMG's earnings profile is that of a diversified alternatives business across private markets and liquid alternatives, characterized by high growth, high fee, high margin and long-duration assets. As we have discussed over recent quarters, 4 secular trends continue to drive our organic growth profile. First, the accelerating client demand worldwide for secondary strategies across private markets. Second, the ongoing client demand for infrastructure strategies broadly. Third, the growing appetite for absolute return strategies within client portfolios; and fourth, the continued expansion of tax-aware investing.

Together, these 4 growth areas, secondary solutions, infrastructure, absolute return strategies and tax-aware strategies contributed to our record alternative inflows in the quarter and have been the driving force behind the $150 billion in net inflows into our affiliates' alternative strategies over the past 6 quarters. Our affiliates' performance across private markets and liquid alternatives has been outstanding. And with clients increasingly seeking differentiated sources of return and diversification against the backdrop of a more complex market environment, we have high conviction that these strategies can be a powerful growth driver for years to come.

More broadly, over the last 12 months, our assets under management have increased by approximately $170 billion or 21%, including $69 billion as a result of new affiliate investments. Following an active first half, including the completion of our investments in BBH Credit Partners, HighBrook Investors and an incremental minority investment in Garda Capital Partners, our investment pipeline remains strong. We are excited to execute on our opportunity set and form additional new partnerships that further diversify our business and drive additional earnings growth. AMG is a strategic partner that can magnify the competitive advantages of partner-owned firms while preserving the very thing that makes them so special, their independence.

No other institutional partner can match our 3-decade track record in meeting the needs of and magnifying the opportunities for independent firms, which is why AMG's unique partnership approach continues to strongly resonate with prospective affiliates. And given our competitive differentiation, our robust capital position and our pipeline of new prospects, we have a sizable opportunity to drive additional earnings growth and further evolve our business profile by forming new partnerships as well as investing in and alongside our existing affiliates. AMG's business is highly diversified across nearly 40 affiliates operating in private markets, liquid alternatives and differentiated long-only strategies.

This unique business profile generates significant unencumbered cash flow, enabling us to navigate periods of uncertainty and changing market conditions while also making accretive investments in new and existing affiliates. In addition, given our forward growth prospects and the strength of our capital position, we have been a buyer of AMG shares in size, repurchasing approximately 2.3 million shares or 9% of the shares outstanding through the third quarter and 30% since the beginning of 2024. And we expect to continue to take advantage of this truly unique opportunity to invest in industry-leading growth through a diversified alternatives business at an extremely attractive price. That is, we will continue to invest in AMG itself.

Our alternatives profile and our ability to invest substantial capital in the areas of highest growth and return across new and existing affiliates and in our own shares provides us with the opportunity to continue to generate a long-term compound annual growth rate in economic earnings per share between 15% and 20% as we have done over the past 5 years. And given the ongoing successful execution of our strategy, that growth rate has accelerated. In 2025, we generated growth in economic earnings per share of more than 20%, and we expect that growth rate to more than double to approximately 50% in 2026.

As we look ahead, our capital allocation decision-making will continue to be by far the most impactful element of our strategy. We expect our cumulative free cash flow over the next 5 to 7 years to approximate our entire current market capitalization enabling us to continue to strategically evolve AMG's business towards areas of growth in our industry. And with our unique partnership-centric cash-generative, return-focused model, we will continue to deploy that capital with discipline, further diversifying and enhancing our earnings power and our ability to create long-term value for our shareholders. And with that, I'll turn it over to Dava.

Dava Ritchea: Thank you, Jay, and good morning, everyone. Our affiliates now manage $338 billion in liquid alternatives, and together with private markets, our alternative affiliates manage approximately $500 billion and contribute approximately 2/3 of our EBITDA on a run rate basis. In aggregate, our third quarter flows further increased the earnings and organic growth contribution from alternatives. Adjusted EBITDA was $354 million, an increase of 41% year-over-year. Underlying fee-related earnings increased 35%, driven by organic growth, investment performance and margin expansion at certain affiliates. Economic earnings per share grew 56% year-over-year to a quarterly record of $9.50, reflecting higher adjusted EBITDA and the benefit of our ongoing share repurchase activity, which has reduced our average economic share count by approximately 11% compared to the prior year period. Our third quarter results build on strong performance in the first half of the year.

For the first 9 months of 2026, adjusted EBITDA grew 41% year-over-year to $987 million, reflecting organic growth, investment performance, margin expansion at certain affiliates and contributions from recent new investments. Economic earnings per share grew 56% year-over-year to $26, further benefiting from share repurchases. Now moving to fourth quarter guidance. This includes recurring fee-related earnings of $335 million to $345 million, up from $325 million in Q3. Our outlook assumes no material private market catch-up fees.

So maybe now I'll turn it to Dava to talk a little bit more about how we're experiencing and what we're experiencing.

Dava Ritchea: Thanks, Jay. And I think that let me just echo a couple of the points that Jay made because they're really starting the foundation of what we have seen as the shift in our business towards alternatives and how that impacts the bottom line EBITDA. So that first shift really coming from moving the alternatives business from about 35% of EBITDA to 70% over time. And that has led to what we believe to be much more durable long-term organic growth trends. The second as Jay mentioned was in many of our alt businesses and particularly some of our largest, we own that underlying margin. And so as our affiliates grow their businesses, we are experiencing that margin expansion.

The third point is, as we're growing in alternatives, it is shifting the business towards higher management fee products, which leads to a higher management fee contribution to EBITDA. These tend to also be in longer locked strategies. And in some cases, they also have future performance fee and longer-dated carry potential. So all of those factors combined are what's driving that overall margin growth rate to be about 2x what we're seeing in our organic flow rate.

You’re not crazy for thinking, “Hasn’t Disney already done AI stuff?” after reading my headline.

In December of last year, the global mass media and entertainment corporation announced a partnership with OpenAI that would let users play around with Sora’s generative AI features to generate short-form videos and images. Those pieces of content were set to incorporate over 200 characters from Disney, Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars. However, that deal ended a lot faster than everyone anticipated when it was called off in March of this year.

Even with that development, Disney isn’t done trying its hand at injecting AI into its everyday operations. Now they’re working alongside Adobe in a newly announced multiyear partnership that’s set to expand Disney’s usage of AI tools.

Here’s how that new collaboration will alter Disney’s creative ventures and businesses.

In an official press release released by Adobe, the multinational computer software company announced the strategic alliance it has now entered into with The Walt Disney Company.

In a bid to “advance creativity, innovation and the art of storytelling through new technologies and experiences,” both companies will use the Adobe Firefly Foundry proprietary AI model to develop models that are specifically tailored to Disney’s animated characters, environments and visual styles.

Both companies promise that those custom models will be trained on those three previously mentioned aspects of Disney, while still generating commercially safe and production-ready outputs that should speed up animators’ workflows and allow for the expanded development of more creative endeavors.

Walt Disney Imagineering Research & Development, which is largely responsible for working on the company’s theme park development, is already using Adobe Firefly Foundry. Their efforts are geared towards using a sketch-to-image model that transforms hand-drawn ideas into fully rendered 2D concept art. They’ve also begun using a custom image model that produces the sort of assets that are on-brand and consistent with Disney franchises.

Adobe and Disney’s AI-themed joint efforts will also affect StudioLAB (Disney’s innovation and technology hub, located in Burbank, California) and the ESPN Edge Innovation Center. Adobe has become a StudioLAB Innovation Partner and will work with its creatives and technologists to observe and expand internal creative workflows. On the sports side of the equation, Adobe and ESPN will work side by side to find the best ways to use AI to enhance fan engagement, how they deliver content and to utilize more of ESPN’s archival content.

In the midst of this announcement comes some less-than-inspiring news, however. More layoffs are reportedly coming at Disney, with some areas aiming to cut costs by up to 20% in the process. These expected layoffs may impact Disney theme parks, Disney Cruise Line, movie studios, television, and technology, but not all evenly.

What makes this latest round of Disney job cuts especially disheartening is the fact that it will be the fifth round of layoffs since Josh D’Amaro took over as the company’s CEO after replacing Bob Iger in March. Those previous layoffs have targeted Disney’s marketing, National Geographic, Pixar, ESPN, technology, human resources/relations and Walt Disney Imagineering departments.

Disney is going big again on AI and looking to expand the technology’s role in improving different portions of its creative business. With a focus on empowering the use of internal creative tools and experimenting with new AI technologies that could benefit them down the line, Disney sounds like it’s planning to stay in this partnership a lot longer than it did with the one with OpenAI. But with even more layoffs looming, it’s hard to get all the excited about the news of Disney tapping into more AI while letting go of the humans that help keep its myriad core businesses running smoothly.

#3143. Uber Parking Lets You Book a Spot Directly in the App. Here’s How

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The new feature is launching in 15 cities before expanding across the US and Canada. It follows Uber's acquisition of SpotHero earlier this year.

Uber is adding a parking reservation option directly within its app.

The rollout of Uber Parking, announced on Monday, comes after the ride-hailing platform’s acquisition of SpotHero earlier this year. Now, you can reserve a parking spot from the Uber app homepage, alongside existing options to book a ride, rent a car or order a meal.

Uber says its acquisition of SpotHero is bringing more than 13,000 garages, lots and valet options across more than 400 cities onto Uber’s platform. The SpotHero brand and app won’t go away, though customers might see branding for SpotHero by Uber on garage signage, for example.

At launch, Uber Parking is available in 15 cities, including Chicago, Nashville, San Francisco, Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, Seattle and Washington, DC.

“Our mission is to help people get around, and this seemed like a very natural thing for us to solve, given how painful parking is today,” Amit Fulay, vice president of product at Uber, said in an interview. “If we can bring that ease that we have for rides into the app, it fits with helping people move. It felt like a very natural extension.”

Uber One members will get 10% back in credits on eligible completed parking reservations, which they can use on future rides and Uber Eats orders. (Uber One costs $10 per month.)

To reserve a spot with Uber Parking, open the Uber app and tap the new Parking icon on the home screen. Enter your destination, and choose a date and time. You’ll then be able to see available nearby parking options via an interactive map, which will show pricing upfront.

You can filter for options like self-parking or valet, as well as a garage or surface lot. You can also select amenities such as on-site staff or re-entry capability.

Fill out your vehicle information, including make, model and license plate number. As with booking a ride, you’ll be able to pay using a payment method in your Uber Wallet.

You’ll then be able to access your “Parking pass” in the Uber app. Depending on where you park, you’ll either scan a QR code or use license plate recognition to get in. You can extend your reservation in the app if you end up staying longer than expected.

Uber says that with most parking options, you can cancel your booking for free before the start time.

Over the coming weeks and months, Uber Parking will expand from 15 launch cities to over 400 across the US and Canada, according to the company.

Uber Parking is the latest example of how the ride-hailing company aims to be known for much more than just that. Uber now has options for everything from car and bike rentals to hotel reservations to food delivery through Uber Eats. The addition of Uber Parking gives people another reason to open the app and, importantly, give more of their dollars to Uber.

The Uber One subscription service is another way the company has worked to entice customers. It includes no delivery fee on food and grocery orders, 5% back on rides and 10% back on hotel bookings, among other perks. Uber says it has over 55 million Uber One members across 47 countries.

Uber’s new parking venture feeds into another area the company is heavily investing in: autonomous vehicles. With more than 30 AV partners, Uber says it plans to “explore leveraging parking spots as staging and waiting locations for AVs, which can reduce deadheading, congestion and vehicle wear while improving fleet efficiency.”

Fulay notes that this network can also be useful for delivery drivers working in areas where parking is difficult to find, or for those with downtime who need a convenient place to stop for a while in dense urban areas.

“Once we have this infrastructure, those are the next set of things we’ll look to explore,” Fulay said.

Ultimately, offering a service within an app consumers likely already have on their phones could make them more inclined to stick with a single company. Uber appears to be betting on just that.

#3142. Apple will monitor your public iCloud links now, starting with iOS 27.3

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Under Apple's new policy, the company will scan publicly shared iCloud links for harmful content - and possibly ban violators.

Be careful what you share in your iCloud. Apple announced it will start monitoring public iCloud links for harmful content — and potentially disable accounts that violate company policy.

Also: How to free up your iPhone storage almost immediately

The change comes with the impending release of Apple’s 27.3 build across its operating systems. If an iCloud user selects “Anyone with the link” when sharing something in a group chat or Discord server, it’s considered a public link; Apple is within its rights to scan for anything that violates company policy or is potentially illegal.

If you try to upload harmful content, Apple says it reserves the right to “move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” your content at any time. Furthermore, Apple outlines possible actions it may take, including:

Apple’s announcement did not explain what “harmful content” would mean in practice. While there are obvious violations like drug sales and child sex abuse material, the new policy’s vagueness is concerning.

Once an iCloud link is shared under the “Anyone with a link” designation, end-to-end encryption is removed, even if either party has enabled Advanced Data Protection, which allows Apple to view the link’s content.

If you select “People you choose,” which limits access to users who have been invited or approved, the encryption remains in place, and Apple won’t be able to see what you’re sharing.

The new policy does not lay out an appeals process if you think your account or content has been falsely flagged as harmful. However, Apple does have a web page that provides information on how to appeal for other reasons. So there is a framework in place to push back if you think you’ve been caught in the dragnet by accident.
