#3141. Ionis (IONS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Launch ramp slows and cash flow breakeven shifts a year to 2029.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (IONS -21.36%) is managing multiple commercial launches while navigating pipeline setbacks and updated sales forecasts. Management reported total revenue of $243 million for the third quarter, a 55% increase year over year when excluding a prior-year onetime payment. The company reduced its full-year TRYNGOLZA net product sales target to approximately $50 million due to a more gradual launch ramp but reaffirmed its total revenue range based on strength in the DAWNZERA franchise and partnership milestones. Recent clinical milestones included approvals for ZANVASTRO and HIBSAGO along with positive Phase 3 readouts for sefaxersen and ulefnersen. Management extended the projected timeline for sustained positive cash flow by one year to 2029, citing the impact of the TRYNGOLZA ramp and setbacks in two late-stage neurology and cardiovascular programs.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to Ionis' Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. As a reminder, today's event is being recorded. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Wade Walke, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations, to lead off the call. Please begin.

D. Walke: Thank you, Chris. Before we begin, I encourage everyone to go to the Investors section of the Ionis website to view the press release and related financial tables we will be discussing today, including a reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP financials. We believe non-GAAP financial results better represent the economics of our business and how we manage our business. We've also posted slides on our website that accompany today's call. With me this morning are Brett Monia, Chief Executive Officer; Kyle Jenne, Chief Global Product Strategy Officer; Holly Kordasiewicz, Chief Development Officer; and Beth Hougen, Chief Financial Officer. I would like to draw your attention to Slide 3, which contains our forward-looking language statement.

During this call, we will be making forward-looking statements that are based on our current expectations and beliefs. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties, and our actual results may differ materially. As a result, you are cautioned not to rely on these forward-looking statements. I encourage you to consult the risk factors contained in our SEC filings for additional detail. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Brett.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Wade. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on today's call. Through the first 3 quarters of 2026, Ionis has continued to evolve and grow as a commercial stage biotechnology company, achieving numerous important milestones. In addition to TRYNGOLZA for FCS and DAWNZERA for HAE, our Ionis-owned commercial portfolio now includes TRYNGOLZA for severe hypertriglyceridemia or sHTG, our first launch in a large patient population and ZANVASTRO, our first independent launch in neurology. Although 2 recent Phase III readouts did not deliver the outcomes we hoped for, we have achieved a number of other important firsts for patients across our business that position us for further growth.

This includes the approval of HIBSAGO for chronic hepatitis B virus in the U.S. and Japan and positive Phase III results for Sefaxersen in IgA nephropathy and ulefnersen in FUS-ALS. Our substantial progress keeps us on track to achieve our full year 2026 total revenue, operating loss and cash guidance, and DAWNZERA's continued positive momentum supports our confidence in achieving its 2026 product sales guidance. For TRYNGOLZA, we are lowering our 2026 full year revenue guidance to approximately $50 million to reflect a more gradual launch ramp than we had anticipated.

As the first and only treatment approved to reduce triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis in people living with sHTG, TRYNGOLZA requires HCPs to adopt a new approach to patient care, which takes time. In these early days, we are encouraged by the fundamentals underlying the launch, including strong physician enthusiasm. We are refining our launch tactics to translate this enthusiasm into action. We've identified key executional priorities and implemented specific initiatives across these priorities, which Kyle will discuss in detail. Importantly, we remain confident in TRYNGOLZA's multibillion-dollar peak sales potential. Beyond TRYNGOLZA, Kyle will provide further perspective on DAWNZERA and share initial insights on ZANVASTRO.

Holly will then go over our recent pipeline progress, and Beth will review our third quarter results and outlook for the rest of 2026. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Kyle.

Kyle Jenne: Thank you, Brett. I'd like to start by recognizing our highly engaged commercial team for their dedication to bringing important medicines to patients. Their deep expertise, strong commitment to each of our launches and clear priorities to expand physician adoption and help patients access treatment gives us confidence in our ability to drive growth across our commercial portfolio. Following TRYNGOLZA's June approval for sHTG, HCPs continue to express strong enthusiasm for TRYNGOLZA's compelling clinical profile, including placebo-adjusted mean reductions in triglycerides of up to 72% and a favorable safety and tolerability profile. These triglyceride reductions resulted in a profound reduction in acute pancreatitis events by up to 91%.

Physicians also appreciate the dosing flexibility and are prescribing both the 50- and 80-milligram doses, allowing them to tailor treatment to individual patient needs. For patients, TRYNGOLZA offers the convenience of a once-monthly auto-injector that can be self-administered in about 10 seconds. We are seeing HCPs prescribe TRYNGOLZA for high-risk sHTG patients who are the focus of our initial commercial efforts. These are patients with triglyceride levels of 880 milligrams per deciliter or higher or 500 or higher with a history of acute pancreatitis or other comorbidities. We are also seeing prescribing beyond our initial focus, consistent with the broad sHTG label. Our post-launch market research reinforces HCP's strong intent to prescribe TRYNGOLZA.

As we establish a new treatment paradigm, we are focused on translating the strong intent to prescribe into action with 3 executional priorities designed to increase prescribing and help patients move efficiently from prescription to treatment. First, we are focused on broadening the prescriber base, specifically among high-priority physicians who care for high-risk sHTG patients. We are accelerating our education efforts across these specialists and practice teams to increase their understanding of the burden of sHTG, the risk of acute pancreatitis and TRYNGOLZA's demonstrated ability to reduce that risk.

In parallel, we are supporting patient education through HCP conversations with their patients and patient support programs so that people living with sHTG better understand their disease, the importance of treatment and the role TRYNGOLZA can play in reducing triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis. Our field teams are meeting more frequently with high-priority HCPs who have not yet prescribed to instill a sense of urgency in patient identification and treatment. The goal is to help physicians incorporate TRYNGOLZA into routine care for appropriate patients. From sHTG approval to the end of September, approximately 1,500 prescribers across all anticipated specialties had prescribed TRYNGOLZA.

In the weeks since our field team put these initiatives into action, our initial prescriber base has started to broaden further. Second, we are focused on increasing the depth of prescribing among HCPs who are early adopters of TRYNGOLZA. Since the sHTG launch through the end of September, approximately 24% of prescribers had written more than one prescription. Prescribers want to see how a patient responds to treatment before prescribing more broadly, consistent with how HCPs often adopt new specialty medicines. We saw a similar pattern when we launched in FCS, where physicians became more confident prescribing TRYNGOLZA as they gained experience and observed its impact.

While the sHTG population is much broader, our FCS experience gives us confidence that TRYNGOLZA's novel mechanism of action and groundbreaking patient outcomes can support broader prescribing over time. Our field team is executing on this priority by following up with prescribers to discuss their initial treatment experience and support them in identifying additional patients who may benefit from TRYNGOLZA. Notably, we have seen recent increases in repeat prescribing, suggesting these efforts are starting to have an impact. Third, we are working to make the path from prescription to treatment more efficient. As expected at this early stage of the launch, a majority of TRYNGOLZA prescriptions required a medical exception.

Some physicians are hesitant to prescribe newly approved therapies broadly before formal coverage is in place, a pattern seen in other specialty launches, especially in the cardiovascular space. To address this, our dedicated access team is educating physician offices on the reimbursement process and payer requirements. Additionally, we have a Quick Start program that enables patients to begin TRYNGOLZA treatment while coverage is being secured. The program has been well received with meaningful utilization to date, and we expect it to continue to expand. Ionis Every Step, our patient support program, also helps eligible patients navigate the insurance process and access treatment. We are working with payers to establish coverage policies and are making good progress.

By the end of September, plans representing 33% of commercial lives had added the sHTG indication for TRYNGOLZA to their formularies. Importantly, all current policies provide coverage aligned with the broad TRYNGOLZA label for adults with triglyceride levels of 500 or higher, extending beyond the high-risk patients who represent our initial commercial focus. As payers review the reimbursement policies for TRYNGOLZA, we are on track for additional policies to take effect this year with more expected throughout 2027. As we address these early launch dynamics, we remain confident in TRYNGOLZA's potential to achieve more than $3 billion in peak annual sales. That confidence begins with the substantial unmet need.

More than 3 million people in the U.S. have sHTG, including approximately 1 million high-risk sHTG patients. TRYNGOLZA's efficacy, dosing flexibility and self-administered auto-injector provide a compelling profile for these patients. As we establish a new treatment paradigm and build the market, our priorities are clear: broaden and deepen prescribing and improve payer access to simplify the path to treatment. While we recognize it will take some time for these initiatives to deliver accelerating prescription volume, we are confident our actions position TRYNGOLZA for future growth. Outside the U.S., Sobi is continuing to advance the launch in FCS while preparing for the upcoming anticipated broader launch in sHTG following the recent positive CHMP opinion. Turning to DAWNZERA.

The launch continues to gain momentum with product sales increasing substantially each quarter since launch. DAWNZERA has continued to capture a meaningful share of the U.S. HAE prophylaxis market where adoption is largely driven by patients switching therapies. We are seeing a growing base of repeat prescribers alongside adoption by patients with different treatment histories. In addition to growth from patients switching from other prophylactic therapies, we have also seen patients initiate DAWNZERA treatment who were previously only using on-demand treatment or who were treatment-naive. Physician and patient feedback has been positive, highlighting DAWNZERA's strong efficacy and favorable safety, differentiated RNA-targeted mechanism and compelling switch data.

Its patient-friendly profile, including dosing every 4 or 8 weeks with a self-administered auto-injector, is also resonating with physicians and patients. DAWNZERA has been a key driver of commercial revenue growth through the third quarter. Its growing base of repeat prescribers and adoption across patients with different treatment histories give us confidence in continued growth ahead. Outside the U.S., DAWNZERA access has continued to expand through our partners. This progress includes the recent approval in Canada and advancement of the European launch with positive reimbursement decisions in multiple countries and additional market access activities underway. Turning to ZANVASTRO.

The recent approval provides children and adults with Alexander disease, the first FDA-approved disease-modifying treatment for this progressive and often fatal neurological disorder. As planned, we were able to get ZANVASTRO into the channel shortly after approval, and I'm pleased to share that the first patients have received commercial treatment. Our launch is centered on 4 priorities. First, we are working to transition patients receiving ZANVASTRO through the clinical study or expanded access program to commercial therapy while ensuring continuity of care. This will take time as patients await their next quarterly dose, institutions navigate reimbursement and some patients move to treatment centers closer to home.

Second, we are engaging physicians who care for patients already diagnosed with Alexander disease to provide education on ZANVASTRO and support access for appropriate patients. Although exact prevalence is not well understood, the U.S. prevalence is estimated to be approximately 300 people with about half identified through medical claims. Third, we are raising disease awareness to help identify additional undiagnosed patients. Our focus is on approximately 25 neurology centers, including 12 leukodystrophy centers of excellence with disease education extending to physicians outside this network. Fourth, we are working with payers and treatment centers to establish coverage and access. ZANVASTRO is administered quarterly by intrathecal injection and reimbursed as a medical benefit.

So providing education on the buy-and-bill process is an important part of our launch execution. Our Ionis Every Step program for ZANVASTRO is tailored to the Alexander disease community, providing education and assistance navigating the reimbursement process for patients and families and access and reimbursement support for health care providers and site staff. We expect uptake to increase as patients from our clinical studies and expanded access program transition to commercial treatment, additional patients are identified and access is established. Outside the U.S., Recordati is planning for regulatory filings in the EU and Japan next year with additional submissions to follow. Across our multiple ongoing launches, our priorities are clear.

Our team is focused, energized and committed to delivering on these priorities for patients. With that, I'll turn the call over to Holly.

Holly Kordasiewicz: Thanks, Kyle. This quarter, we made important progress across our wholly owned and partnered pipeline, advancing medicines with the potential to transform care for people with serious diseases. At the European Society of Cardiology Congress in August, we presented new data, reinforcing our leadership in the management of severe hypertriglyceridemia. This included positive long-term data for TRYNGOLZA, the first and only approved treatment to reduce triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis in adults with sHTG. In the CORE and CORE2 open-label extension study, TRYNGOLZA delivered substantial and sustained triglyceride reductions for up to 2 years of treatment. More than 90% of patients achieved levels below 500 mg/dL and nearly 60% achieved normal levels.

Patients also achieved persistent reductions in the risk of acute pancreatitis and the safety and tolerability profile remained favorable. These findings further strengthen TRYNGOLZA's clinical profile, reinforcing its durability and long-term safety profile, both of which are essential in treating a chronic disease like sHTG. Beyond sHTG, our leading neurology pipeline continues to make exceptional progress, highlighted by the recent approval of ZANVASTRO. ZANVASTRO is the first and only disease-modifying treatment for Alexander disease, an ultra-rare progressive and often fatal neurological disorder. We were pleased that the FDA approved ZANVASTRO with a broad label for children and adults. This approval builds on our long history of discovering and developing first-in-class treatments for rare neurological diseases.

Today, our leading neurology pipeline includes 7 wholly owned medicines targeting challenging diseases such as Dravet syndrome, prion disease, and Angelman syndrome. In light of the recent results from the ASPIRE study of apazunersen, I'll review obudanersen for Angelman syndrome and our design of the Phase III REVEAL study. Obudanersen is a product of Ionis chemistry and know-how in delivering breakthrough treatments for CNS diseases, experiences that led to SPINRAZA, QALSODY and ZANVASTRO, groundbreaking approved medicines for devastating neurological diseases. We are evaluating an 80-milligram dose in REVEAL, which was the maximal dose we evaluated in the Phase I/II HALOS open-label extension study.

Based on our data, we believe that the apazunersen dose in ASPIRE was not high enough to be efficacious. Equally important is our choice of endpoints. The primary endpoint in our REVEAL study is expressive communication, measured using the Bayley-4. We selected this endpoint because expressive communication remains stable in natural history data, but showed robust improvement with obudanersen treatment in HALOS. With up to 2 years of treatment data in HALOS, we continue to see durable improvement in expressive communication and other functional domains relative to natural history. We plan to publish an update of our long-term extension study soon and look forward to Phase III results in the second half of next year.

While our partner pipeline had 2 Phase III disappointments, it also delivered recent approvals and 2 positive Phase III readouts since our last update. HIBSAGO, partnered with GSK, was recently approved in the U.S. and Japan as the first-in-class treatment offering unprecedented functional curates in chronic hepatitis B, a disease affecting millions of people worldwide. Sefaxersen, partnered with Roche, met the primary endpoint in the interim analysis of the Phase III IMAgINATION study in adults with IgA nephropathy with favorable safety and tolerability consistent with prior data. Roche plans to share the data with health authorities with a potential U.S. approval next year.

We also announced positive Phase III FUSION top line results for ulefnersen, partnered with Otsuka in people with FUS-ALS, a rare and rapid progressive form of ALS that affects a broad age range. These results bring us closer to what could be the first disease-modifying treatment for FUS-ALS. Looking ahead, our pipeline offers multiple opportunities to build on our progress. Next year, in addition to the Phase III results for obudanersen, our growing mid-stage pipeline of wholly owned medicines are advancing to a proof-of-concept data readout that could enable us to further expand our late-stage pipeline. We also anticipate further regulatory progress that will expand the global reach of our marketed medicines.

This includes the planned launch of TRYNGOLZA for sHTG in the EU and the continued launch of HIBSAGO and potential approvals and launches for sefaxersen and ulefnersen next year. Our recent progress reinforces the strength of our R&D engine and our confidence in the next wave of opportunities to reach more patients. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Beth.

Elizabeth L. Hougen: Thank you, Holly. The substantial progress we've made this year is reflected in our third quarter financial results with growing revenue across our diverse revenue streams and continued investment in our launches and pipeline to drive future growth. And recent advances in several late-stage partnered programs provide additional opportunities ahead. Overall, our results and outlook keep us on track to achieve our full year total revenue, operating loss and cash guidance. Revenues in the third quarter and year-to-date were $243 million and $757 million, respectively, representing year-over-year growth of 55% and 64% compared to the same period last year, excluding the $280 million onetime payment we received for sapablursen last year.

Commercial revenue increased to $136 million in the third quarter and $363 million year-to-date, up 18% and 23%, respectively, from the same period last year. Notably, commercial revenue outpaced R&D revenue in the third quarter. These increases were driven primarily by DAWNZERA with product sales of $37 million in the third quarter and $79 million year-to-date. DAWNZERA product sales have increased each quarter since launch, including increasing approximately 40% in the third quarter. TRYNGOLZA generated product sales of $9 million in the third quarter, its first full quarter following the approval for sHTG and $41 million year-to-date. As Brett mentioned, we are lowering our full year TRYNGOLZA net product sales guidance to approximately $50 million.

With the launch underway, our third quarter results also included initial product revenue for ZANVASTRO. Our partner portfolio continues to serve as a financial amplifier, generating revenue of $107 million in the third quarter and $394 million year-to-date, reflecting milestones from multiple partners as programs advanced. Operating expenses increased as expected in the third quarter and year-to-date compared to the same period last year, driven by investments in the commercialization of TRYNGOLZA, DAWNZERA and ZANVASTRO. We also continue to invest in our advancing wholly owned pipeline supporting the next wave of opportunities. We ended the third quarter with $1.9 billion in cash and investments.

Our year-to-date results and fourth quarter outlook keep us on track to achieve our 2026 total revenue of $875 million to $900 million, underpinned by strong momentum from DAWNZERA and substantial contributions from our partnered programs. We continue to expect DAWNZERA net product sales of $110 million to $120 million. As we establish a new treatment paradigm in sHTG, our updated TRYNGOLZA net product sales guidance reflects a more gradual initial launch. Our guidance also takes into account the expansion of our Quick Start program, which helps patients begin treatment while coverage is being secured. We expect this program will support both broader adoption and revenue growth over time as patients transition to paid therapy.

Importantly, we remain confident in TRYNGOLZA's potential to deliver sustained long-term revenue growth and multibillion-dollar peak sales. Our partner programs also continue to deliver meaningful value through R&D revenue and royalty streams. For example, in the fourth quarter, we earned a $30 million milestone payment following HIBSAGO's recent U.S. approval, and we expect to begin earning royalties as the global launch gets underway. On the expense side, we continue to expect full year operating expenses to increase in the low teens percentage range compared to last year, driven primarily by sales and marketing investments in our ongoing launches.

We project R&D expenses to remain consistent with last year as several late-stage studies conclude and resources are deployed across our advancing wholly owned pipeline. With strong revenue generation from multiple sources and prudent expense management, we continue to project a non-GAAP operating loss of $425 million to $475 million. This is similar to our 2025 operating loss after adjusting for the onetime sapablursen license. And finally, we continue to project a year-end cash balance of greater than $1.6 billion. Our financial outlook reflects the strength of our diversified revenue streams with growing commercial revenues and contributions from our partnered programs. It also reflects investments in our advancing pipeline to drive continued growth.

Importantly, we remain committed to achieving sustained positive cash flow and continuing to create value for patients and shareholders. And with that, I'll turn the call back over to Brett.

Brett Monia: Thank you, Beth. Our growing commercial portfolio and the continued progress across our rich diverse pipeline demonstrate the strength of Ionis's science and its potential to address the significant unmet needs of patients. For TRYNGOLZA, we remain confident in its multibillion-dollar peak sales potential, and we are taking action to translate HCP enthusiasm into broader adoption. DAWNZERA continues to demonstrate a significant growth trajectory and ZANVASTRO extends our leadership in neurology. With a growing portfolio of marketed medicines, a rich pipeline and a team with the capabilities to deliver, we are executing on multiple value drivers for continued growth.

We're confident in Ionis' outlook and are committed to turning these opportunities into sustained positive cash flow and creating lasting value for patients and our shareholders. And with that, we'll open the call up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And today's first question comes from Jay Olson with Oppenheimer.

Jay Olson: For TRYNGOLZA, could you help separate physician adoption from the operational steps between prescription and paid treatment? And maybe talk about where you see the greatest friction today in terms of identifying appropriate patients or securing coverage or converting prescriptions into starts? And which leading indicators should we keep an eye on?

Brett Monia: Thanks, Jay. Kyle, do you want to touch on the key challenges that we're addressing for TRYNGOLZA launch as well as the KPIs?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Jay. Let me first by just addressing the market overall. There is a significant unmet need here in this market, obviously, greater than 3 million patients overall and greater than 1 million that are at high risk for sHTG, which is our initial launch focus. We've got a differentiated label. We've got very strong clinical data, including a 72% reduction in triglyceride levels, up to 91% reduction in pancreatitis events and numbers needed to treat of approximately 20 in the overall patient population and 4 in the highest risk patient population. The focus here, obviously, in the first quarter, is to build a market with the first-of-its-kind treatment in this large population.

We had approximately 1,500 prescribers as of the end of September. 24% of those prescribers had written more than one prescription. And this is the only approved treatment right now to reduce triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis in people living with sHTG. So it's taking some time for HCPs to adopt this new approach to see the response from patients once they put the patient on to TRYNGOLZA for the first time. And we've got a couple of key priorities that I referenced in my remarks, but I'll reiterate.

First and most importantly is to get more HCPs to prescribe for the first time so that they can gain this experience with a new modality and see the outcome in that patient that they're treating. Number two, those that have prescribed one time, we're trying to broaden the depth of prescribing, helping them to understand additional patients in their practice that might be able to benefit. So deepening that base and increasing repeat prescribing. And then the access component, and Jay, you were just asking about that. We had 33% of commercial plans come on board in the first quarter of the sHTG launch.

So they obviously have added sHTG to their policy and included the 50-milligram dose along with the 80-milligram dose, which is important for HCPs to have dosing flexibility, which they very much appreciate with the profile of the drug. So our real focus here is on those 3 components, getting HCPs to gain initial experience, those that gain experience to treat more patients. And then finally, the ease of access and getting payer policies to come on board, which is exactly what we're executing against. I continue to be very encouraged by the enthusiasm from HCPs as we do build this market with the compelling profile that TRYNGOLZA has and the early experiences that we have in the first quarter.

We want to build on that and make sure that, that continues through the end of this year. And 2027 is going to be a very important year for us as we continue to establish this brand in a new market.

Brett Monia: And Jay, the metrics to continue to monitor are really the ones that we highlighted so far today. I mean, our prescriber base, repeat prescribers, payer coverage and, of course, quarterly revenue.

Operator: And the next question comes from Yanan Zhu with Wells Fargo.

Yanan Zhu: I was wondering -- and thanks for the color on the TRYNGOLZA launch. I was wondering, looking at the 4Q -- implied 4Q number, it seems to be flat from third quarter. Does that -- it seems to imply no new patients added. Is that a function of estimate being very approximate? Or is there any other dynamics? And in general, can you comment on what has the trends been since the beginning of the fourth quarter?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Yanan. This is Kyle. I'll address that. There are a few factors, I think, that could impact Q4 revenues, and Beth mentioned this in her remarks. Number one is the Quick Start program. We believe that, that program will be used and has been used effectively up to this point and will continue to be used in Q4. So it's the timing of those patients starting and the use of Quick Start. Number two, we're still navigating the medical exception process, which can take time for many of these patients, right?

We are very encouraged by our payer access and the way that payers are coming on board and the fact that payers are adding TRYNGOLZA for the labeled indication of greater than 500. The payers are also when they're putting policies in place, the criteria for use is consistent with the clinical trial design. So being on background therapy, for example, of a fibrate or omega-3 compliance with diet, et cetera. So the policies are coming on board, but that will take time. And then the third component is just around seasonal dynamics. We've got the holidays and things that are happening right now. So there could be just some limited number of days with patients coming into the office.

But I think that the first signs of progress, I think, that everyone should be looking to is what Brett just emphasized is that we want to see more prescribers come on board, which we are seeing in the fourth quarter already. We want to see more repeat prescribing, which we are seeing already in the fourth quarter. And then we want to see that payer access and coverage continue to improve, which I believe will happen not only in the fourth quarter, but also as we advance the launch in 2027.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Kyle. Just to add to that, Yanan, I just want to make the point, the obvious point, is demand is increasing for TRYNGOLZA. And we're also very pleased with the persistency that TRYNGOLZA is demonstrating. Patients are staying on TRYNGOLZA, we're quite encouraged by that. It's really -- that's all matched up against the dynamics that Kyle highlighted specifically as well as the fact that we're still very early on in a launch in a market that we're creating, right? It's a brand-new market. We have a fantastic drug that is going to -- we believe is addressing the needs of a very large patient population with high unmet need.

But we're balancing demand, persistency along with the dynamics that Kyle highlighted.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jason Gerberry with Bank of America.

Jason Gerberry: Maybe 2 for Beth. Just curious how investors should be thinking about maybe cash runway, your burn level against sort of the $2 billion cash on hand and need for any additional licensing or financing instruments. Is that contingent on launch trajectory? I know there was some prior breakeven commentary. So just curious how to think about it in that context. And then how do you foresee the launch evolving in 2027 from a revenue recognized perspective? Just any commentary you guys are willing to provide on the current consensus, which is roughly, I think, $370 million.

Elizabeth L. Hougen: Well, let me start with that one, Jason. On the 2027 guidance, if you will. We'll look forward to providing that guidance when we get to the February year-end earnings call as we always do. So stay tuned for that. As far as cash runway goes, we ended this quarter with $1.9 billion. We anticipate ending the full year with greater than $1.6 billion. Obviously, that's all really important for us to continue to invest and execute on the commercial launches, in particular, TRYNGOLZA as well as advancing the pipeline and our technology. We'll continue to be in a period of investment for the next short while as our commercial products ramp towards peak.

And so we'll be obviously very aware of ensuring that we're well capitalized to be able to support that investment. And that means we'll be looking, as we always do, at our needs for financing. And if we do, we'll be very careful and very cognizant of cost of capital and dilution as important factors and considerations. So just -- as far as positive cash flow, that's still something we're highly committed to. We want to achieve sustained and -- achieve positive cash flow and sustained positive cash flow. And obviously, the timing of that is dependent on the TRYNGOLZA launch ramp.

But based on the recent Phase III setbacks and the slower-than-anticipated TRYNGOLZA launch, we do expect the timing to shift from 2028 to 2029. However, our goal is to continue to balance investment and growth with operating discipline and to achieve that sustained positive cash flow.

Operator: The next question is from Gary Nachman with Canaccord Genuity.

Gary Nachman: Just back on TRYNGOLZA. So what portion of the physicians that you're targeting are high priority docs? And how often do you need to communicate with them in terms of frequency to increase their prescribing? And if you want to expand breadth and depth of prescribing, do you have the right sales team in place in order to be able to do that? And then just if there is some net pricing pressure that we're seeing into 4Q, maybe from Quick Start, just how should we think of that? And when could it normalize? Would it be next year, the year after now that you have that program in place?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Gary. A couple of things. Field force size is absolutely adequate for the size of the opportunity for the high-risk sHTG patient population that we're starting with. We've got a couple of hundred representatives out there that can address about 20,000 of the highest sHTG treaters in the United States. Now the increasing frequency that we're focused on are on our Tier 1 HCPs, which are a subset of that. And we know that these HCPs see the highest volume of high-risk sHTG patients.

So we're trying to do exactly what you described, which is deploy those representatives to those offices more frequently so that HCPs will get their first experience with the first patient and then broaden the prescribing from there. We also have a field access team that is supporting the reimbursement and access process with those offices, which is the other dynamic here. And so we believe that when HCPs gain experience using this new modality and they see the clinical outcomes with these patients, combined with a smooth process in terms of getting those patients started on treatment, we believe that, that will unlock more patients for them to be able to treat appropriately with TRYNGOLZA.

In terms of frequency, it varies, right? The -- some of the early adopters, you're seeing 5 or 6 times. I think some of the others may take upwards of 10-plus times to be seen before they come on board. Part of that is education around the product. Some of that is education around reimbursement and some of that is around the appropriate patient to treat. And we really are focused on the high-risk sHTG patient population that are at the highest risk of having an acute pancreatitis event.

In terms of the Quick Start program, that will be an ongoing situation for us because those will be patients that are able to go on free drug for a period of time while reimbursement comes into play for that patient or access is secured. So we'll see that now and moving forward in terms of patients benefiting from that program and helping them get on drug quickly while they're navigating the reimbursement process.

Operator: And the next question comes from Joon Lee with UBS.

Unknown Analyst: It's reassuring that the demand for TRYNGOLZA is increasing. But as you broaden the prescriber base, is there a particular specialty you're targeting? And is it different than the prescribers you were already targeting for FCS indication? And for the prescribers who need educating -- "education", what exactly is the difficulty in understanding the value proposition of TRYNGOLZA? And finally, what were some unexpected hurdles that led you to cut your guidance?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. In terms of the specialties, very consistent with FCS, but a broader number of HCPs that we're reaching at this point. We were reaching about 3,000 mix of cardiologists, endocrinologists and lipid specialists for FCS. As we expanded the sales team last year, we're now reaching, as I mentioned, about 20,000 cardiologists, endocrinologists and lipidologists. The largest percentage of those is cardiology just because of the size of that specialty population. The education is just more about building a market here, right? There is HCP enthusiasm when they learn about TRYNGOLZA. They do see that TRYNGOLZA has a compelling profile. It has a broad indication of greater than 500.

It also has acute pancreatitis as outcomes and reduction in AP in the indication statement. So there is HCP enthusiasm and a belief in a compelling profile. When you get down to the underlying numbers, reductions of triglycerides of up to 72% on top of standard of care that they're using today, up to a 91% reduction in acute pancreatitis and getting approximately 50% -- or excuse me, 60% of patients to goal is very encouraging for these HCPs. So the education is more about which patients do I treat? When am I going to see those patients? And then when am I going to prescribe TRYNGOLZA for the first time in order to gain this clinical experience.

And that just takes a little bit of time is what we're learning here.

Brett Monia: Yes. And on the guidance, it's really nothing more, [indiscernible], than the slower-than-expected launch ramp. We're very pleased with the enthusiasm by HCPs to prescribe. Demand is increasing, and we're very pleased with payer coverage to date. We're getting coverage on agreements that we haven't gotten in place so far to label, which means a very broad label, 500 milligrams per deciliter of triglycerides and above. So the metrics are lining positively. It's just a slower launch ramp than what we initially expected.

Operator: Your next question is from Mike Ulz with Morgan Stanley.

Michael Ulz: Maybe another one on TRYNGOLZA. It looks like out of the gates, you're getting some nice breadth there in terms of the prescribers and starting to see some depth. But as we kind of move forward into next year, what's the key to sort of driving greater depth? Is it just more experience? Is there something else? Is it education? Maybe a little bit more color on your thoughts there.

Kyle Jenne: Yes. I think there are a couple of things there, Mike. Experience is one. And what we're seeing is some of these HCPs are treating the most severe patient first, right, history with AP, for example. So I think that they potentially could start with the highest risk patient and then start moving beyond that to patients that are just greater than 880 or patients that are over 500 with comorbidities, for example. But we believe that really to help these HCPs unlock these patients, they need to see the clinical outcomes of using this new treatment that they've never had access to.

And number two, the process in order to get coverage and access needs to be smooth and straightforward for their offices. And those are the 2 really key things that we're working through these offices with here on the outset and then talk to them about more patients that could potentially benefit and how they could broaden their prescribing.

Operator: The next question is from Jessica Fye with JPMorgan.

Jessica Fye: You've been talking about the TRYNGOLZA launch just progressing a little bit slower than you initially thought. Can you talk about how you think about the time line to get to that $3 billion U.S. peak target? And then my follow-up sort of still related to TRYNGOLZA would just be, can you talk about the specific Quick Start expansion change that you're making is?

Kyle Jenne: So I'll touch on peak, Jess. And we have not, up to this point, provided any insight in towards -- to time to peak. But what I'll mention is the large patient population that is addressable here of greater than 3 million patients, 1 million of which are at high risk of acute pancreatitis. And there's an opportunity for TRYNGOLZA to address a significant unmet need here. And I've been through the profile a couple of times in terms of what the strength of the profile of TRYNGOLZA represents. But we do believe that we will continue to build this market. The HCP enthusiasm will continue to grow.

We will get more experience with new prescribers and those prescribers that have written will prescribe more and access will open up over time. But this is a function of building a new market that has never been in existence before. The Quick Start expansion point, I don't want to get into a lot of the details there just because it's a competitive space. But obviously, we have a number of different programs to make sure that patients can get on treatment and get on treatment quickly and able to stay on treatment long term. And I think that's important for our patient services program, and it's important for the patients that can benefit from those types of programs.

Brett Monia: And on the time line, I'll just add. Thanks, Kyle. Jess, it's really important to remember that we are 3 months into -- these numbers represent 3 months into a launch, delivering a medicine that is providing benefit to patients that physicians have never had experience with before, right? And that requires education, that requires patients -- physicians to bring patients in to get the triglycerides measured and then get them on to medicine. We're looking forward to 2027. We think 2027 will be a very important year for TRYNGOLZA.

Operator: Our next question comes from Eric Joseph with Citi.

Eric Joseph: Just a couple more on TRYNGOLZA. I'd be curious to know on the payer access dynamic so far, if you could speak to the success rate of getting on formulary. Have there been any refusals by any plans to cover TRYNGOLZA for sHTG? And what's your expectation as to when the outstanding formulary reviews could complete?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Eric. So we have not had significant pushback or challenges or issues related to our payer negotiations up to this point. As I mentioned, the end of Q3 through the end of September, we had 33% of commercial plans within a 3-month period already begin putting policies in place for sHTG and adding the 50-milligram dose, so the 50 milligrams and 80 milligrams were available. We believe on a pricing standpoint, we priced at $40,000 WACC, and that took place on April 1 of this year. We priced exactly for this reason, which was to make sure that we had coverage to label, which is for all patients greater than 500.

And we wanted to make sure that we reduce the blocks and limitations where payers didn't put in place restrictions around history of AP or being a high-risk patient over 880, for example. And I think we've been very successful at working with payers and talking about the patient population that's addressable here and putting policies in place that reflect the broad label and also, obviously, the prior authorization criteria being consistent with the clinical trial design, which is typically what we are seeing with these plans. So we're very encouraged by payer access coming on board. We believe we will have more coverage and access open up at the end of this year and going on throughout 2027.

So we're in a good place as it relates to access.

Operator: The next question comes from Akash Tewari with Jefferies.

Akash Tewari: So this is what I'm trying to kind of sparse out. I think in September in an investor transcript, you were saying July and August were good months when you're thinking about scripts for TRYNGOLZA. And then obviously, the implied guidance cut today is a pretty stark contrast. Can you talk about -- when you were talking about July, August being good months, how are you defining that? And then what really kind of broke down? And I think my concern is really if July and August were good months that we're actually seeing a downward trajectory in terms of demand as we got into September and the back half of the year?

And then also, I know you went away from PantherRx to multiple specialty pharmacies. How much of that maybe has played a role with uptake here? Do you feel like patients need more high-touch service?

Brett Monia: Thanks, Akash. So early comments -- comments during the early part of the launch really reflected the data that we had available at the time. We were very pleased with the label we received with the indication statement, including acute pancreatitis reduction. And we also -- were seeing a great deal of enthusiasm by HCPs for the overall drug profile and their desire to prescribe at the time. But remember, we were a few weeks into the launch at that time. So it was really based on what we are hearing from the HCP community and their enthusiasm for TRYNGOLZA, which continues today. Now we just have to bring these patients through and get them on to covered drug.

With regard to the pharmacies, specialty pharmacies and so on, Kyle, would you take that?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. The multiple SPs, Akash, we have the right programs in place. We have the Ionis Every Step program, right, our patient support program to make sure that patients are educated from the disease state standpoint, product standpoint and that we also have programs in place to help financial situations, if necessary, in order for those patients to get on and stay on treatment. So I think we've got the right programs there. As it relates to expanding the SPs, the SPs are doing very well. We've got 4 SPs that address some of the largest payers as well.

And we believe that we've got the right SPs to help us make sure that the prescription process gets navigated and we get drug to patient. But we've also got our field access team out there working directly with offices on the reimbursement process and making sure that we're educating around which plans have policies in place and what the criteria for use are for those respective plans. And so that HCP office education is another key component to this beyond just the SP expansion as well.

Operator: And the next question comes from David Lebowitz with BMO Capital Markets.

David Lebowitz: When you try to bucket how the launch is going in various groups, there's a lot of talk about the high-risk patients above 880, about the patients above 500. What about the patients that specifically have had pancreatitis events? Have we seen any uptick -- notable uptick in that group?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, David. We are absolutely laser-focused on the high-risk sHTG patients here out of the gate to establish TRYNGOLZA and to begin building this market. The patients above 500 with history of AP are a cornerstone of that focus. And our sales team and our medical affairs team, obviously educating HCPs around the need to treat those patients and the risk now that these patients have had one AP event of subsequent events going up exponentially in terms of risk potential. So we are seeing those patients get prescriptions. Some of it is an office dynamic of when those appointments are scheduled and when those patients are coming in to see their HCP. So it's a timing situation.

But that is a really strong focus of our communications and our education and the launch in order to build this market and get TRYNGOLZA treated or get patients treated with TRYNGOLZA for the right reasons.

Operator: And the next question comes from Ellie Merle with Barclays.

Eliana Merle: Maybe just to take a step back, could you kind of highlight like, I guess, what exactly contributed to the slower-than-expected launch versus what you had initially anticipated? Is this driven by like reimbursement factors, use of free drug? Or is this slower-than-expected demand? And if you could kind of break that out or characterize that a little bit, I think that would be helpful. And then just again on the Quick Start program, you did mention that there's been meaningful utilization. If you could give us any color or characterize, I guess, what proportion of overall starts are on free drug?

And I guess your expectations for the average duration that patients will have -- will be on free drug before converting to paid.

Brett Monia: Kyle, do you want to reiterate what's driving the slower-than-expected launch?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Ellie. I'll just revert back. We're building a market here. That's the first thing, right? HCPs, the majority, some that have treated FCS have experience using TRYNGOLZA. But the majority of these HCPs that we're calling on are learning about a new modality, a new product and trying to make sure that they understand which patients to treat and the potential value of treating those patients. So it's about market building and creating this market. It requires HCP education, which is exactly what we're doing with our field team with personal promotion.

It also takes nonpersonal promotion like our omnichannel capabilities and the way that we are educating through digital means, which is really important here as well to drive awareness and an understanding of sHTG and TRYNGOLZA. And then there's also the patient dynamics. So we're doing a lot of work to educate patients, not only through omnichannel, but also through our patient advocacy work and the engagements that we're having with different groups in order to make sure people understand what sHTG is, what risks are associated with sHTG and the potential benefits of being treated with TRYNGOLZA would look like. So that's really what's taking time, I think, in terms of the process to build the market.

In terms of Quick Start, I don't want to get into really any more details surrounding that program. I mean it's a program that I think is important for patients to be able to get on treatment quickly and for HCPs to be able to assess how patients are doing and to make sure that patients can stay on treatment long term. So it's an important program for patients and HCPs.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Kyle. Thanks, Ellie. And I think we have time for one more question, please.

Operator: And the next question comes from Myles Minter with William Blair.

Jake Batchelder: This is Jake on for Myles. Should Redemplo be approved in sHTG, do you expect them to take similar headwinds in initial uptake? Or is this just sort of the cursor being the lead blocker here? And then maybe a follow-up for Beth. You changed your breakeven guidance from 2028 to 2029. Just wanted to confirm that the TRYNGOLZA uptake was the key driver there and that there were no other factors for updating that guidance.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Jake. I'll start, Beth, feel free to jump in. But as Beth said in her prepared remarks, our shift to 2029 cash flow breakeven was related to the slower-than-expected ramp -- launch ramp for TRYNGOLZA, but it was also impacted as was stated by the disappointment -- Phase III disappointment for eplontersen in ATTR cardiomyopathy and pelacarsen for Lp(a) CVD. That guidance to achieve cash flow breakeven will be driven among -- in addition to pipeline successes in large part by the TRYNGOLZA launch as we go forward. As far as competitor programs, we have no comments on what they should expect.

We see no reason why they would be in any different position than we are with respect to the dynamics that we're facing for the TRYNGOLZA launch to date. What we're thrilled about, of course, is the compelling product profile that we have for TRYNGOLZA, which has shown unprecedented reductions in triglycerides, reductions in acute pancreatitis, all with good safety, tolerability and convenience. So stay tuned. We're looking forward to 2027 for the launch of TRYNGOLZA. It's a very important year. And like I said, we're very much looking forward to it. With that, I think we're going to end the call. Thanks, everybody, for joining us today.

We look forward to sharing our progress as we further advance our launches and the next wave of medicines from our pipeline. Have a good day, everybody.

Jeremy Latcham does have a long history with the MCU

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a sudden and surprising move, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran announced they were stepping down today (Nov. 11). The unexpected move (via Variety) comes just as Skydance acquired Warner Bros. Discovery for $111 billion in October.

The duo had led WB's attempt at revitalizing its comic book movies for the last four years and are being replaced by a former Marvel producer, Jeremy Latcham.

Under Gunn and Safran, it's been a mixed bag. Last year's "Superman" was a massive hit while this summer's "Supergirl" bombed out of the box office, even if we liked it more than most. However, the just-released body-horror R-rated "Clayface" has been a modest success.

In our Clayface review, we found Matt Hagen's performance and the practical effects entertaining, even if it didn't feel like a DC film. However, as Alix Blackburn noted, "I can't help feeling that “Clayface” leaves some serious potential untapped."

There are also the TV shows "Peacemaker" and "Lanterns", divisive but interesting projects that are worth your time.

So, who is Jeremy Latcham, and what does his hiring say about the future of the DC Universe?

Latcham only has 12 credits on his IMDB page, but he was on the ground floor at the beginning of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Variety reports he joined Marvel in 2004 and worked his way up to an associate producer on "Iron Man" and a co-producer on "Iron Man 2."

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Later, he became an executive producer on the first and second Avengers movies as well as Guardians of the Galaxy and Spider-Man: Homecoming. Gunn directed and wrote the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy.

"We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter," Gunn and Safran said in a statement.

If there was a golden era of Marvel movies, the run from the first Iron Man to "Avengers: Endgame" is it, and Latcham was there for most of it, reportedly working closely with Marvel head Kevin Feige.

Latcham went solo around 2018 with the Tarantino-esque "Bad Times at the El Royale," which is too long and probably too clever by half, but a solid evening. He also produced the D&D movie "Honor Among Thieves," a personal favorite even if it didn't set the box office on fire.

That movie came out in 2023, and Latcham's most recent credit is the deeply boring Nate Bargatze vehicle "The Breadwinner."

I suspect Latcham is expected to bring a Marvel structure and formula to the DC Universe, which has been scattershot even under Gunn.

The difference between the DC Universe and what Marvel has built over the last 18 years is the characters. DC is defined by inherently mythological heroes, whereas Marvel, outside of some of its more operatic teams, has tended to be more character-driven.

It makes for archetypes that people have strong opinions about, and I'm not sold on the idea that the Marvel formula can work with the myths of DC. As with Marvel, DC's best successes have come from characters that aren't part of the holy trinity or the Justice League, à la Peacemaker or Gunn's Suicide Squad, and I guess the first Shazam.

We're still waiting for the delayed "The Batman: Part 2" with Robert Pattinson, which paused production in October as director Matt Reeves deals with a family matter.

James Gunn's is directing his Superman follow up "Man of Tomorrow." And on the TV side of things, "The People v. Gorilla Grodd" show is expected to launch in 2027 starring Jimmy Teatro and Skyler Gisondo.

It may be a year or two before we really see what Latcham has in store for the DC Universe.

#3138. Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

#3136. Berkshire Kept Buying Back Stock as Shares Hit Records. Here’s What the Price It Paid Tells You.

Berkshire’s own filing shows the prices at which management found its stock attractive, and how far the shares have climbed since.

One of Warren Buffett's investing lessons has been that the price you pay for a stock matters as much as the company you're buying. Greg Abel, his successor at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.36%) (BRKB +0.76%), looks to be following the same philosophy.

Berkshire posted its quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission over the weekend. In it, the company disclosed that it spent $9.6 billion repurchasing its own shares during the third quarter of 2026, more than double the $4.5 billion it spent in the second quarter. That's an eye-opening amount of money, even for a company with Berkshire's incredible financial resources.

But the amount isn't the most interesting part of the story.

Berkshire has strict rules about when it can repurchase shares. And by examining what Abel was willing to pay, investors can get an idea of where management sees value in the stock.

Most large companies regularly repurchase shares, sometimes spending billions of dollars regardless of whether their stocks are trading at attractive valuations.

Berkshire operates differently. Its third-quarter regulatory filing states that repurchases are permitted when the CEO, after consulting with the chairman, believes the purchase price is "below Berkshire's intrinsic value, conservatively determined." Intrinsic value is simply an estimate of what a business is actually worth, based on its assets and ability to generate cash over time.

So, Berkshire isn't buying shares because it has money available or because it wants to support its stock price. Management must believe the company is worth more than the price it's paying.

There are other restrictions. Berkshire won't repurchase shares if doing so would reduce its combined cash, cash equivalents, and Treasury bill holdings below $30 billion. But there's no maximum amount Berkshire can spend, and it isn't obligated to buy anything.

Abel has considerable flexibility to repurchase shares. When Berkshire spends billions buying its own shares, investors have good reason to pay attention.

The company's latest filing provides a monthly breakdown of its repurchases of Berkshire stock, including the average price paid for each class.

In July, Berkshire purchased approximately 3.1 million Class B shares at an average price of $496.24, along with about $1.84 billion in Class A shares. The average purchase price for Class B shares increased to $503.99 in August, when the company bought another 1.5 million shares, in addition to $66 million in Class A shares.

September was particularly interesting. Berkshire purchased approximately 7.7 million Class B shares at an average price of $506.64. It also acquired 1,983 Class A shares at an average price of $758,332.88.

Remember that one Class A share represents the same economic ownership as 1,500 Class B shares. September's average Class B purchase price was therefore equivalent to $759,960 per Class A share. Altogether, Berkshire spent about $9.6 billion on purchases in the quarter.

Those figures don't establish Berkshire's intrinsic value. Management presumably believes the business is worth more than the prices it paid, but it hasn't disclosed by how much. But it tells us that Abel was comfortable committing billions of dollars to Berkshire stock at those valuations.

And the company wasn't exactly running short of money. Berkshire's insurance and other businesses held approximately $352.3 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and Treasury bills, net of related payables, at the end of September.

Berkshire's stock continued climbing after the third quarter, with Class A shares eventually surpassing $863,000. That's nearly 14% above the average price Berkshire paid for its Class A shares in September.

The Associated Press reported that the rally may have prompted Berkshire to halt share repurchases. The company hasn't confirmed that, and its latest filing only covers purchases through September. But the possibility makes sense given Berkshire's repurchase policy.

A stock that looks attractive at $758,000 doesn't necessarily offer the same value now, particularly when management insists on a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.

But investors shouldn't assume Berkshire has established a firm ceiling for its stock price, either. Intrinsic value changes as the underlying business grows, and management's assessment can change along with it. Nor would a pause in repurchases automatically mean Abel believes Berkshire is overvalued. It might simply mean the discount isn't large enough to justify spending shareholders' money. Or the company chose to pause buybacks as Buffett announced his retirement as chairman in September.

So, Berkshire's third-quarter purchases don't provide an official price target or guarantee future returns. They do, however, establish a useful reference point for evaluating the stock.

If shares retreat toward the levels where Berkshire was aggressively buying, investors will have evidence that management recently found those valuations attractive.

And that's considerably more informative than simply knowing the stock has fallen from its highs.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

'Notify when left behind' is making its way to Android - but to limited devices for now.

A much-needed update — “Notify when left behind” — is rolling out to Google’s Find My hub. The feature sends a notification when a registered device is separated from your phone, except when you leave it at your house.

Also: 7 Galaxy settings I always change to boost my battery life

According to 9to5Google, this feature was first previewed in October, with the notification available for Chipolo trackers and Moto Tag.

This feature is not yet available for other peripherals such as headphones. I tried to see if my Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones or Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 have it — they don’t. Hopefully, support is on the way. In the meantime, here’s what we know.

“Notify when left behind” is my all-time favorite device tracking feature on iOS. Any device set up on my Find My network is compatible with this feature, including my MacBook Air, AirPods Pro 3, and Apple Watch, three devices I often take out of the house — and have indeed left behind once or twice.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

If these devices are separated from my phone in an unsaved location, I’ll get a notification of which device I left and where. In iOS, you can customize which locations are “safe,” and won’t notify you if you leave them there.

On Android, this feature is currently limited to only notifying you when a device is left at a location other than the home address registered to your Google account. Hopefully, location customization is on the horizon.

Right now, this feature appears to be limited to specific Bluetooth trackers. Photos shared by 9to5Google show compatible trackers have a “Notify when left behind” tab at the bottom of their menu in the Find Hub, so it’s expected that future supported devices will operate the same way.

9to5Google reports that previous updates to Google Play Services indicated this feature’s existence. According to 9to5Google, “Notify when left behind” should be a feature that users can enable when registering a new device with their Find Hub.

Also: I’m an Apple Maps fan, but I switch to Google Maps for these 3 tasks

Once Google matures and fully rolls out this feature, there should be a setting inside the Find Hub to enable these notifications on every device in your hub.

Android’s breadth of compatibility with third-party manufacturers is its most significant advantage over Apple. Regarding device tracking, you can add Sony headphones, Motorola trackers, and Samsung Galaxy smartwatches to the same Find Hub.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

However, my Beats headphones that appear in my Find My hub are not currently supported by this new feature. If Google can expand this feature to all Fast Pair-compatible devices, such as Bluetooth trackers, headphones, smartwatches, laptops, and more, it’ll be easier for consumers to keep tabs on their ever-growing armory of devices.

#3131. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

#3130. Bluetooth Core 7.0 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.
